See Resources a service consumes Usage Contract One file, pacto.yaml, that says what a service offers, who owns it and which other services it calls. See the contract reference Contract Contract graph All your contracts together: who calls whom and which versions each accepts. See Operational graph Graph cosign The Sigstore command-line tool that signs artifacts in a registry and verifies their signatures. pacto publish signs in the same format, so cosign verify checks a version, and cosign verify-blob-attestation checks a record. See Verify a record — Delivery The opt-in part of Pacto, also called the delivery component, that decides which version of each service runs in each environment. It is a separate install. See How delivery works Delivery Digest The fingerprint of one exact published artifact (sha256:...) — Domain The business domain a service belongs to, such as payments, declared as service.domain. The operational graph groups services by it. A service that declares none is listed under No domain, and one whose domain Pacto cannot tell under Domain unknown. See Business domains Domain DRI Directly responsible individual: the one person a contract names as accountable for the service (service.owner.dri). When a contract names no team, the DRI is its owner. See OwnerInfo — Earned autonomy Raising a Stage's level after enough good changes, confirmed by a person. See Earned autonomy — Environment A place a service runs, such as test or prod. In Kubernetes it is a namespace of the same name Environment Evidence What was observed about a running service, such as which ports listen or which services it called. See Evidence Evidence Evidence Server The service that receives evidence and stores it in your registry next to the contract it is about. See Evidence Server — External dependency A dependency outside this Pacto system, such as a managed database or a model. It has a contract and a range, or only a version, and then anything relying on it is Unknown. See External dependencies — Finding One result of comparing a contract with the evidence: a contradiction such as INTERFACE_ABSENT, or a reason Pacto could not tell, such as EVIDENCE_STALE. See Compliance model Findings Fleet All your services together, as Pacto sees them from contracts, clusters and registries. See Fleet views Fleet Flux The GitOps tool that applies each version in the cluster. Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto a Flux OCIRepository. See How a change moves — Follower A Stage in another cluster that takes the versions an upstream Stage verified, by reading that Stage's stream. See Follow a Stage in another cluster — Freeze Stop automation moving a Stage until a person unfreezes it. See When a Stage is frozen Frozen GitlessOps Signed artifacts in your registry and evidence decide which version runs where, while your code and manifests stay in git. See What GitlessOps means — GitOps Keeping a cluster in line with files in git, with a tool such as Flux or Argo CD. Pacto works with it — Golden path A contract your platform team publishes as a starting point for new services, marked by service.template. pacto init --from copies it into a new service that records it as its service.origin. See Create a service from a golden path Golden paths Held change A change waiting for a person to decide. See Why you were asked Inbox in-toto A standard format for signed statements about software. Every record is an in-toto statement. See What a record says — Inferred contract A contract the operator publishes for an external system nobody declares, at <registry>/pacto-inferred/<identity>: the hosts, ports and client majors Pacto sees, signed with the installation key. A range against it is always unknown and never clears a gate. See Inferred contracts Inferred contract Invalid The compliance state of a contract that fails validation. It ranks worse than NonCompliant. Invalid Interface One way a service is called, such as an HTTP API described by an OpenAPI file. See interfaces Interfaces Kustomization The Flux object that applies a set of Kubernetes files, such as the files a version ships, as the ServiceAccount it names. See Manifests and the levels — Level How much a Stage lets Pacto do on its own: observe, advise, auto for non-breaking (auto-nonbreaking) or autonomous. Also called autonomy level. See The four levels Level MCP Model Context Protocol, the standard way an AI agent finds and calls tools. pacto mcp is an MCP server. See Drive Pacto from an agent — Mediated A Stage condition that says whether only the pointer decides what runs. See What the pointer guarantees — Node agent The Pacto collector that runs on every Kubernetes node and watches with eBPF which ports each service listens on and which services it calls. It is a program in the cluster, separate from an AI agent. See Runtime conformance — NonCompliant The compliance state of a valid contract when the evidence contradicts it, for example a declared interface that is absent. Non-Compliant OCIRepository The Flux object that points at one artifact in a registry, whose files a Kustomization applies. Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto it. See How a change moves — Operator The Pacto controller you install in a cluster. It checks that each running service matches its contract. See Kubernetes overview — oras A command-line tool that lists and fetches artifacts and referrers in a registry. See Check one record without Pacto — Organization index The repository <registry>/pacto-index, where pacto publish and pacto push write one entry per published version naming its bundle and dependencies. pacto impact reads it to find every declared consumer with no --root list. See Consumers from the organization index — Owner team The team a contract names under service.owner. Pacto asks its members about that service. See OwnerInfo Owner Pactify Give a service a contract and connect it to delivery. See Pactify a service — pactoVersion The contract format version in each pacto.yaml, "2.0", "2.1", "2.2", "2.3", "2.4" or "2.5". It is separate from the Pacto core and operator release versions. See Versions — Plan What Pacto would do with a change, and who must agree, before anyone asks. See Plan, propose and approve Plan Platform offering The kind of offering a service provides to other teams, such as postgresql, declared as service.offering. Any organization defines its own slugs, such as security-scanning. The operational graph lists providers of the same offering together. See Platform offerings Offering Pointer The digest a Stage moved its environment to (status.pointer). See What the pointer guarantees — Policy A rule a contract must follow, such as "every service names an owner", checked with the contract. See policies Policy Promote Move a Stage to a newer version Promote Promoter The part of delivery that plans each change, runs its checks and moves the pointer. It holds no signing key. See How a change moves — Provisioning status What a provider adapter last reported about a resource a consumer's contract asked for, per environment: Requested, Provisioning, Ready, Failed or Deleting. It is observed evidence and reads Unknown until a current report arrives. See Follow provisioning status — Proposal The next level Pacto suggests for a Stage, with its evidence or what blocks it. See Earned autonomy — Proposed range A dependency range or ref pacto ci proposes in pacto.inferred.yaml, from the provider version the service runs with or from the organization index. It publishes as compatibility: unknown until an acceptance record accepts it. See Accept proposed ranges — Readiness assessment A dated statement in a contract of which readiness claims are done, with evidence. It counts for nothing once it expires. See Readiness Readiness Recent sign-in An opt-in rule: deciding on a held change needs a login newer than delivery.promoter.authFreshness. Off by default, so a person decides with the sign-in they have. See A recent sign-in to decide Sign in again to decide Record A signed account of one finished change, stored in your registry and checkable without Pacto. See Verify a record Record Recorder The part of delivery that signs records. It is the only part that holds the signing key, and it is off until you turn it on. See Signed records and history — Referrer A file a registry stores attached to an artifact, listed by the OCI Referrers API. Evidence and delivery records are stored this way; on a registry without that API, delivery records are write-once tags. See What delivery needs — Registry The place your container images are stored. Pacto stores contracts, versions and records there too. The registry path, such as ghcr.io/acme, is part of each service's key in the operational graph Registry Resource (consumed) Something a service uses from a provider through a dependency or a configuration reference, such as a database. Its request is declared in the consumer's contract and its provisioning status is observed from provider reports. A resource's phase is never the service's health. See Resources a service consumes Resources Resource health Whether the resource a consumer asked a platform offering for, such as its database, is ready, read from its provisioning status. One consumer's failed resource leaves the offering's availability unchanged. See Provisioning status — Rollback Put back the version that ran before. See What happens to a change and Roll back by hand Roll back Routed An acceptance record signed by a person who is not the service's declared owner. It never counts and names who may accept. See Announced breaks — Service Something you run and other things call, such as payments Service Session What a shared dashboard keeps after a person signs in: their token, held on the server behind a cookie until dashboard.auth.session.idleTimeout or maxAge ends it. See Sessions Sign out Shadow consumer A service seen calling another at runtime that no contract declares. See Observed dependencies — Sign-in How a person proves who they are to a shared dashboard, with your identity provider or a pasted Kubernetes token. Every view and action then runs with their Kubernetes RBAC, and the delivery views need it. See Dashboard authentication Sign in Stage One service in one environment, such as payments in prod, and the version it runs there. See Stages and records Stages Step-down Dropping one level after a version Pacto shipped with no person fails. See Step-down — Stream The numbered history of one Stage's records, each naming the one before it, hung on the Stage's anchor. See Streams, stand-ins and gaps — Successor What replaces a deprecated service, declared as service.lifecycle.successor. Pacto resolves it to a revision in the fleet and checks each consumer's range against it. See Deprecated providers and successors — Target One running deployment of a service, such as payments in one cluster. See Three identities Targets Target snapshot A signed list of the targets one cluster runs, which its operator publishes to <registry>/pacto-targets:cluster-<uid> every 5 minutes. CI reads it to find the consumers that run, with registry access and no cluster credentials, and trusts it only under a key scoped to that cluster. See Where consumers come from — Transitive closure A service's dependencies, their dependencies and so on to the last one. pacto.lock pins all of them by digest. See Lockfile — Transparency log Sigstore's public, append-only log of signatures, which anyone can read. pacto publish writes each signature there unless told otherwise, so a private or throwaway key can stay out of it. See Signing — Unknown The answer when Pacto could not see enough to decide. A check answers Unknown instead of Pass or Fail, and a contract's compliance state is Unknown when its evidence is missing or inconclusive. Unknown never counts as a pass. See What Unknown means Unknown Version One published copy of a contract, such as payments 2.4.0. It never changes once published. See Publish a version Version Write-once tag One tag per delivery record in the streams repository, written once and naming the record by content, used where the registry serves no Referrers API. See Write-once tags — Would have On observe, what Pacto would have done with a change. It is advice only. See Cold start —

docs.title: Golden paths reference
docs.text: This page describes how the operational graph treats golden paths and the services created from them. The operational graph reference covers sources and queries.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
A golden path is a service the graph treats as a starting point for new services. A service is a golden path when:

  • the newest revision Pacto can read declares service.template;
  • the service has no operational target;
  • every source that reports targets (Kubernetes, the Evidence Server and a target state file) is available and complete, so Pacto knows the service runs nowhere.

While such a source is unavailable or partial, a service without targets stays an ordinary service, so an outage never drops a running service from impact. A running service that declares service.template also stays a service and raises GOLDEN_PATH_DEPLOYED (warning, category golden-path). With no target source in the fleet, Pacto cannot tell a golden path from a service that runs elsewhere.

A golden path's dependencies and references describe what services created from it need. They are never consumption:

  • impact, graph traversal, dependents, the neighborhood and offering consumers leave the path out;
  • the path has no offering membership and never joins OFFERING_CONFLICT;
  • the Overview service, owner, domain, readiness and attention summaries leave it out and count it in goldenPaths and invalidGoldenPaths; their links carry template=exclude, so a count matches its list;
  • an owner or domain that holds only golden paths has no row in the owner or domain list, and its own page still answers with zero services;
  • the path's detail lists the same edges as requirements, through the offerings they reach.

docs.title: Declared origins
docs.text:
A service's origin is the service.origin of its newest readable revision. Pacto resolves it to the golden path revision whose content digest (lock.HashFS of the bundle, the digest pacto.lock records) or registry digest matches. An origin that matches no golden path, or more than one, keeps its ref and digest with a reason and links nowhere. Every origin is labelled declared.

A service created from a directory records as ref the coordinate the path's publish.bundle and version name, which Pacto does not check against the registry. A path with no publish.bundle records a path relative to the new contract, or only the folder name when that path would climb above the home folder, so no host folder such as /Users/<name> is published.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Parameter Values Effect template (entities) only, exclude only keeps golden paths and, with no kinds, lists services only; exclude leaves them and their revisions out. Absent lists every service and marks golden paths template createdFrom (entities; MCP created_from) a service key, (none) or (unresolved) Keeps the services whose origin resolves to that golden path. (none) keeps the services that declare no origin and (unresolved) those whose origin resolves to no golden path in the view. A hidden, absent or non-path key answers an empty list sort (entities) created Golden paths that created the most services first, then the most non-compliant of those, then by name template (search) only, exclude The same filter on search; the default keeps golden paths, each hit marked template

A golden path row in an entity list carries created, the number of services created from it, golden paths derived from it left out like the Services list leaves them out, nonCompliant, how many of those are non-compliant, and its signature status: not-checked when no source that read the path checks signatures, and the path's detail then has no signature.

docs.title: Services by golden path
docs.text:
The aggregate of an entity list over services carries origins, which partitions the matched services that are no golden path by their declared origin, over the whole population before paging:

Field Counts byPath Up to 10 golden paths, the most services created first, each with services, nonCompliant and hidden paths Golden paths that created at least one matched service beyond Services created from the golden paths past the ranking unresolved Services whose origin resolves to no golden path in the view (createdFrom=(unresolved)) none Services that declare no origin (createdFrom=(none)) hidden Services created from a golden path that the viewer cannot see, in no other count

The services of byPath, beyond, unresolved and none sum to the matched services, and their nonCompliant counts sum to the non-compliant ones. pacto fleet entities prints the ranking under the list, and the dashboard's Golden paths page draws it.

docs.title: Creation checklist
docs.text:
A service with an origin carries creation, a checklist derived from what the fleet holds. Each step is done only on its signal:

Step done when Otherwise signature never unknown: a verified signature names a signer a publisher rule, pin or policy accepted, and an unverified one a signer none of them covers, which is no failure contract a revision was read validation the newest revision is valid with no *_UNVERIFIED or *_NOT_ENFORCED finding unknown listing those codes; failed when invalid plugin never unknown: Pacto does not observe what a plugin wrote published a registry served a revision unknown: seen only in local files fleet always, naming the sources deployed the fleet observes a target unknown provisioning every provider reports Ready failed on any Failed; unknown without reports; not-applicable when nothing provisions

The delivery step appears only in the step list pacto init --from --delivery and pacto_create with delivery return. It is planned, then done, when the Pacto resource and every Stage were planned. Otherwise it is unknown with the reason.

docs.title: Golden paths in a restricted view
docs.text: A namespace-scoped viewer sees a golden path that has no Kubernetes target, like a declared offering provider, with only the revisions that declare service.template. Nothing in the view resolves to the older revisions it drops. Services created from it that the viewer cannot see are counted in hiddenCreated, and its requirements on services the viewer cannot see in hiddenRequirements, never named. A visible service whose golden path is hidden keeps its declared ref and digest and links nowhere, with the reason "the golden path it names is not in this view".

docs.title: Create a service from a golden path
docs.text:
A golden path is a contract your platform team publishes as a starting point for new services. It is an ordinary signed Pacto bundle whose contract declares service.template. A developer finds it, reads what it requires and creates a service from it with pacto init --from. The fleet then links the new service back to the path it came from.

This guide follows the http-service path of the demo from both sides.

docs.title: Publish a golden path
docs.text:
A golden path holds the contract and files every new service of its kind starts with:

pactoVersion: "2.4"
service:
  name: http-service
  version: 1.0.0
  owner:
    team: platform
  summary: An HTTP API on the platform runtime with a PostgreSQL database
  template:
    plugins:
      - name: dockerfile
        description: A Dockerfile for a Go HTTP service
      - name: github-actions
        description: A CI workflow that validates and publishes the contract
        options:
          go-version: "1.27"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/postgresql
    required: true
    compatibility: ^16.0.0

Beside the dependency, a configuration reference requests a database from the PostgreSQL offering:

configurations:
  - name: database
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/postgresql:16.1.0
    configuration: provisioning
    required: true
    values:
      size: small
      storageGi: 20
  • service.template marks the contract as a golden path. Each entry of plugins names a plugin the path offers to run, with the options it receives.
  • service.summary is what the Golden paths list shows.
  • The configuration references and dependencies point at the offerings every service created from the path requires, and policy references at the platform rules it must meet. The fleet lists them as the path's requirements.
  • Files such as interfaces/openapi.yaml or docs/ are copied into each new service.

Publish each version with pacto publish, signed with the key under publish.sign, so developers can check who signed it.

docs.title: Find one
docs.text:
A golden path runs nowhere, so no Pacto resource points at it. Make your paths visible on each surface by naming their repositories:

  • CLI: pacto fleet ... --oci oci://ghcr.io/acme/paths/http-service.
  • MCP: pacto mcp --fleet --oci oci://ghcr.io/acme/paths/http-service.
  • Local dashboard: the repository as an argument, pacto dashboard oci://ghcr.io/acme/paths/http-service, or a comma-separated list in PACTO_DASHBOARD_REPO.
  • Operator dashboard: the dashboard.repositories chart value, a list of oci:// references.

Developers then list the paths with pacto fleet entities --template, pacto_fleet_entities with template: only or Golden paths in the dashboard's sidebar. Search results mark each path; pacto fleet search --template keeps only paths and --template=exclude leaves them out. Each path shows its summary, its requirements, its plugins, its signature and a command to copy, pinned to the path's digest when a registry served it.

A golden path never counts as a running service or as a consumer: Overview, owner and domain counts, attention, impact and offering consumers leave it out. A viewer restricted to some namespaces still sees a path that runs nowhere. Services created from it that the viewer may not read appear only as a count.

A service is a golden path only while it runs nowhere. A deployed service that declares service.template stays a service, keeps its dependents and raises GOLDEN_PATH_DEPLOYED until someone removes the field or stops running it.

docs.title: Create a service
docs.text:
pacto init gift-cards --from oci://ghcr.io/acme/paths/http-service:1.0.0 \
  --owner checkout --domain commerce --registry ghcr.io/acme --plan

--from takes an oci:// reference or a directory, and --owner is required. --plan shows the contract, the files and the step list and changes nothing; run the command again without it to write them. A tag is resolved to a digest first, so the bytes checked are the bytes copied.

The new contract keeps the path's interfaces, dependencies, configurations, policies, workload, state and capabilities. Pacto resets the identity:

  • service.name is the folder name or --name, and the version is 0.1.0;
  • service.owner is --owner and service.domain is --domain;
  • the path's offering, summary, lifecycle, readiness, metadata.repo and metadata.summary are dropped, each with an Unknown line that names it;
  • publish.bundle and every artifact move under --registry, or under the registry.example placeholder;
  • publish.sign names the new service's own key, cosign.key.

--values files, then --set entries, change any field before the identity is set; a null removes a field. service.origin records the path's reference and the content digest of its files; the reference says what a directory records. A directory may hold only regular files. YAML comments are not kept, and the path's pacto.lock is not copied: run pacto lock.

Pacto validates the result strictly, with every reference resolved, before it writes anything. A configuration reference it cannot resolve fails with CONFIG_REF_UNRESOLVED, and values the provider's schema rejects fail with CONFIG_VALUES_VALIDATION_FAILED. It only adds files: a folder that already holds a pacto.yaml is refused and any other file there is left as it is. A path or plugin that gives a file under .git or a private key is refused.

An agent creates a service the same way with pacto_create and from, owner, domain, values, set, run_plugins, delivery and dry_run. from works only when pacto mcp runs over stdio, beside the agent and under its own credentials.

docs.title: Plan its delivery
docs.text: --delivery also plans the cluster pieces from the new contract, as pacto init --delivery does, with --env, --registry-secret and --insecure-registry. An agent passes delivery to pacto_create. It needs a path that publishes manifests under publish.deploy. Without it, the delivery step says unknown and names the missing field. The demo's http-service path publishes no manifests, so it plans none. A Stage also needs the version that runs: in a new folder, with no workload manifest, only delivery/pacto.yaml is planned and the step says why. Files already there are kept as they are, and the path's own delivery/ files are left out.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
Pacto checks the signature against the template keys of a trust config, read from --trust or PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST (pacto mcp --delivery-trust for an agent). A template key has role: template and lists in streams the path.Match patterns of the repositories it may sign for, such as ghcr.io/acme/paths/*; empty means every repository. It takes no untilSeq, untilRecord or providers: to stop trusting a signer, remove its entry. A bare PEM key given to --trust is a template key for every repository. A bare PEM key in PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST or --delivery-trust stays a record key and never verifies a golden path, so an agent needs a trust config with a role: template key. See Check who signed a golden path for an example.

When the trust config names a template key, a path that no matching key signed creates nothing. When it names none, or the path is a directory, the signature step says unknown: Pacto did not check who signed the path. Unknown is neither a pass nor a failure. To check the same signature without Pacto, run cosign verify --key platform.pub on the path's repository@sha256:....

The fleet shows a path's signature as Verified when its signer is accepted by a publisher rule, a pin or a signed policy (which publishers Pacto accepts). A service created from the path keeps its signature step unknown, and a signer none of them covers (unverified) is no failed step. Only the creation step, checked against your template keys, can say done.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Each plugin the path names appears in the step list with the binary it resolves to, or as not installed. Pacto never fetches a plugin. Only the ones you name run:

pacto init gift-cards --from oci://ghcr.io/acme/paths/http-service:1.0.0 \
  --owner checkout --run-plugins dockerfile,github-actions

Every name must be one the path lists, and nothing runs under --plan. When the trust config names a template key, plugins run only from a path a template key verified. A plugin reads a temporary copy of the planned files, never your folder, and the files it returns are added like the path's own. A plugin is how a platform team adds a repository, a CI workflow or any other file it wants a new service to start with.

docs.title: Follow the creation
docs.text:
pacto init --from ends with the step list: signature, contract, validation, each plugin, delivery with --delivery, publishing, the fleet, deployment and provisioning. A step is done only when Pacto established it. Publishing, the fleet and deployment stay unknown at creation, since no source has observed the new service yet.

Once a fleet source reads the service, pacto fleet entity service gift-cards and the dashboard show its declared origin, the golden path revision whose content digest matches and the same steps as a checklist derived from what the fleet observes. pacto fleet entities --created-from http-service and pacto_fleet_entities with created_from list every service created from a path.

The golden paths reference lists how each checklist step is derived.

docs.title: Impact consumers and evidence
docs.text: Impact analysis walks the declared dependencies of the changed service. This page covers the consumers it finds through other edges and how it judges the age of the evidence behind each one.

docs.title: Configuration-reference consumers
docs.text:
A service that takes a configuration schema from the changed service by ref is a consumer too. Pacto selects its configuration in the new revision and checks its inline and environment values against that schema. With a dependency too, the stricter of the range and values verdicts speaks.

  • Values that pass give compatible.
  • Values that fail give incompatible, and the note lists each violation as configuration <name>: <violation> against <provider>@<version>.
  • A selection that fails in a 2.4 consumer gives incompatible.
  • unknown remains when the consumer's values or the new schema cannot be read, or an older consumer's selection fails, and the note says why.

These consumers carry declared confidence and feed the release gate: a BREAKING change with one of them never ends clear.

A configuration reference that is neither digest-pinned nor locked cannot be placed on a revision. When such references name the changed service, by repository or by name, the answer adds a CONFIG_REF_CONSUMERS_UNRESOLVED limitation and its completeness is partial, so the gate stays unverified.

docs.title: Policy referrers
docs.text:
A service that references a policy the changed service publishes is a consumer too, with via: policy_reference. Pacto checks the referrer's contract against the new revision's policy:

  • A contract that passes gives compatible.
  • A contract that fails gives incompatible, whatever the classification. The gate is blocked when the referrer runs on a known target and unverified otherwise.
  • unknown remains when the check cannot decide, and the answer adds a counted POLICY_REFERRERS_UNCHECKED limitation.

A BREAKING change with referrers never ends clear. Policy references that are neither digest-pinned nor locked add POLICY_REF_CONSUMERS_UNRESOLVED and make the answer partial. A change of any classification with an unchecked or unresolved referrer ends unverified: the diff can miss a policy the provider tightened, so a referrer Pacto could not check is never taken as safe. A referrer the viewer may not see is never named; the answer counts it in hidden (consumers.hidden in the dashboard).

A golden path that references the policy runs nowhere, so it is never a consumer and never holds the gate. The answer lists it in templates to review: a service created from it checks against the new policy.

docs.title: Observed consumers
docs.text: Observed edges come from OpenTelemetry traces via --traces <file>. Beyond corroborating declared consumers, traces surface observed-only (shadow) consumers: services seen calling the changed service without declaring the dependency. With traces they appear as direct consumers at observed confidence.

docs.title: Consumers from the organization index
docs.text:
Every pacto publish, pacto push and pacto ci --publish writes one entry per published version to <registry>/pacto-index. <registry> comes from the provider reference as for the target snapshot: ghcr.io/acme/contracts/ledger tries ghcr.io/acme/pacto-index, then ghcr.io/pacto-index. --index names another <registry>/pacto-index, with no tag or digest, and --index none reads none. Any --root skips it, since --root names the consumers. A --local tree that holds the changed service also skips it: impact judges that local copy, which the published consumers do not depend on.

pacto impact lists the index by tag and reads each service's newest entry. It refuses an entry not bound to its tag, its index host and its service's bundle repository, then pulls each selected consumer's bundle by digest and judges its declared dependency. Each code below makes the answer partial, so a BREAKING change never ends clear on the index alone:

Code Meaning CONSUMER_INDEX_NOT_FOUND No candidate holds an index CONSUMER_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE The registry refused or failed the listing CONSUMER_INDEX_TRUNCATED A read bound or the timeout stopped the read CONSUMER_INDEX_ENTRY_INVALID Entries malformed, unbound or unconfirmed by their own repository were not used; a service whose newest entry is refused counts as not indexed CONSUMER_INDEX_UNCHECKED No target snapshot to check the index against: only a snapshot adds the running revisions with their dependencies CONSUMER_NOT_INDEXED A published declared consumer the fleet holds has no usable entry; it stays in the answer

The answer reports the read in consumerIndex. pacto_impact over stdio reads the index; over HTTP and in the dashboard it is never read.

docs.title: Target snapshot consumers
docs.text:
The operator of each cluster publishes a signed target snapshot to <registry>/pacto-targets:cluster-<uid> every 5 minutes, where <registry> is the operator chart's top-level registry value; with no registry it publishes none. It publishes whether or not delivery runs. pacto impact and pacto ci read it with registry read access alone, so CI finds the consumers that run without a kubeconfig. See Where consumers come from for how Pacto finds the repository and pins a cluster.

A snapshot carries every target source the installation accepted, each as its own fleet source with its own asOf and completeness:

  • targets-<uid>, kind target-snapshot: the Pacto resources of the cluster, read from their status. Their consumers carry declared confidence.
  • targets-<uid>-workloads, kind kubernetes-workloads: workloads no Pacto targets, as inferred services. An inferred service never counts as a consumer and its health never gates impact.
  • targets-<uid>-evidence, kind evidence-http: the targets the cluster's Evidence Server accepted from any producer, pacto agent included. They count as observed targets, as --evidence-url does.

The installation key signs the snapshot. Build the cluster's trust entry from the public key in the installation key Secret, which only the operator writes, or copy the one the helm upgrade notes print. The detected ConfigMap names the cluster:

kubectl -n pacto-operator-system get secret pacto-operator-installation-key \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.public\.b64}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system get configmap pacto-operator-detected \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.detected\.json}' | jq -r .cluster

Wrap the key at 64 characters between -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- and -----END PUBLIC KEY----- for publicKey, name the entry installation-<first 8 characters of cluster> and scope it with streams: ["<cluster>/pacto-targets/snapshot"].

A snapshot counts only when a trust entry scoped to its cluster verified its signature and its asOf is less than 15 minutes old. Otherwise every section reads partial, stale or unavailable with a TARGET_SNAPSHOT_* limitation (see Sources), and a BREAKING change with consumers ends unverified. A section the publisher could only read in part, such as an Evidence Server that did not answer, makes its own source and the answer partial, and the other sections still answer.

docs.title: Announced breaks
docs.text:
A provider announces a deliberate break in breaks. On a BREAKING change each announced, direct and declared consumer carries a break state, printed under it:

    break: announced for reports, not accepted; waiting for the owner of reports: ana@acme.com
  • accepted: the consumer's declared owner signed a counted acceptance of exactly this break (provider, version and the digest of its announcement) with pacto accept --break, or the consumer's own published ranges admit the new version, a source shows where it runs and no revision that refuses it runs there. An accepted consumer never blocks.
  • announced: nothing accepts it. A record by somebody other than the declared owner, or signed by CI or an agent, names who may accept.
  • expired: the announcement's expires, else the date pacto ci recorded (commit time + 30 days), has passed, or no date is recorded (expiry unknown: run pacto ci or declare expires).

A listing of acceptances that could not all be read makes the answer partial (ACCEPTANCES_TRUNCATED), never accepted. An HTTP MCP server and a dashboard viewer who is not signed in read no acceptances: the answer notes ACCEPTANCES_NOT_READ and the break reads acceptances not read.

docs.title: Range coverage
docs.text:
ranges counts the direct declared consumers of the changed service: declared when the consumer declares a range, accepted when a counted acceptance accepts it and is not yet published, else unknown, listed with the range its inferred record proposes (20 at most):

Ranges: 3 declared and 1 accepted of 5 dependency edges (80%)
  unknown: reports -> ledger (proposed ^2.4.0)

policy echoes the --policy the answer was held to, and a warn policy that applies adds a POLICY_WARNING note.

docs.title: A possible break on an inferred interface
docs.text:
When a spec file is only inferred (an interfaces[api], interfaces[events] or interfaces[grpc] entry in pacto.inferred.yaml and no interface of that name in pacto.yaml), Pacto runs the same spec diff it runs on a declared interface, between the old and the new file. Its breaking findings become an advisory in advisories: the interface, the inferred source path:line, the findings, the direct consumers (each inferred, with compatibility unknown) and the YAML that declares the interface. The CLI prints one line after the gate:

possible break (inferred) payments api openapi/v1.yaml:1: openapi.paths[/payments].methods[GET].parameters[currency:query] GET /payments query param 'currency' added; consumers (inferred, unknown): web

An advisory never blocks and never clears. It never changes the classification or the version pacto publish requires. A change that is not BREAKING reads unverified with the gate code INFERRED_POSSIBLE_BREAK; a BREAKING change keeps its own gate. Without the old record or a spec file that reads, Pacto reports no advisory. To classify the change, add the declare YAML to pacto.yaml. pacto diff, pacto ci, pacto_impact and Change analysis show the same advisory.

docs.title: Evidence freshness
docs.text:
Impact judges evidence against the 24 hours before the snapshot's asOf. A consumer whose target evidence is older, or missing, gets confidence unknown, an evidence entry that says how old it is and a counted CONSUMER_EVIDENCE_STALE limitation. Stale evidence never raises confidence. An observed call last seen before that window, in the snapshot or in a --traces file, no longer corroborates. Its caller stays in the list with confidence unknown, so it cannot drop out of the answer. A live source such as Mira reports no window, and its evidence says "no observation window".

With --include-observed and no observed edge anywhere, the answer adds OBSERVED_EVIDENCE_ABSENT: observed-only consumers cannot be found. An observed call to a name that matches more than one service, or that is neither a service nor an external system, raises OBSERVED_IDENTITY_UNRESOLVED and makes the answer partial. A call to an external system that the external catalog or a host name identifies, such as api.stripe.com, is no consumer of a service and raises nothing.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Impact analysis: the analysis these consumers feed, its confidence model and its release gate
  • Ask what happens if: impact for a service that becomes unavailable, is removed or regresses

docs.title: Ask what happens if (pacto impact --unavailable)
docs.text: Impact analysis answers who a contract change reaches. The same analysis answers what happens if a service becomes unavailable, is removed or regresses, over the same snapshot and with the same answer shape.

docs.title: Ask from the CLI
docs.text:
Three flags ask about the service as it is, with no contract change. Each takes a fleet service key and no positional arguments:

pacto impact --unavailable redis --local examples/demo/bundles
pacto impact --removed postgresql --local examples/demo/bundles
pacto impact --regressed payments-service@sha256:<digest> --local examples/demo/bundles

Event answers always read the snapshot's observed edges and its callers with no contract, because availability is a runtime question. Each consumer carries an effect, graded over every path from it to the service:

effect When breaks Some path holds only required dependencies. may-degrade Every path holds an optional dependency. These consumers have their own lane and never count as unaffected. unknown The path holds a hop known only from a configuration reference or an observed call, or the caller has no contract.

No version is judged, so every compatibilityVerdict is unknown.

docs.title: Ask about an offering
docs.text:
--unavailable and --removed also take offering:<name>, which asks the same question of every service that provides a platform offering:

pacto impact --unavailable offering:postgresql --local examples/demo/bundles

Each consumer appears once, with the worst effect over the providers it reaches. A provider is never its own consumer. providers lists the providers the answer covers. In the dashboard answer the offering's own reference fills both offering and service, and each provider carries its owner. A regression belongs to one revision, so --regressed takes no offering. When no visible provider exists, the answer raises OFFERING_NOT_IN_FLEET. Providers the viewer cannot see are counted in a HIDDEN_PROVIDERS limitation that makes the answer partial. The pacto_impact MCP tool takes offering in place of service, the dashboard API takes offeringKey and the offering page links here with What if it becomes unavailable?.

docs.title: The event gate
docs.text: An event never blocks: only a contract change has a version a consumer can refuse. The gate is unverified (exit 2) when anything depends on the service or the answer is partial. It is clear (exit 0) only when the complete snapshot holds no consumer, and its reason names the observation sources consulted, since a service with no contract can still call it. The reason names the consumers that break on fresh targets first. A consumer whose target evidence is stale was last seen there more than 24 hours before asOf.

docs.title: Removal and regression evidence
docs.text:
--unavailable and --removed list each consumer's resources: what it asked the service for, with the provisioning status per environment. When the service declares its lifecycle, such as deprecated or sunset, each consumer cites it as lifecycle evidence. Policy referrers join a removal as unknown, since their next revision fails validation. Golden paths that reference it are listed under templates, never as consumers.

--regressed grades consumers like --unavailable. When the revision is an artifact digest (sha256:...), Pacto reads delivery's recorded failures of that digest with your own cluster credentials: Fail verdicts, failed digests and rollbacks, at most 50, under regression. A DELIVERY_EVIDENCE_TRUNCATED limitation counts the facts beyond 50. A rollback line read from a Stage's status is marked "from status, not signed". A version names no single artifact, so it reads nothing. Whenever delivery cannot be read in full, the answer carries a DELIVERY_EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE limitation with the reason. An unread Stage never reads as "no failure recorded".

Two answers about one change differ in time. A delivery record carries the pacto.impact verdict signed when the change shipped: the impact recorded at the time, shown in pacto delivery history and on Delivery history. An impact answer projects the change onto today's graph, so its consumers may differ from the recorded ones. Pacto never rebuilds a past graph; see a service's changes.

docs.title: From an agent
docs.text: The pacto_impact MCP tool takes event (unavailable, removed or regressed) with service, and revision for a regression, in place of old_ref and new_ref. Only a stdio server reads delivery evidence, a traces path or a local ref, so run pacto mcp --fleet over stdio beside the agent to cite delivery's recorded failures; see Fleet query safety.

docs.title: In the dashboard
docs.text: Switch the workspace to What if this service… to ask the same events. The service page and the graph's selected-service panel link to it with What if it becomes unavailable?. The answer draws one lane per effect, plus the sources it could not read, and the gate sits under the lanes that decide it.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Impact analysis: the fields every consumer carries and the release gate of a contract change
  • Impact consumers and evidence: policy referrers, observed callers and the 24-hour freshness rule

docs.title: Impact analysis (pacto impact)
docs.text:
Impact analysis answers the question a reviewer asks before merging: if this revision ships, who is affected? Give it the old and new contract and it lists the services that depend on this one, whether each still works with the new version, where they run and who owns them.

pacto impact ./payments-api@1.4.0 ./payments-api@2.0.0 --local ./services

It joins two things Pacto already has. The semantic diff says how the contract changed (change classification). The operational graph says who depends on the service and where it runs. The CLI command, the MCP tool and the dashboard's Change analysis workspace run the same analysis and, given the same snapshot, return the same answer.

docs.title: Diff × graph → impact
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    OLD["Old revision<br/>contract + files"] --> DIFF["Semantic diff"]
    NEW["New revision<br/>contract + files"] --> DIFF
    DIFF --> CLASS["Classification<br/>NON_BREAKING · POTENTIAL_BREAKING · BREAKING<br/>breaking and potentially-breaking, kept separate"]

    SNAP["Operational graph<br/>immutable read model"] --> GRAPH["Dependents traversal<br/>direct + transitive"]

    CLASS --> IMPACT["Impact result"]
    GRAPH --> IMPACT
    IMPACT --> CONS["Affected consumers<br/>compatibility verdict · confidence"]
    IMPACT --> TARGETS["Active targets<br/>where the change lands"]
    IMPACT --> OWNERS["Owners to notify"]

A change can break consumers while every spec stays identical, such as an amount switching from cents to euros. Raise the interface's compatibilityEpoch and the diff classifies the revision BREAKING, so its consumers are listed.

The diff is computed once over the old→new revision. The changed service is then looked up in the graph and traversed in the dependents direction, direct and transitive, over declared dependencies and resolved configuration references. Each dependent becomes an affected consumer, annotated with the evidence Pacto has for that edge, and the result rolls up the active targets the change would land in and the owners to notify.

Every answer inherits the snapshot's asOf time, completeness, limitations and sources, so a partial fleet always reads as partial. When no fleet source holds the changed service, pacto impact adds the new revision to the snapshot so the services that depend on it are found, and the answer carries newRevisionAdded: true. A snapshot it cannot add to, such as the dashboard's published snapshot, answers with a SERVICE_NOT_IN_FLEET limitation, no consumer list and an unverified gate.

docs.title: What an affected consumer carries
docs.text:
For each dependent the analysis records:

Field Meaning service / domain / owner Who is affected and who owns them. owner is the display label. ownerKey The owner's canonical key, such as team:shop. Group and link by it: two owners can share a label. via The edge types that make the service a consumer: dependency, configuration_reference, policy_reference or observed. depth / direct / path depth is the shortest distance from the consumer to the changed service: 1 is a direct dependent and >1 is transitive. A consumer that depends on the changed service directly is direct even when it also reaches it through another dependent. path is a shortest dependency chain from the consumer to the changed service. required Whether the consumer declared this dependency as required. compatibility The consumer's declared compatibility range against the changed service. compatibilityVerdict Whether the new version satisfies that range. compatible and incompatible both need a declared range and a range and version semver can parse; without all three the verdict is unknown, because an unreadable or absent range is uncertainty. provenance Where the edge came from: declared, observed, declared+observed or inferred. confidence How strongly the evidence supports the claim (see below). status / targets The consumer's aggregate status and the operational targets it runs in. unmet Each guarantee the consumer requires that the new version does not meet, with both values. evidence The facts behind the consumer and their age, newest first: its targets, observed calls, unreachable findings, the file its inferred record read the dependency from and, for a removal, the provider's declared lifecycle. Stale evidence is marked. effect In an event answer, what the event does to the consumer: breaks, may-degrade or unknown. resources In a removal answer, what the consumer asked the removed service for, with one provisioning status per environment, at most 20 (resourcesTotal counts them all). note A plain-words qualifier. On a BREAKING change a compatible verdict only means the range accepts the new version, so the note says to check that the consumer does not use what the change removes. An open range such as >=1.0.0 accepts every new major version, and the note says so.

docs.title: Confidence model
docs.text:
Confidence grades how strongly the available evidence supports each affected-consumer claim.

Confidence Exact meaning contractual A declared dependency with a usable compatibility range. The consumer's own contract says it depends on this service and pins the versions it accepts. declared A declared dependency without a usable compatibility range. The dependency is stated, but no version constraint was pinned, so Pacto cannot compute a compatibility verdict. observed Runtime use of the dependency was observed in a window. Requires --include-observed. corroborated The declared dependency and an observed one agree. This is the strongest grade: contract and runtime say the same thing. inferred A transitive effect reached through another affected service (depth > 1). It follows from the graph. unknown A direct edge with no declaration and no observation. The effect is possible but unverified.

An inferred path is a lead to verify. Pacto reaches a transitive consumer through the graph. It tells you where to look; confirm whether the consumer breaks before you act on it.

Observed evidence only raises confidence when you opt in. Without --include-observed the analysis is declared-only. Runtime observations then let a direct edge become observed or corroborated.

A partial snapshot is incomplete knowledge, an unknown verdict is uncertainty and an inferred consumer is a lead to verify. Evidence older than 24 hours before asOf makes confidence unknown; see evidence freshness.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
pacto impact <old> <new> --local .

<old> and <new> are the two revisions to compare: bundle paths or refs. They are separate from the fleet snapshot and may be oci:// references either way.

pacto impact reads the fleet through the same source flags pacto fleet does, --local included, which defaults to .. Point it only at offline sources and the whole analysis stays offline.

Turn on runtime corroboration with --include-observed, or supply an OTLP/JSON trace export with --traces, which implies it:

pacto impact ./payments-api@1.4.0 ./payments-api@2.0.0 \
  --local ./services \
  --traces ./traces.json

The output reports the classification, then the breaking and potentially-breaking changes in separate lists, so a potential break never counts as a confirmed one. It then lists each affected consumer with its owner, verdict and confidence, the active targets and a warning when the snapshot is partial. The JSON output also carries owners and completeness as fields.

Pacto finds consumers only in the sources it reads. With an oci:// revision and no other source of targets, it reads the signed target snapshot each cluster publishes beside that registry and prints a Registry: line saying where it looked; --target-snapshot off turns that off. With --local alone it sees only the contracts in those folders. A BREAKING change that none of them depends on ends clear and exits 0, so No affected consumers. covers only those folders.

docs.title: Release gate and exit status
docs.text:
Every answer ends in a release gate, gate, with the reason in gateReason. The CLI exits on it, and the MCP tool returns it:

gate Exit When blocked 1 The change is BREAKING and reaches a consumer that does not accept the new version, or has an unmet guarantee, and is active. Or a policy referrer that fails the new policy is active, whatever the classification. Or a --policy set to fail meets an unknown range or an uncontracted caller. unverified 2 Nothing is shown to block the change, but the answer cannot clear it: a BREAKING change whose answer is partial or whose consumers none is shown to be safe, or a policy referrer that fails the new policy and runs nowhere known, could not be checked or could not be resolved. clear 0 The change is not BREAKING and every policy referrer was checked and passes the new policy, or the snapshot is complete and no service depends on the changed one, or every consumer accepted the announced break (BREAKING_ACCEPTED).

A command that could not run also exits 1, with nothing on stdout.

The answer also carries:

  • ranges: the range coverage of the changed service's consumers
  • each announced consumer's break state
  • an advisory when a changed spec is only inferred

Active means the snapshot knows of somewhere that consumer is deployed: at least one operational target. Compatibility is a statement about contracts; active is a statement about the world.

unverified exists because a breaking change with consumers is never safe by default. A consumer can be incompatible on paper with no known target, declare no range, or match only by range. --local bundles declare no targets, so a declared-only run of a breaking change with consumers exits 2:

$ pacto impact ./api-v1 ./api-v2 --local ./fleet
Impact: api 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Ranges: 1 declared and 0 accepted of 1 dependency edges (100%)
Affected consumers (1):
  web                          direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=frontend
    path: web > api  provenance: declared  via: dependency
By outcome: 1 incompatible, 0 unknown, 0 compatible
Most affected owners: frontend 1 (1 incompatible)
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 1 consumer depends on api, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart
$ echo $?
2

Give the snapshot a source that knows where things run, with evidence from the last 24 hours, and the same command blocks:

$ pacto impact ./api-v1 ./api-v2 --local ./fleet --target-state ./targets.yaml
Impact: api 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Ranges: 1 declared and 0 accepted of 1 dependency edges (100%)
Affected consumers (1):
  web                          direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=frontend
    path: web > api  provenance: declared  via: dependency
    evidence: target production/kubernetes-workload/shop%2Fweb 10m0s before asOf
By outcome: 1 incompatible, 0 unknown, 0 compatible
Most affected owners: frontend 1 (1 incompatible)
Active targets (1): [production/kubernetes-workload/shop%2Fweb]
Release gate: blocked
breaking changes affect active consumers, which run on known targets and do not accept api 2.0.0: web
$ echo $?
1

docs.title: Gating in CI
docs.text: In CI that is one of two deliberate choices. Fail on any non-zero exit and an unverified breaking change stops the job as a blocked one does. A promotion pipeline that gates on deployed impact alone can treat 2 as a pass, as long as the job supplies targets. Gate on the JSON instead (--output-format json, then classification == "BREAKING") and you gate on the contract alone, which is what you want before anything is deployed. That JSON carries schemaVersion: pacto.dev/impact/v1, the compatibility contract to branch on before reading any other field. Put it in your repository has a pull-request step that gates on the JSON. The file --target-state expects is documented under target-state fixtures.

docs.title: Against what runs
docs.text:
pacto impact --running <new> judges <new> against every running revision of its service, keeping the worst gate, as the Argo CD plugin does:

pacto impact --running . \
  --target-snapshot oci://ghcr.io/acme/pacto-targets:cluster-<uid> \
  --delivery-trust trust.yaml
  • Domain. A local <new> takes the fleet domain holding its service name; several exit 1 (judge the oci:// reference instead), none is unverified with SERVICE_NOT_IN_FLEET.
  • Ranges. A running consumer whose range rejects <new> blocks, whatever the classification. A partial answer never clears.
  • First version. With nothing running, a consumer range that rejects <new> blocks; a complete answer clears.
  • Unread. A revision Pacto could not link, pull or trust, a tag-only link, an inferred workload or an unreadable workload source makes the answer unverified at best. A failed pull names only the ref: a registry error can carry credentials.
  • Hosts. Revisions are pulled only from the snapshot hosts, an oci:// <new> and PACTO_RUNNING_REGISTRIES (or running-registries in the config file).
  • Itself. A target already running the digest of an oci:// <new> is never its baseline, so a post-deploy gate, such as a Kargo verification, passes oci://<repo>@<digest>.
  • Bounds. At most 8 running revisions are judged and 32 unread lines are listed; the last line counts the rest, and the answer never clears over them.
  • Output. running lists the revisions that run and those Pacto could not read.

docs.title: The MCP tool and the dashboard
docs.text:
Agents get the same analysis as the read-only pacto_impact MCP tool. It belongs to the fleet query family and shares that family's boundaries: it projects the operational graph. It is read-only and grants no permission. It analyses over the same snapshot as the pacto_fleet_* tools, so an impact answer and a graph answer from the same interval carry the same snapshotId, unless the impact answer carries newRevisionAdded: true. Its event argument and the workspace's event mode ask what happens if.

In the dashboard the analysis is one half of the Change analysis workspace, served by /api/fleet/impact. It is entered from the service or revision you are already looking at, and the analyzed pair is in the URL so the answer is shareable. It opens on a one-line answer: what kind of change it is and who it reaches. What changed, the affected consumers, owners and targets and the evidence gaps are folded below it, each with its count. It reads the currently published snapshot, the same one the Operational Graph shows, so its snapshotId matches the graph. The include-observed control is enabled only when the host declares an observation source, because observed evidence needs a real source. Plan… offers what you may do (act on what you found).

docs.title: Which refs a shared dashboard reads
docs.text:
A dashboard that serves other people, signed in or open, takes only oci:// refs of revisions in your view and reads each one's digest-pinned ref, as pacto_impact does over HTTP. Only a local dashboard reads local folders.

Over stdio pacto_impact also reads the organization index and reports it in consumerIndex; over HTTP and in the dashboard it is never read.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Ask what happens if: impact for a service that becomes unavailable, is removed or regresses
  • Impact consumers and evidence: configuration and policy referrers, observed callers and evidence freshness
  • The Pacto Operational Graph: the read model impact projects onto, and the knowledge vocabulary every answer carries
  • Change classification rules: the semantic diff impact composes with the graph
  • MCP integration: the fleet query tool family pacto_impact belongs to

docs.title: Inferred contracts for external systems
docs.text: This page describes the inferred contracts Pacto publishes for the external systems your services call, such as Stripe or a legacy host. An inferred contract records what Pacto sees of a system nobody in your organization declares. A consumer can point a dependency at it, and Pacto never checks a version range against it.

docs.title: What the operator publishes
docs.text:
Once the chart's registry value is set, for example ghcr.io/acme, the operator publishes one inferred contract for every external system with at least one consumer, to <registry>/pacto-inferred/<identity>:

oras repo ls ghcr.io/acme | grep pacto-inferred

acme/pacto-inferred/stripe
acme/pacto-inferred/host/corp-legacy.example

The operator runs the publisher every 5 minutes and needs no other value: no flag, no extra chart key and no Git access. Without registry nothing is published. registry needs a path below the host: with a bare host such as zot:5000 the operator publishes nothing and logs why, because readers take zot:5000/pacto-inferred/stripe for an organization named pacto-inferred. The operator log reports each run, and the metrics pacto_inferred_contracts_published_total and pacto_inferred_contracts_publish_errors_total count pushes and errors.

docs.title: The bundle
docs.text:
Each revision holds two files. pacto.yaml names the service, a version and the external system it describes in service.external:

pactoVersion: "2.5"
service:
  name: stripe
  version: 0.0.3
  external: stripe

pacto.inferred.yaml holds the surface: the hosts, ports and client majors the fleet sees, each with the sources that saw it, the digest of the catalog that classified it and when it was first and last seen:

format: pacto.inferred/v1
inputs:
  pacto: 4.6.0
  discovery: "1"
  sources: []
  catalog: ["default sha256:9c1f..."]
surface:
  identity: stripe
  class: vendor-api
  asOf: "2026-11-20T09:15:00Z"
  completeness: {state: complete}
  catalog: {origin: default, digest: "sha256:9c1f...", entry: stripe}
  hosts:
    - value: api.stripe.com:443
      sources: [prod-workloads]
      catalog: "sha256:9c1f..."
      firstSeen: "2026-11-02T08:00:00Z"
      lastSeen: "2026-11-20T09:10:00Z"
  ports:
    - {value: "443", sources: [prod-workloads], catalog: "sha256:9c1f..."}
  clients:
    - {value: stripe-go/76, sources: [org-repositories]}

The bundle never names a consumer. Who calls the system stays in the fleet, where restricted views apply. The version is a count of surface changes and never a vendor version.

docs.title: When a revision is published
docs.text:
A new 0.0.<n> tag is pushed only when the surface changes: a host, port or client added or removed. A new caller adds a source and publishes nothing, and so do changed sources, times, asOf and completeness. Tags are never overwritten.

asOf says when the surface was computed and completeness whether the fleet snapshot was complete. A partial snapshot never removes a value: the operator keeps every value the last revision it signed holds and only adds new ones. Removing a value needs a complete snapshot. An operator that watches only some namespaces always publishes a partial snapshot, with TARGET_SNAPSHOT_SCOPED.

At most 20 contracts are pushed per run; the rest wait for the next run.

docs.title: The signer
docs.text:
The operator signs every revision with the installation key, the key it creates once in the Secret pacto-operator-installation-key, and annotates the manifest with run.pacto.contract.provenance: inferred for registry UIs, oras and other readers. Pacto itself reads the location and the signature, never the annotation.

An operator signature never makes a publisher. Readers name the operator's signer from the snapshotKey the pacto-operator-detected ConfigMap advertises (--detected on the CLI, a file or the ConfigMap), even when delivery is off or there is no cluster. A revision only the operator signed shows its signature as unverified with source operator, even when its publish.sign names the operator. A declared revision that an accepted publisher also signed keeps that publisher's verdict. A revision under pacto-inferred reads as inferred from its location alone, signed or not.

Pull access to pacto-inferred is a separate audience that the registry's ACL governs: restricted views cover Pacto's own answers, never direct registry pulls. A restricted view never shows the surface (surfaceHidden: true).

docs.title: A range against an inferred contract
docs.text:
A dependency whose ref names <registry>/pacto-inferred/<identity> joins that external system. When it declares a compatibility range, the range reads rangeStatus: unknown with rangeReason: INFERRED_PROVIDER, even when the version would satisfy it:

pacto fleet get external:stripe --output-format json \
  | jq '.external.provider.rangeStatus,.external.provider.rangeReason'

"unknown"
"INFERRED_PROVIDER"

Every gate reads it as unverified. Impact gives each consumer the verdict unknown and the gate unverified, and delivery's move-first checks and the Stage environment gate never pass it. A range against a revision only the operator signed, wherever it is published, reads the same way. An inferred contract never clears a gate.

docs.title: Declare instead
docs.text:
Each external system with such a range raises one attention item, INFERRED_PROVIDER, in the knowledge category: "2 services check a range against stripe's inferred contract". Its next action is declare. pacto declare reads only workloads, so for an external system write a contract with service.external: <identity>, publish it outside pacto-inferred and point the ranges at its repository: the reason then disappears.

The External page on the dashboard shows the inferred contract in a collapsed block after Consumers: what its signature check established, when the surface was computed, whether that run was partial and, for each value, when it was last seen. Each list shows its first 12 values.

docs.title: Publish without an operator
docs.text:
An installation with no operator, such as the Compose demo or a Docker host, publishes with pacto fleet publish-inferred:

pacto fleet publish-inferred --registry ghcr.io/acme --key installation.key \
  --oci oci://ghcr.io/acme/checkout

--key takes a PEM private key or a pacto evidence keygen seed. Readers recognise its signature as the operator's only when their --detected advertisement names its public key. Never run it against a registry an operator already writes. No MCP tool publishes inferred contracts: agents never sign as the installation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: A provisioning or usage key scoped with allowedProviderRepos never matches a pacto-inferred repository, and the Evidence Server refuses provider evidence about one; see Evidence. Declare a contract for the external system first.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the pacto command-line tool (CLI). Use the installer script: it installs pacto and the plugins with one command. The other two ways need Go and suit contributors.

Method Installs pacto version reports Installer script pacto plus both official plugins the release you installed go install pacto only dev, with commit and date unknown From source pacto only version, commit and date from your checkout

To look first, open the live dashboard demo. It runs Pacto in your browser.

docs.title: Via installer script
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh | bash

This puts three programs in /usr/local/bin: pacto, pacto-plugin-schema-infer and pacto-plugin-openapi-infer. The script checks each download's SHA-256 checksum first. If a plugin fails to install, the script warns and still installs pacto.

Pass --version for a specific release: bash -s -- --version v4.0.0. The CLI, the charts and the images each have their own version numbers. See Versions.

If the script cannot find a version (GitHub API rate limit)

The script asks the GitHub API for the latest version. Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests per hour per IP address, so on a shared network it can fail with Failed to fetch latest version. Set GH_TOKEN to any GitHub token and run it again:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh \
  | GH_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" bash

docs.title: Installing without sudo
docs.text:
The installer calls sudo to write to /usr/local/bin. To install into your home directory with no sudo at all:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh \
  | PACTO_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" bash -s -- --no-sudo

$HOME/.local/bin must be on your PATH, and the directory must already exist.

docs.title: Via Go
docs.text:
go install github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@latest

Requires Go 1.27.4 or later. The binary is placed in $GOBIN (typically ~/go/bin).

go install builds report as dev

pacto version prints Pacto: dev and pacto update refuses to run. Use the installer script if you need version metadata.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Requires Go 1.27.4 or later, make and git.

git clone https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto.git
cd pacto
make build

make build installs into $GOBIN (typically ~/go/bin) and stamps the version, commit and build date.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Pacto uses three version numbers:

Version What it versions Current major pactoVersion The contract format, set in each pacto.yaml "2.0", "2.1", "2.2", "2.3", "2.4" and "2.5" Pacto core The pacto CLI and the Go library github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4 4.x Kubernetes integration The operator, its Helm chart and delivery 6.x

The version selector at the top of these docs follows Pacto core.

A contract with pactoVersion: "2.1" needs Pacto core 4.1.0 or later and operator 6.1.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.2" needs Pacto core 4.3.0 or later and operator 6.3.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.3" needs Pacto core 4.4.0 or later and operator 6.4.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.4" needs Pacto core 4.5.0 or later and operator 6.5.0 or later. A contract with pactoVersion: "2.5" needs Pacto core 4.6.0 or later and operator 6.6.0 or later. Older releases reject it. The integration's version compatibility table lists the current releases.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
pacto version

The first line should match the release you installed, or say dev if you used go install. If it names an older release, an earlier copy is ahead on your PATH: which pacto shows which one won.

docs.title: Installing the official plugins
docs.text:
The two official plugins (pacto-plugin-schema-infer and pacto-plugin-openapi-infer) are separate binaries from the pacto-plugins repository.

Install method Plugins Installer script Installed (best-effort) go install Not installed From source Not installed

Without them, pacto generate schema-infer fails with plugin "schema-infer" not found. To install by hand, download from pacto-plugins releases and put them on your PATH. See Plugins.

docs.title: Update the CLI
docs.text:
pacto update              # latest release
pacto update v4.0.0       # a specific version

This verifies the new binary's SHA-256 before replacing the current one. A go install build cannot use it; re-run go install github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@latest instead.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Pacto has no uninstaller. Remove the binaries, then the state they wrote:

# 1. The binaries (adjust the directory if you set PACTO_INSTALL_DIR, or use
#    ~/go/bin if you installed with `go install` or `make build`).
sudo rm -f /usr/local/bin/pacto \
           /usr/local/bin/pacto-plugin-schema-infer \
           /usr/local/bin/pacto-plugin-openapi-infer

# 2. Registry credentials and the update-check timestamp.
rm -rf ~/.config/pacto

# 3. The pulled-bundle cache.
rm -rf ~/.cache/pacto

The last two follow XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_CACHE_HOME where you set them. Removing ~/.config/pacto deletes stored registry credentials; run pacto logout <registry> first if you would rather drop them one registry at a time.

docs.title: Supply chain: signatures, provenance and checksums
docs.text:
Check what ships with each release artifact before you rely on a signature:

Artifact What ships with it ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/operator Cosign signature (keyless) and SLSA build provenance ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator Cosign signature (keyless) ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/delivery Cosign signature (keyless) and SLSA build provenance ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard Cosign signature (keyless) and SLSA build provenance ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/external-catalog Cosign signature (keyless) CLI binaries on the GitHub release checksums.txt (SHA-256), an SPDX SBOM and SLSA build provenance. No Cosign signature. ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/dashboard-contract Nothing. Unsigned. The demo contract bundles (ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/<service>) Nothing. Unsigned.

The release workflow signs the three images, the chart and the default external catalog with Cosign "keyless" signing: the signature is tied to the GitHub workflow that built the image, so you store no key. Verifying it proves who built it:

cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/TrianaLab/pacto/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/operator:<version>

A successful run prints the certificate subject and the workflow ref it was issued to. Any other output, including no signatures found, means do not deploy it.

docs.title: Build provenance
docs.text:
The release workflow records SLSA build provenance as GitHub artifact attestations for the CLI binaries, checksums.txt and the three images. The provenance names the workflow, the run and the commit it built from. Verify a binary or an image with the GitHub CLI. First look up the commit the version's tag points at, then pass it to --source-digest. Use v<version> for the CLI and the dashboard, integrations/kubernetes/v<version> for the operator and delivery images:

sha="$(git ls-remote https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto refs/tags/v<version> | cut -f1)"
gh attestation verify pacto_darwin_arm64 --repo TrianaLab/pacto \
  --cert-identity https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --source-digest "${sha:?tag not found}" --deny-self-hosted-runners
k8s_sha="$(git ls-remote https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto refs/tags/integrations/kubernetes/v<version> | cut -f1)"
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/operator:<version> --repo TrianaLab/pacto \
  --cert-identity https://github.com/TrianaLab/pacto/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --source-digest "${k8s_sha:?tag not found}" --deny-self-hosted-runners

An empty --source-digest turns the commit check off without a warning. ${sha:?tag not found} stops the command when the tag lookup returned nothing. The identity pins the release workflow on main, and --source-digest pins the tag's commit.

The command exits with status 0 and prints ✓ Verification succeeded! when the provenance verifies. Any other exit status means do not run it. Scripts should check the exit status, or add --format json and read .[].verificationResult.statement.predicateType, which is https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1.

Core v4.5.0, Kubernetes v6.5.0 and earlier releases carry no attestation. The first attested release is the one whose core changelog or Kubernetes changelog entry announces SLSA build-provenance attestations.

To check that a download matches the release page, use the checksum:

shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing

pacto update performs the checksum check, and gh attestation verify proves who built the binary. For a release without an attestation, checksums.txt proves only that the download matches what the release published and says nothing about who built it, so build from source at the tag if that matters.

Next: Quickstart.

docs.title: Investigate a problem with Mira
docs.text: When a service misbehaves, an engineer or an agent starts from that service and asks what changed, what it depends on, who depends on it and who owns them. Pacto answers from contracts, delivery records and the operational graph. Mira, an OpenTelemetry trace store, answers from the traces your services send: when the problem started and which signals show it. This guide maps each question to the tool that answers it and says what to cite.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
Run one Pacto server for fleet and delivery questions beside Mira's own, and give your agent both:

# Fleet questions, with Mira's service map as observed calls, and delivery
# questions over the cluster your kubeconfig points at
pacto mcp --fleet --k8s --mira-source http://mira:4318 \
  --dashboard-url https://pacto.example.com --delivery

# Mira's own tools, served by Mira at POST /mcp
#   http://mira:4318/mcp

Each family keeps its own authorization in the one Pacto server. Fleet answers can be restricted to what a caller may read. Delivery reads run as the caller against the cluster. Mira has no authentication. Pacto reads only Mira's service map, and only from the URL the operator passes with --mira-source; no tool argument can point it anywhere else.

For the dashboard, set PACTO_DASHBOARD_MIRA_SOURCES (space-separated URLs) to add Mira's service map to the fleet, and --mira-url to link a service page to Mira.

docs.title: Questions and tools
docs.text:
Question Tool What to cite When did the problem start? Mira list_alerts, query_metric, correlate. The frame.from of a correlate answer is the start of the window you asked for; read the onset from alert times and metric points. Alert times and metric points Which signals indicate degradation? Mira query_metric, list_alerts, get_trace Series and exemplar trace ids Which deployments or changes happened around then? pacto_delivery_history with service, since and until, or correlation_id for the changes of one incident; pacto_delivery_explain for verdict citations; pacto_impact with include_observed=true on a suspected change Record ids, applied, cause, completeness and affected consumers Which dependencies are involved? pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_neighborhood with views=differences; Mira service_map Edge provenance, reconciliation and observedSources Which other services are affected? pacto_fleet_neighborhood with direction=dependents and depth=2 (views default to expected,observed); pacto_fleet_graph with direction=dependents and transitive=true; pacto_fleet_attention with category=undeclared and service, for the callers with no contract that the neighborhood does not list Nodes, attention items and hiddenDependents. A restricted viewer sees only a count of hidden services and callers. Which teams own the affected components? pacto_fleet_neighborhood owners, pacto_fleet_entity with kind=owner Owner keys What is the likely cause?
