The agent or person concludes; Mira render_rca writes it up with citations Every citation above What evidence supports the conclusion? Every answer above meta.asOf, snapshotId, sources, limitations, delivery record ids and Mira queries with absolute times

From the CLI, pacto fleet neighborhood <service> and pacto delivery history --all --service <service> --since 2h answer the same questions. When the changes of an incident share a correlation id, pacto delivery history --all --correlation-id <id> (correlation_id in pacto_delivery_history) lists exactly those, and --cause finds the changes a verdict or reason caused.

To ask what a service looked like before, run pacto delivery history --all --service <service> --at <time> (at in pacto_delivery_history): it names the revision each Stage ran then, from signed records, and a Stage with no record before that time reads unknown. Each history line carries the pacto.impact verdict its record signed at the time. Rerun pacto_impact on the same two revisions to see who the change reaches against today's graph.

docs.title: Act on what you found
docs.text:
The dashboard plans a change from the page where you found the problem:

  • A target page offers what you may do on the Stage that delivers its environment, such as a promote or an undo of the change that Stage runs.
  • A revision page offers the promote of that revision's artifact, matched by its contract digest, so another artifact with the same version is never offered.
  • A Change analysis answer offers the promote of the new revision, or the undo on a Stage that runs the regressed artifact.

Each Plan… button shows only an action you may take now. It plans and proposes nothing: the panel shows the plan, and Propose sends it with your identity. A ?correlationID=CHG-2041 in the page's URL fills the panel's "Ticket or incident id" field, for example #/fleet/targets/<target>?correlationID=CHG-2041.

Fleet attention items whose fix is a contract edit carry nextAction ({"verb": "edit-contract", "tool": "pacto_edit"}). Pacto infers it from the item's code, and it grants nothing.

An agent plans with pacto_delivery_operation_plan, then proposes with pacto_delivery_operation_propose, the plan's intent digest, the person who asked in on_behalf_of and the incident in correlation_id. The CLI runs pacto delivery plan, then pacto delivery propose with the same flags and --intent-digest.

To tie a change to an incident, write its id when you plan or propose it: --correlation-id in the CLI, correlation_id in pacto_delivery_operation_plan and pacto_delivery_operation_propose, or the "Ticket or incident id" field of the dashboard's propose panel. The automatic rollback, freeze or step-down the promoter raises after that change inherits the id, so the history of the incident lists them too. A rollback you ask for carries it the same way:

pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type rollback \
  --undoes <operation> --correlation-id CHG-2041 --reason "error rate after 2.4.1"

docs.title: Read the evidence
docs.text:
Unknown is never healthy. Treat these as limits on what an answer proves:

  • A partial answer may be missing a change or an edge. A failed Mira read marks its source unavailable, and a truncated, empty or unattributable map marks it partial.
  • Mira's map is sampled, covers only instrumented services and only the last 15 minutes, so an edge it did not see may still exist. A declared dependency that Mira or any other source saw is matched; one Mira did not see stays insufficient unless a --traces export also observes calls.
  • A Mira node behind mira proxy cannot serve the map. Mira keeps traces for 7 days by default.
  • Mira names carry no namespace. An observed edge between two services you can see counts every namespace's traffic under those service names, including namespaces you may not read.
  • A restricted Pacto view hides every caller that has no namespace, whichever source saw it, and every caller in a namespace the viewer may not read. It counts each one in hiddenDependents.
  • The dashboard shows "Open in Mira" only to viewers with nothing hidden, because Mira has no authentication. In Open mode the dashboard serves the whole fleet to everyone.

docs.title: Revisit and share
docs.text:
• With --dashboard-url, fleet answers carry an href to each entity's page, and pacto_impact consumers link to their service pages.
  • A dashboard delivery history URL keeps its window, for example #/delivery/history?service=payments&since=2026-11-05T09:00:00Z&until=2026-11-05T11:00:00Z.
  • pacto fleet snapshot --output-format json > snapshot.json keeps the whole graph as you saw it.
  • Mira render_rca writes the incident report with its citations.

docs.title: Lockfile
docs.text:
pacto.lock pins the exact version of every contract yours depends on, so every build and every teammate resolves the same thing. Run pacto lock, commit the file and Pacto refuses to continue if a dependency later changes under you. It plays the same role as other lockfiles:

Tool Lockfile What it pins Go go.sum Module hashes Helm Chart.lock Chart versions and repository URLs npm package-lock.json Exact package versions and integrity hashes Pacto pacto.lock OCI digests for dependencies and references

It records a digest (a content hash) for every dependency and every configuration or policy reference, including the ones your dependencies pull in. When the lock is present, Pacto checks each one against its pinned digest. Any mismatch is an error: you cannot validate, graph, diff or push a bundle whose lock no longer matches.

The lock is optional. Without a pacto.lock next to pacto.yaml, Pacto resolves dependencies fresh each time. With one, pacto pack and pacto push include it in the bundle, so the dashboard can show pinned digests and drift for services read from a registry or a cluster too. To keep the lock out of a pushed bundle, list it in .pactoignore.

docs.title: What the lockfile pins
docs.text:
A pacto.lock file records:

  • Every dependency, all the way down: every dependency declared in dependencies[], recursively resolved through the dependency tree, pinned by OCI digest.
  • Every reference, all the way down: every config/policy reference declared in configurations[].ref and policies[].ref, followed through each referenced bundle, pinned by OCI digest. One entry per declared reference occurrence, tagged with the contract that declared it, so a root contract's settings reference and a referenced bundle's own settings reference stay distinct pins.
  • Local dependencies and references: file-based deps and refs pinned by their content hash (sha256:...) so local changes invalidate the lock.

The lock does not capture configuration values (configurations[].values), runtime metadata or scaling parameters. It only pins the structural dependencies and references that form the contract's external boundary.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: See the CLI reference for the full flag list; this section explains what each mode does.

docs.title: pacto lock
docs.text:
Creates or refreshes pacto.lock in the current directory. Resolves the full dependency and reference closures and writes the result to disk. Existing pins are preserved on rewrite when the dependency's constraint is unchanged; a consistent lock is left untouched.

# Create or refresh the lockfile
pacto lock

# Operate on a specific directory
pacto lock ./my-service

The lock command respects --values and --set overrides like validate and graph, so the lock you generate matches the contract as it would be evaluated at command time.

docs.title: pacto lock --update
docs.text:
Re-resolves the entire closure from scratch, ignoring existing pins. Use this when you want to bump all dependencies and references to their latest compatible versions.

# Re-resolve everything
pacto lock --update

The --update-name flag re-resolves only the named dependency (repeatable) to the newest version its constraint allows, leaving every other dependency pin untouched.

docs.title: pacto lock --check
docs.text:
Checks that the lockfile is up to date without changing it, and exits non-zero if it is stale or has conflicts. Run it in CI: the step fails until someone runs pacto lock after editing dependencies or references.

If a dependency points at a tag (not a digest) and that tag is republished, its digest changes and lock --check fails. Fix it with pacto lock --update or --update-name <dep>. Plain pacto lock keeps pins whose constraint did not change, so it does not clear this drift.

pacto lock --check

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
When a pacto.lock file exists in a contract directory, the following commands verify the lock before proceeding:

  • pacto validate
  • pacto graph
  • pacto diff
  • pacto push
  • pacto publish

If any resolved dependency or reference produces a digest that does not match the pin in the lock, the command fails with one of these error codes:

Code Description LOCK_DIGEST_MISMATCH A resolved OCI ref's digest does not match the lockfile LOCK_LOCAL_DRIFT A local file's content hash changed since the lock was written LOCK_STALE The lockfile is missing a newly added dependency or reference LOCK_CONFLICT The dependency closure requires the same service at two incompatible versions LOCK_UNRESOLVED A ref in the lockfile could not be resolved (network error, registry unreachable, bundle deleted) LOCK_MISSING pacto lock --check was run but no pacto.lock file exists. It is the only command that treats a missing lock as an error; the commands listed above skip verification entirely when there is no lock to verify LOCK_AMBIGUOUS_REFERENCE One declared reference would have to be pinned to two different destinations, so the lock cannot record it LOCK_DUPLICATE_DECLARATION A contract in the closure declares the same configuration or policy name twice, so it holds two declarations the lock cannot tell apart LOCK_ERROR Fallback for a lock failure that carries no more specific LOCK_* code, for example a lockVersion outside the supported range

A lock below lockVersion 3 is reported as LOCK_STALE: re-run pacto lock to rewrite it. Rewriting is the whole migration: Pacto re-resolves the closure from the contract and ignores the old lock's content.

docs.title: Example pacto.lock
docs.text:
lockVersion: 3
pacto:
  version: v3.2.1
root:
  name: payments-api
  version: 2.1.0
dependencies:
  - name: auth-service
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/auth-service-pacto
    constraint: ^2.0.0
    version: 2.5.1
    digest: sha256:abc123...
    dependsOn:
      - crypto-lib
  - name: crypto-lib
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/crypto-pacto
    constraint: ~1.2.0
    version: 1.2.0
    digest: sha256:def456...
  - name: shared-lib
    source: local
    path: ../shared-lib
    constraint: ^1.0.0
    version: 1.5.0
    contentHash: sha256:789abc...
references:
  - kind: policy
    name: org-security
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/org-security-policy
    version: 1.3.0
    digest: sha256:fff111...
  - kind: config
    name: shared-config
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/shared-config
    version: 2.0.0
    digest: sha256:222eee...
  - from: oci:sha256:222eee...
    kind: config
    name: limits
    source: oci
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform-limits
    version: 4.0.0
    digest: sha256:333ddd...

The lockfile starts with lockVersion (schema version), pacto.version (the CLI version that wrote the lock) and root (the contract's name and version).

Each dependencies[] entry records the source (oci or local), the full ref or path as written in the contract, the constraint and resolved version and the digest (for OCI) or contentHash (for local). The lockfile's constraint is the dependency's compatibility range copied from pacto.yaml. The dependsOn field captures the dependency chain so Pacto can rebuild the full graph structure from the lock without re-resolving upstream refs.

The references[] section records config and policy refs with their kind, source and digest. Only dependencies carry a constraint. Local file-based refs appear here with a contentHash instead of an OCI digest. A contract that declares no config or policy refs produces a lock with no references key at all.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text: • The operator does not gate on the lock. The lockfile is a CLI-side reproducibility guarantee. The Kubernetes operator resolves contracts independently from CRD specs and does not consult the lockfile.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Moving a new version into an environment is still a pull request: someone bumps a tag in git, someone else approves it and a GitOps tool applies it. That made sense while a person wrote every change. Agents now produce changes faster than people can review them. The approval also rarely answers the real question: whether this version breaks the services that depend on it.

Answering that question needs a description of each service as an operating thing, and the pipeline has none. A reviewer approves a one-line diff, and the safety of the change rests on whoever remembers who calls whom.

Pacto moves that one line out of git and decides it from evidence. The contract graph says who depends on a service and which versions each accepts, checks say whether the new version behaves and a person is asked only when the evidence runs out.

docs.title: What GitlessOps means
docs.text:
GitlessOps means signed artifacts in your registry and evidence decide which version runs where, while your code and manifests stay in git. GitlessOps is three principles, and each one holds only under its stated condition:

  1. Desired versions are immutable artifacts in a registry. Every version Pacto promotes is an OCI digest that pacto publish signed. Which digest runs where is a pointer Pacto writes onto a Flux OCIRepository or an OCI-sourced Argo CD Application. Source code and manifests stay in git, and Flux or Argo CD still apply them.

  2. Evidence moves a change on a Stage set to an automatic level. A person is asked only when the evidence runs out, and only the team concerned; Why you were asked lists every case.

  3. Every decision can be verified without Pacto. With the recorder on, each finished operation leaves a signed in-toto record as an OCI referrer, checkable with oras and cosign; see Verify a record.

docs.title: Contracts are the foundation
docs.text:
A service's operational knowledge is real, but it has no home.

The API surface has an OpenAPI spec. The container has a registry. The deployment has a Helm chart. The service as an operating thing has no document: what it is, what it exposes, how it is configured, what it depends on, what compatibility it guarantees and whether reality still matches. Those facts are spread across artifacts built for other jobs, with no links between them:

  • OpenAPI describes one HTTP interface.
  • Helm charts encode how one orchestrator deploys the service.
  • Kubernetes manifests carry health checks and wiring with no link back to a service definition.
  • Configuration lives in .env.example files, wikis or nowhere.
  • Dependencies live in Slack threads and in the heads of the people who wired them.
  • READMEs go stale the day they are written.

Every consumer that needs to understand a service reassembles that picture from those fragments and fills the gaps with assumptions. The consumers: a platform, a CI pipeline, a controller, an on-call engineer, increasingly a program acting on someone's behalf. The picture is expensive to rebuild, different every time it is rebuilt and wrong the moment any fragment drifts.

docs.title: Contracts record version ranges
docs.text:
A Pacto dependency records which versions of another service a revision accepts, for example auth ^2.0.0. pacto.lock pins the rest of the transitive closure by digest. A catalog entry such as dependsOn: auth records only that the edge exists.

The range lives in a versioned artifact, so you can compare it with the previous revision, with the rules your platform sets for every contract (policies) and with what is deployed. A CI job, a controller or an agent needs that comparison before it concludes anything.

docs.title: Tenets
docs.text:
Pacto tells you which services a change breaks before it ships, and checks what is actually running. These tenets decide its design questions. They are in priority order: when two conflict, the earlier one wins.

  1. Every feature answers who a change breaks. A feature belongs in Pacto when it makes that answer more accurate, available earlier or easier to act on.
  2. A confirmed contradiction is an error. A missing observation is Unknown. Pacto reports a pass only for what it checked, and says so when it cannot see.
  3. The contract describes the service you already run. Pacto works with existing services in any language, and adopting it never requires a change to service code.
  4. Declaration stays separate from observation. The contract records author intent. Collectors gather runtime state, and Pacto evaluates that state against the contract, so one contract is validated at authoring time, compared in CI and checked against a running system.
  5. Every dependency states what it relies on. A dependency names the provider, the versions it accepts and the behavior it needs from it. CI can evaluate a range, and a bare edge gives it nothing to evaluate.
  6. Compatibility is computed from the contract. The diff rules, the version ranges and the lock decide whether a change is compatible. A version number is a claim that Pacto checks.
  7. Contracts travel through existing infrastructure. Each revision is an immutable OCI artifact, carried by the registries and the auth that already move container images. A contract references the schemas its interfaces already have, so it stays correct when they change.
  8. The core observes. Acting is opt-in. The core never changes what runs. The opt-in delivery component moves a version only when this change's compatibility, its impact on the consumers and its checks back it. A Stage earns the right to move on its own one level at a time, and a person confirms each level. When Pacto cannot see enough, it holds the change and asks a person on the teams concerned.
  9. People, CI and agents take the same path. They get the same checks, the same answer and the same next step.

docs.title: Agents take the same path
docs.text:
An agent, like any automation, reaches its goal by whatever path is open to it. Pacto gives agents building blocks that it checks and, with the recorder on, records. An agent creates a service through the same checked building blocks as a person. Those blocks are the only way Pacto makes a change.

Every change Pacto makes goes through the same checks for its type and the same admission policies, whether a person, a CI job or an agent over MCP asks for it. Agents get no approve tool, and the policies refuse an approval from an agent.

docs.title: What stays outside the path
docs.text: The admission policies decide who may write an Operation, an Approval and a pointer's digest. They do not cover workloads, objects without the pointer label or anyone allowed to delete the policies. RBAC alone limits kubectl apply on a workload. Your platform closes the rest with RBAC and its own admission. The delivery security model gives the detail.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: Pacto builds on ideas from others. The Flux team pioneered Gitless GitOps in 2022: container registries hold desired state as OCI artifacts and controllers read it from there. On Flux, Pacto moves a version by writing its digest onto an OCIRepository. ConfigHub treats configuration as data in a database behind an API. Pacto stores only "which version runs where" that way. Anthropic's Scion addresses stored content by what it holds, moves a pointer with one compare-and-swap and tests after a change merges and before it deploys. The contract graph is ours, and all of it is open source under the MIT licence.

docs.title: MCP publish and delivery tools
docs.text: This page lists the tools pacto mcp --publish and pacto mcp --delivery serve. The MCP reference covers the other modes, how they combine and the tool-call log.

docs.title: The publish server
docs.text: --publish adds pacto_publish_plan (what publishing would write and which checks refuse it, without writing) and pacto_publish (publishes the version the same way pacto publish does, with this process's registry credentials, always to a new tag) beside the authoring tools and pacto_capabilities, which reports the publish mode with writes true. It runs over stdio only. Both tools take path and revision; for a contract with no publish section they also take image, registry, sign_key and no_transparency_log, the flags of the same name on pacto publish.

docs.title: The delivery server
docs.text: --delivery serves the delivery tools over the cluster your kubeconfig points at: pacto_delivery_status, pacto_delivery_operation_types, pacto_delivery_candidates, pacto_delivery_operation_plan, pacto_delivery_get, pacto_delivery_explain, pacto_delivery_history, pacto_delivery_blame, pacto_delivery_undo_plan, pacto_delivery_record_get, pacto_delivery_record_verify and pacto_delivery_lifecycle for everyone, plus pacto_delivery_operation_propose and pacto_delivery_cancel only when the cluster says the caller is an agent. Delivery mode has no approve tool on any server: agents read approval records with pacto_delivery_record_get and pacto_delivery_record_verify, and a person approves with pacto delivery approve or the dashboard. Over stdio the two record tools also take ref, a record reference (<repository>:<tag> or <repository>@<digest>) read with your own registry credentials and no kubeconfig, in place of namespace, stage and record; the HTTP server has no ref. Over HTTP the server needs token exchange.

docs.title: The delivery read tools
docs.text: Seven read tools answer what the dashboard's delivery views show, with the route's own parameters and answer: pacto_delivery_caller, pacto_delivery_inbox, pacto_delivery_environments, pacto_delivery_autonomy, pacto_delivery_published, pacto_delivery_refusals and pacto_delivery_trust. pacto_delivery_trust answers which publishers each service accepts: the installation's rule or signed policy, the signers a person pinned, the signers waiting for a person and the newest verdicts, each naming its source (which publishers Pacto accepts). They run the dashboard's route code in the server with the caller's identity, so the API server decides what each caller reads. With --fleet they also follow the caller's fleet view, and the fleet --namespace limits them to one namespace, as on the dashboard. A list answer carries asOf and completeness. It covers the namespaces the caller may list Stages in; namespaces outside the caller's permissions are left out without being named. unreadable names a namespace that refused the list, and without --fleet the inbox names owners there, since no owner is known and every Stage is shown as the caller's.

docs.title: Candidates, plans and history
docs.text:
pacto_delivery_candidates lists the versions a Stage may take, with their digests. The to input of plan and propose takes a version (3.0.0), a tag or a digest; a version or a tag must name exactly one of those candidates, or the tool refuses it and says why. A plan's next says what proposing it leads to, as plan, propose and approve describes, and pacto_delivery_get repeats it while an operation is held. Propose with the plan's intent digest and the same reason and on_behalf_of: the digest binds them, and PlanStale names the one that differs when it can tell.

  • on_behalf_of on plan and propose: the person an agent acts for, as the Kubernetes username the cluster authenticates them as, asserted and never verified. An agent must name one when it proposes, never itself, a service account, a system user or the promoter, and that person may not approve the change (agents). Planning needs none.
  • correlation_id on plan and propose: a ticket or incident id of at most 128 printable ASCII characters, kept with the change and its record. The automatic rollback, freeze and step-down the promoter raises after the change inherit it. It does not change the intent digest.
  • cause_verdict on plan and propose: a verdict you cite as the cause. The intent digest binds it, so a changed cause makes the plan stale.

pacto_delivery_history takes since and until (an RFC 3339 time or a duration such as 2h), cause, correlation_id and, without a stage, service and domain. Each line carries impact, the pacto.impact verdict its record signed, and the answer's revisions map each artifact digest to its revision key. at (same time forms, without since, until, cause or correlation_id) answers which revision each Stage ran at that time instead, with each Stage known, partial or unknown. pacto_delivery_blame adds the digest's revision. Every revision key on these tools is derived from the contract's digest and name, not checked against a fleet. Status, progress and lifecycle covers the status, lifecycle and record tools.

docs.title: Drive Pacto from an agent
docs.text:
This page is for an engineer who wants an AI agent, such as Claude, Cursor or Copilot, to use Pacto. It covers how to connect the agent, what it can do and the limits that keep it safe. Every tool and input is listed in the MCP reference.

Words in links are defined in the glossary: MCP, contract, bundle, fleet, delivery and change.

docs.title: Connect your agent
docs.text:
Install the pacto command first (Installation) and check that pacto version works. Every agent then starts pacto mcp and talks to it over its standard input and output. Pick yours:

Claude CodeClaude DesktopCursorGitHub Copilot

Add to your project's .mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to claude_desktop_config.json (~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\Claude\ on Windows):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

Add to .vscode/mcp.json (requires VS Code 1.99+ and the Copilot Chat extension):

{
  "servers": {
    "pacto": { "command": "pacto", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}

That starts the default server. To pick another, add its flag to args, for example ["mcp", "--delivery"].

docs.title: Pick what the agent may do
docs.text:
How you start the server decides what the agent can reach. A bundle, --fleet and --delivery combine in one server; --root and --publish each start a server of their own. The agent's first call can be pacto_capabilities, which lists what the server serves and who the caller is to it.

Start it with The agent can It can change pacto mcp Write and check contracts in local folders Contract files on disk pacto mcp --root oci://... Read published contracts and what they depend on Nothing pacto mcp --fleet Everything the default does, plus answer questions about your fleet Contract files on disk pacto mcp ./my-service --base-url https://... Everything the default does, plus call the service's own API, one tool per operation. The bundle is a folder or an oci:// reference; --base-url is where the running service answers Contract files; the live service only with --allow-writes pacto mcp --publish Everything the default does, plus publish a version to your registry Contract files and your registry pacto mcp --delivery Everything the default does, plus read delivery state and, if the cluster counts it as an agent, ask for or cancel a change Contract files and its own requests; it can never approve pacto mcp --fleet --delivery Both in one session: answer questions about your fleet, read what the dashboard's delivery views show and ask for a change Contract files and its own requests; it can never approve

If the agent must change nothing at all, use --root.

Files. The contract tools run over stdio only. They write to the folder the agent names in each call, relative to the folder the server was started in. Pacto does not limit which folder, so start the server in the project the agent should work on, as a user that can write only there. Claude Code and Cursor start it in your project; for Claude Desktop, have the agent pass full paths.

Fleet. --fleet reads the sources you name with more flags, such as --local ./contracts for folders, --oci <ref> for published contracts and --k8s for your kubeconfig's cluster. Over stdio it also reads the bundles under the folder it was started in (--local .); over HTTP it reads local bundles only from the --local roots you name. See pacto mcp. Ask questions about your organization lists the questions an agent can answer with it, and Investigate a problem with Mira pairs it with Mira's traces during an incident.

Credentials. --publish, --root and --fleet use the registry logins of pacto login. A bundle's API calls use --auth name=value for the service's own sign-in, as its OpenAPI document declares it.

docs.title: Delivery: who counts as an agent
docs.text: --delivery acts on the cluster your kubeconfig points at, as the identity in it. Every service account counts as an agent, and so does anyone the platform team's groups name as one; see Who counts as a person, an agent or a team. Only an agent gets the tools to ask for and cancel a change; a person gets only the read tools. So give the agent a kubeconfig for its own service account, never yours: an agent holding your credentials is you to the cluster. Have the agent fill on_behalf_of on pacto_delivery_operation_propose with the person it works for: then that person cannot also approve the change, which keeps two people on every change.

docs.title: What keeps it safe
docs.text:
• An agent never approves. In delivery mode it can ask for a change, and Pacto's checks and the owning team decide (Who may approve). There is no approve tool.
  • Calls to your service are read-only by default. Only GET and HEAD operations become tools unless you pass --allow-writes. Each call stops after 30 seconds and follows no redirect.
  • Tools carry safety hints. Every tool says in MCP whether it is read-only or destructive. Hints guide your client; --allow-writes and the stdio-only rules decide what runs.
  • Partial answers say so. Fleet answers carry asOf, the time they describe, and completeness, complete or partial. When a source was unreachable the answer says partial, and "not found" then means "not known".
  • Most answers are frozen at start. --root and a bundle (the ./my-service argument) are read once when the server starts. Restart it to see newer services or versions. --fleet rebuilds its snapshot when a call arrives 30 seconds or more after the last rebuild attempt.
  • Over the network, callers must sign in. By default the server talks over standard input and output. With -t http it serves HTTP on this machine only, and every request carries the bearer it prints at launch. Serving other machines needs --auth-issuer and --resource, so every request carries a token from your company sign-in, and the server then refuses --auth and --allow-writes, which would lend one credential to every caller. With --fleet or --delivery it exchanges each caller's token (--exchange-client-id) and the API server names the caller, as the dashboard does. See agents over the network.
  • Over HTTP the only contract tool is pacto_schema. pacto_create, pacto_edit and pacto_check read and write the server's folders, read its kubeconfig and follow refs with its registry credentials, so they run beside the agent with pacto mcp over stdio.

docs.title: Which tools exist
docs.text:
Tools Mode Read or write pacto_create, pacto_edit every mode but --root, over stdio only Write contract files. pacto_create with pactify: true does what pacto init does for a folder or a cluster (see Pactify a service) pacto_check every mode but --root, over stdio only Read pacto_schema every mode but --root Read pacto_capabilities every mode but --root Read: what this server serves and who the caller is pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status, pacto_fleet_explain, pacto_fleet_entities, pacto_fleet_entity, pacto_fleet_attention, pacto_fleet_neighborhood, pacto_fleet_versions, pacto_fleet_revision_document, pacto_fleet_overview, pacto_impact, pacto_stats --fleet (pacto_stats over HTTP only with --stats-read-registry) Read pacto_catalog_revision, plus two MCP resources (documents the agent reads): pacto://catalog and pacto://catalog/closure, the contracts you named plus everything they depend on --root Read One tool per API operation, named by its operationId (or <method>_<path>) a bundle Calls your service: read-only, or its write operations too with --allow-writes pacto_skill a bundle Read: returns the notes a bundle ships for agents in skills/*.md pacto_publish_plan --publish Read pacto_publish --publish Writes to your registry pacto_delivery_status, pacto_delivery_operation_types, pacto_delivery_candidates, pacto_delivery_operation_plan, pacto_delivery_get, pacto_delivery_explain, pacto_delivery_history, pacto_delivery_blame, pacto_delivery_undo_plan, pacto_delivery_record_get, pacto_delivery_record_verify, pacto_delivery_lifecycle --delivery Read pacto_delivery_caller, pacto_delivery_inbox, pacto_delivery_environments, pacto_delivery_autonomy, pacto_delivery_published, pacto_delivery_refusals, pacto_delivery_trust --delivery Read: what the dashboard's delivery views show, with the caller's identity pacto_delivery_operation_propose, pacto_delivery_cancel --delivery, agents only Ask for or cancel a change

Pacto skips any API operation named pacto_*, so the prefix always means a Pacto tool. Inputs and outputs are in the MCP reference.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
You:    Create a contract for a stateful Go HTTP API called user-service
        that stores data in PostgreSQL
Claude: [writes pacto.yaml with an HTTP interface and marks the service as
         keeping data that survives a restart]

You:    Add a dependency on payments-api
Claude: [calls pacto_edit with add_dependencies]

You:    Check the contract in ./user-service
Claude: user-service is valid.

Pacto adds a dependency only from calls it observed, which pactify does when the node agent runs in the cluster. The node agent is a Pacto program on each Kubernetes node, separate from the AI agent that calls these tools. Add any other dependency yourself, as in the second prompt.

docs.title: If the tools do not show up
docs.text:
1. Run pacto version to check Pacto is installed and on your PATH.
  2. Check your MCP configuration file for JSON syntax errors.
  3. Ask your agent to list its tools (in Claude Code, /mcp).
  4. Add -v to args to see what the server does while it starts, such as reading a bundle from a registry. It logs nothing per tool call.

docs.title: MCP reference
docs.text: This page lists the tools, inputs and limits of pacto mcp. For a walkthrough, start with Drive Pacto from an agent.

docs.title: Three tool families and their boundaries
docs.text:
Family Tools What they do Safety boundary Authoring pacto_create, pacto_edit, pacto_check, pacto_schema Create, edit and validate Pacto contracts. Operate on contract files only. pacto_edit writes only after validation. Over HTTP only pacto_schema is served. Generated service Derived per operation from a bundle's OpenAPI interfaces (getUser, createRefund, …) Invoke the live service the contract describes. Read-only (GET/HEAD) unless you pass --allow-writes; every call has a 30-second timeout and follows no redirect, so a 3xx comes back to the agent as the result. Fleet query pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status, pacto_fleet_explain, pacto_fleet_entities, pacto_fleet_entity, pacto_fleet_attention, pacto_fleet_neighborhood, pacto_fleet_versions, pacto_fleet_revision_document, pacto_fleet_overview, pacto_impact Read-only queries over the operational system: services, revisions, targets, owners, business domains, offerings, external systems, relationships and what needs attention. pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph and pacto_fleet_explain take external:<identity>, and pacto_fleet_entities lists them with kind: external. pacto_impact projects a contract diff onto that system to report which consumers a change affects, or asks what happens if a service becomes unavailable, is removed or regresses. pacto_fleet_get returns each revision's bundle signature check and OCI referrers as provenance, and the service's ownerProvenance: where its owner comes from, declared, declared-via-target, attested or inferred, with ownerSource, the file, commit and CI signer an attested owner was read from. pacto_fleet_revision_document reads one document a revision's bundle carries, as the dashboard's revision page does. pacto_fleet_overview answers "how healthy is the organization and how much do we know" in one call, as pacto fleet overview does: a target is failing when its own health check reports it is not healthy and unknown when Pacto cannot tell, and a failing check leaves compliance Unknown; see Organizational health and knowledge. The fleet tools mark target evidence older than 24 hours as stale unless --freshness says otherwise. pacto_fleet_entities takes consumes to list the services that use an offering, and with phase and environment only those whose provisioning status in that phase is in that environment. For a service, pacto_fleet_entity lists the resources it consumes with providerOwner, providerAvailability, requested (declared) and consumption, plus hiddenProviders, and its changes in version order; reached: true on a stdio server adds when each change reached a Stage, from delivery records, and any other server answers times: not-read; pacto_fleet_attention and pacto_fleet_status report PROVISIONING_FAILED and PROVISIONING_STALE in the provisioning category. pacto_fleet_status also carries providers, the providers Pacto detected with their evidence, what each is used for and their status, and providersTruncated when the list was cut. With --detected, pacto mcp --fleet adds the rows the operator detected, each provenance: inferred with its asOf and without its hint. Always read-only: they write nothing. They still make network calls, and the server that hosts them may also register write tools; see Fleet query safety. Catalog mode is the only server with no write tool. Fleet query: statistics pacto_stats Totals the unsigned run records of a stats repository for a window. See the stats answer. Always read-only. Over HTTP it appears only when the server was started with --stats-read-registry and reads only that repository; a signed-in caller sees only records of services in their view.

Outside these families: pacto_capabilities (what this server serves, see Combine modes), pacto_skill (a bundle's skill files) and pacto_catalog_revision (one revision from the catalog, see Catalog mode). The publish and delivery tools, including the seven delivery read tools (pacto_delivery_trust among them: which publishers each service accepts), are listed in MCP publish and delivery tools.

These tasks are CLI-only: inspecting a registry contract, resolving a dependency graph, diffing revisions, generating docs and the two non-query pacto fleet operations, reconcile (declared dependencies against observed traffic) and snapshot (the whole read model as one document). Only pacto_publish pushes, and no tool deploys. In delivery mode an agent asks for a change; Pacto's checks and people decide. Server modes lists which tools each invocation registers.

Annotations are hints

Every tool carries MCP annotations. pacto_check, pacto_schema, pacto_skill, pacto_fleet_*, pacto_impact, pacto_stats, pacto_catalog_revision, pacto_publish_plan and the delivery reads set readOnlyHint. pacto_edit sets destructiveHint: it removes entries in place. A generated tool takes its hints from its HTTP method: GET and HEAD are read-only, PUT is idempotent and DELETE is destructive. Every other method leaves destructiveHint unset, which MCP clients read as destructive. Hints are advice to the client; --allow-writes and the stdio-only rules decide which write tools exist. A bundle cannot claim a pacto_ name: Pacto skips every bundle operation whose name starts with pacto_.

docs.title: Fleet query safety
docs.text:
• They are read-only. They project the Pacto Operational Graph and write nothing. Every fleet tool, pacto_impact included, answers from one shared snapshot. Over stdio pacto_impact resolves both refs with your credentials; when no source holds the changed service, it rebuilds the snapshot with the new revision added, reaching every source (your cluster too if --k8s is on), and it reads the organization index, reported in consumerIndex; an HTTP server never reads it. An HTTP server, whether its callers sign in or not, reads no traces path and accepts only oci:// refs that name a revision in the caller's view, by requested ref, resolved ref or digest; it then reads that revision's own digest-pinned ref. A revision read without a recorded digest has no pinned ref, so it is refused. It also reads no delivery evidence: a regressed event over HTTP carries DELIVERY_EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE. Run pacto mcp --fleet over stdio to read them with your own credentials. The fleet snapshot of an HTTP server holds local bundles only from the --local roots it was started with; over stdio --local defaults to the folder the server was started in.
  • Target snapshots are read over stdio only. On a stdio server pacto_impact reads the change's signed target snapshot, as pacto impact does, unless the server names a target source of its own (--k8s, --target-state, --evidence-url, --target-snapshot) or was started with --target-snapshot off, and returns registry (the pacto-targets repositories it tried and the one it read) and targetSnapshots (each snapshot's pinned ref, signer, cluster and status). pacto mcp --fleet --target-snapshot <oci://ref> adds snapshots to every fleet tool. A server over HTTP refuses --target-snapshot at startup and its pacto_impact reads none, because restriction reviews a viewer in the local cluster only.
  • running needs the whole fleet. pacto_impact with running and new_ref alone judges new_ref against the revisions of its service that run on known targets, as pacto impact --running does, and returns running naming each ref, the one judged and the unread ones. A server whose answers are restricted to your view refuses it, because a hidden target could hide a running revision. Over HTTP it takes only an oci:// new_ref in your view.
  • They expose knowledge only. They never grant, scope or revoke a permission.
  • A nextAction is a suggestion. An attention item whose fix is a contract edit names edit-contract and pacto_edit in nextAction, and INFERRED_PROVIDER names declare and pacto_declare (attention categories); Pacto infers it from the item's code, and the edit itself decides.
  • rangeReason: INFERRED_PROVIDER is never a pass. A rangeStatus: unknown with that reason means the provider is an inferred contract; treat the range as unverified.
  • Partial or stale results are incomplete knowledge. Every answer carries an asOf time, a completeness value and structured limitations. Branch on those before trusting an answer.
  • Each cluster has its own status. When the snapshot knows a cluster, every fleet answer's meta lists clusters: each cluster's id, name, status, access (why a restricted view shows nothing of it) and targets. pacto_fleet_entities takes cluster, a cluster id, to keep that cluster's targets and the services and revisions that run there. See Multi-cluster.
  • Under partial coverage, a missing result means unknown. If a source was unavailable, "not found" means "not known here".
  • The snapshot refreshes on demand. A call 30 seconds or more after the last rebuild attempt rebuilds it first, reaching your sources again. Calls inside that interval share one snapshotId; a failed rebuild keeps the last good snapshot.
  • The server keeps no state. Durable evidence lives in an Evidence Server; the MCP server's state ends with its process.

--fleet names its sources the same way pacto fleet does; see the pacto mcp reference:

pacto mcp --fleet --k8s --oci ghcr.io/acme/payments-api-pacto:2.1.0

--mira-source <url> adds the calls Mira saw.

docs.title: Link answers to the dashboard
docs.text: With --dashboard-url <url>, each entity in a pacto_fleet_* answer except pacto_fleet_get and pacto_fleet_explain carries an href to its page on that dashboard, as does each contracted pacto_impact consumer.

docs.title: Combine modes
docs.text:
A bundle reference, --fleet and --delivery combine in one server:

pacto mcp --fleet --k8s --delivery

--root and --publish each start a server of their own. Pacto registers its own tools before a bundle's, so a bundle never replaces one, and the instructions describe only the modes the server serves.

pacto_capabilities reports modes, the contract tools in authoring, writes, transport, asOf and the keys fleet, impact, observed and delivery of the dashboard's GET /api/capabilities. caller.callerSource says how Pacto knows caller.user: reviewed by the API server, a verified token (user is then unknown) or local (stdio or the loopback launch bearer). With delivery, caller.class is the actor class as read at caller.classAsOf (startup over stdio); caller.policyError marks policy defaults.

docs.title: Tool-call log
docs.text: With --verbose, the server logs one mcp tool call line per call to stderr for the people who run it: tool, caller, callerSource, readOnly, outcome (ok, error or failed), durationMs, snapshotId for fleet answers and argsDigest, an HMAC-SHA256 of the arguments under a per-process key, so the log holds no value an agent passed. A call to a tool the server does not serve, or with arguments its input schema refuses, runs nothing and logs no line.

docs.title: The authoring tools
docs.text:
Every mode except --root carries these four, pacto_declare and pacto_accept over stdio. Over HTTP only pacto_schema and a planning pacto_declare.

Tool Description pacto_create Create a new contract from intent-level inputs. Supports dry run. pacto_edit Edit an existing contract, including its configuration references, environments and their values and the service lifecycle. Supports dry run. pacto_check Validate a contract and return errors, warnings and suggestions. A contract with an older pactoVersion gets the info warning CONTRACT_BEHIND and a suggestion that says whether raising it keeps the contract's meaning. pacto_schema Return the full JSON Schema reference.

Structured inputs are JSON-encoded strings. Every input that carries structure has the MCP wire type string, and the value is JSON serialised into a string:

{
  "name": "orders",
  "interfaces": "[{\"name\":\"api\",\"type\":\"openapi\"}]"
}

Warning

Passing a real JSON array or object where the JSON-encoded string is expected is a silent no-op. The argument is discarded, the call still succeeds, changes comes back null and nothing is written. Check the result's changes and summary. pacto_check's own "add an interface" suggestion carries add_interfaces as a real array, so an agent that forwards that tool call verbatim hits this case.

pacto_check is pacto validate. It runs the same validation, including pacto.lock verification and recursive policies[].ref resolution, so a contract it accepts passes CI. Its result carries the same stages and next as pacto validate --output-format json, and each error carries line and column when Pacto can locate it.

pacto_check compares environments:

  • environments takes two or more distinct comma-separated names, such as production,pr-482, and the result also lists the configuration values those environments disagree on, as pacto explain --environments does.
  • Left empty, it compares every declared environment when the contract declares two or more.
  • comparedEnvironments names the environments compared. When it is present and environmentDifferences is absent, the environments agree.

add_config_properties writes the schema. pacto_edit merges the properties into the first configuration's local schema file (configuration/schema.json when it has to declare one). A property already in the schema is replaced and required names are unioned.

pacto_edit edits configuration references, environments and the lifecycle:

  • add_configuration_refs adds references to published contracts whose configuration the service takes. Each entry's configuration picks one of the referenced contract's configurations and values holds the service's values for it. Either field raises pactoVersion to 2.4.
  • remove_configuration_refs removes references by name or ref, and removes their values from every environment file.
  • add_environments declares environments and creates each missing file holding {}. Each entry may set lifetime (temporary or persistent), expires (an RFC 3339 time, only with temporary) and owner ({team, dri?, contacts?}). It raises pactoVersion to 2.3, or to 2.4 when an entry sets lifetime, expires or owner; see temporary environments.
  • remove_environments removes environments by name, such as ["pr-482"], and deletes each file no remaining environment names. Nothing in a cluster changes.
  • set_environment_values merges values into environment files. Objects merge key by key and a null removes its key.
  • lifecycle sets service.lifecycle (deprecated, sunset, successor), and {"clear": true} removes it. Setting it raises pactoVersion to 2.4.
  • template sets service.template, which makes the contract a golden path: {"plugins": [...]} replaces it, an empty plugins list writes template: {} and {"clear": true} removes it. Either raises pactoVersion to 2.4. No input sets service.origin: only creation from a golden path writes it.
  • A field that needs a newer pactoVersion raises it only when validation finds nothing new at that version, and changes reads set pactoVersion to "2.4" (was "2.3"). When the raise would add a finding, such as ENVIRONMENT_VALUES_MISSING, the edit fails with that finding and writes nothing. When the contract already fails validation, the edit fails naming its first error; run pacto_check.

Value edits are checked first. Adding configuration references or environments, or setting environment values, writes only after pacto_check passes.

docs.title: What an edit leads to
docs.text:
• pacto_edit returns impact, chain and executor, with dry_run or without. impact is who the edit affects, analysed like pacto_impact from the contract on disk (oldVersion) to the edited one (newVersion) for the service the fleet holds under that name: classification, gate, gateReason, affected (the consumer count), hidden, owners, templates (golden paths to review), approvals, completeness, asOf, snapshotId and limitations. approvals names the owners of the consumers the edit breaks and always ends with the promote's own plan deciding. A gate is never clear when the fleet holds no revision at oldVersion or no source holds the service. impact is present only on a server that also serves pacto_impact (pacto mcp --fleet over stdio); when the session has no snapshot, the snapshot holds no single service of that name or the analysis fails, it is absent and the first chain step says who the edit affects is not known.
  • chain: the steps that carry the edit to running, in order: pacto_impact when impact is not known (after a dry run, run it once the edit is written), then pacto_publish_plan, pacto_publish and pacto_delivery_operation_plan. Each step has command (the CLI form), why, tool and, for the publish steps, args with the contract's path. A step whose tool this session does not register leaves tool empty and its why says so.
  • executor: who acts on the published revision. For configuration references and environments it is the provider (an adapter or a GitOps tool); otherwise Flux or Argo applies the version a Stage points at.
  • pacto_create from intent-level inputs (without pactify or from) returns chain too, from publish on: a new service has no published revision to compare with. A consumer that already declares it lists that dependency as unresolved until it is published. Neither tool runs a step of the chain.

docs.title: How pacto_create reads a description
docs.text:
description is matched against fixed keyword lists, case-insensitively and on whole words. A match only fills in what the call left unsaid: explicit interfaces or workload always win, and every inference is listed in the result's derived.

Keywords Inferred REST, HTTP, API, web a public openapi interface named http-api gRPC an internal grpc interface named grpc-api event, kafka, nats, pubsub, queue, message, rabbit an asyncapi interface named events worker, consumer, processor a job workload cron, scheduled, periodic, batch a scheduled workload (wins over job)

The match is a keyword heuristic: "no HTTP" still matches HTTP. State is never inferred: naming postgres declares a database dependency and leaves the service stateless.

docs.title: Declare a running service
docs.text:
pacto_declare plans what pacto declare would publish for a running workload.

  • It is the first tool of the agent write contract, which every MCP tool that writes to a registry for an agent follows. pacto_publish_plan and pacto_publish stay outside it.
  • It takes service, namespace, dir (stdio only), registry, accept, on_behalf_of, dry_run, intent_digest, max_items and call_window.
  • dry_run defaults to true: the call returns the plan and its intentDigest.
  • A write needs dry_run: false and the intent_digest of the plan the agent reviewed. The digest binds what would be declared, never the cluster facts read at the time, so a re-read with the same content keeps it.
  • Every MCP caller is an agent, so a write is a write-once draft-<n> tag that names the person in on_behalf_of (required, asserted and never verified). acceptCLI is the pacto declare --from-draft command that person runs to read the workload again and sign. A draft is never a version and the fleet never lists it.
  • Over stdio the draft is signed only by an ambient CI or agent token. A person's ambient token is never used by an agent, so that draft and one with no token are unsigned.
  • Over HTTP the plan reads the cluster with the caller's own exchanged token and only the registries --oci names. It returns the baseline only when the caller may see the service. A write is refused with ExecuteNeedsStdio.
  • A plan that changes service.owner lists who may set it in mayAccept; see Who may set a service owner. An HTTP server leaves it out, with a generic refusal, for a caller who may not see the service.

A refusal carries code, an enum in the output schema, message and cli, the command a person runs:

Code Meaning PlanStale The plan changed since the intent_digest was reviewed IntentRequired A write passed no intent_digest WorkloadNotFound No workload has that name, or dir holds no cluster draft WorkloadAmbiguous Several workloads have that name: pass namespace/Kind/name AlreadyDeclared A Pacto already describes the workload: change it with pacto publish RangeNotProposed An accept name has no proposed range NoRegistry No registry, or over HTTP one outside the installation's registries RegistryUnreadable Listing or reading the registry failed VersionConflict The version is taken, or no tag is signed by a publisher the installation trusts SignerNotAllowed The signer is outside the installation signer policy SignerUnverified The pushed signature does not name the planned signer; nothing was tagged DraftNotFound The draft tag does not exist or holds no draft of the service ExecuteNeedsStdio An HTTP server only plans: run the cli command BaselineNeedsMigration The baseline is below pactoVersion: "2.5": run pacto migrate BundleRepoMismatch The baseline publishes to another repository than registry OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_PERSON Only a person sets service.owner: an agent, CI or workload signer never does, whoever it acts for OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_ALLOWED The person is no member of the current owner and no default approver OWNER_POLICY_UNVERIFIED No verified owner policy was read, so who may set service.owner is unknown OWNER_SIGNER_UNVERIFIED No signature of the owner-setting version verified

docs.title: Accept proposed ranges and breaks
docs.text:
• pacto_accept plans what pacto accept would sign for the newest published version of a service and follows the same agent write contract as pacto_declare. It is served over stdio only.
  • It takes service (a bundle repository or a checkout folder), proposed, fields, break (<provider>@<version>), from, on_behalf_of, dry_run and intent_digest.
  • The plan names each field with its value and source, or the break, the acceptances already attached, who may accept (the service's declared owner) and the intentDigest.
  • A write writes a write-once pacto-accept-draft-<n> tag in the service's bundle repository carrying on_behalf_of, never a signed acceptance, even with a person's ambient token. acceptCLI is the pacto accept <service> --draft <ref> command that person runs to sign.
  • Its refusals add these codes to the table above:
Code Meaning AcceptNothingProposed The newest published version proposes nothing to accept FieldNotAcceptable The field is no proposed dependency ref or compatibility: declare it with pacto declare BreakNotAnnounced The provider version announces no break for this service, published or in from NotPublished The service has no published version to attach the acceptance to PersonSigningUnavailable Accepting a draft needs a person's interactive Sigstore login

docs.title: Bundle capabilities
docs.text:
Pass a bundle reference and Pacto turns that bundle's OpenAPI operations into executable agent tools:

pacto mcp ./my-service --base-url https://api.example.com

Each operation becomes a tool named by its operationId (or <method>_<path>).

The pacto_ names are reserved. A contract declaring operationId: pacto_check would take over the authoring tool. Pacto skips such operations.

Read-only by default. Only GET/HEAD operations are exposed unless you pass --allow-writes. The live host comes from --base-url, falling back to the spec's servers[0] URL. When you supply credentials, --base-url is required.

Service authentication (--auth). Credentials are supplied per OpenAPI security scheme with --auth name=value:

Scheme type How the credential is applied apiKey Sent as the declared header or query parameter http bearer (and oauth2 / openIdConnect) Authorization: Bearer <value> http basic Authorization: Basic <value> (supply pre-encoded user:pass)

pacto_skill lists a bundle's skills/*.md files and returns their content.

What a session freezes. Bundle mode and --root resolve their inputs once at startup; restart to pick up changes. Two exceptions: pacto_skill reads from disk on every call, and the authoring tools act on whatever is on disk.

docs.title: Catalog mode
docs.text:
pacto mcp --root <ref> starts a read-only contract catalog: the roots you name, plus their dependency closure, resolved once at startup and then frozen for the life of the process.

# One published platform, one contract you are still working on
pacto mcp \
  --root oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform:1.4.0 \
  --root ./experimental-platform

--root is repeatable and takes a local bundle directory or an oci:// reference. It never crawls a registry, guesses repository names or reads a catalog file.

The surface is two MCP resources (pacto://catalog and pacto://catalog/closure) plus one tool (pacto_catalog_revision). The catalog resource carries the schema version (pacto.dev/catalog/v1), catalog id, generation time, bounds, completeness and every requested root, resolved or not and why. The closure resource carries every deduplicated revision (content identity, rank and retained paths), every dependency edge and every conflict and cycle.

Catalog mode registers nothing else, so it cannot modify a contract. A root or a dependency that could not be resolved stays visible with a category such as NOT_FOUND, AUTH_FAILED or UNAVAILABLE in place of the raw registry error, and the whole answer is marked partial. Under partial, a revision missing from the answer is unknown.

docs.title: Create a service's files with pactify
docs.text:
pacto_create with pactify: true does what pacto init does for a folder holding a service: it reads the Dockerfile and Kubernetes files and writes the contract. See Pactify a service.

  • describe_only: true makes the next steps say how to validate the contract instead of how to publish it, for a request to describe a service. delivery: true also writes the cluster files and is refused with describe_only.
  • domain, registry, environments, fleet_roots, insecure_registry and registry_secret match the CLI flags, and dry_run plans without writing. max_items, call_window and continue match the CLI flags too and go with cluster. no_transparency_log applies with from only: it writes transparencyLog: false under the golden path's publish.sign.
  • The contract has no publish section and no service.version: pacto ci --publish derives both.
  • External dependencies are classified with the catalog the server was started with (--external-catalog).

Without pactify, pacto_create refuses a folder that already holds pacto.yaml (change that contract with pacto_edit) and leaves any interface or schema file already there as it is, listed in kept.

docs.title: Create a service from a golden path
docs.text:
• pacto_create with from creates a service from a golden path, like pacto init --from.
  • from is an oci:// reference or a directory. name and owner are required; domain, path, registry, describe_only, delivery, environments, registry_secret, insecure_registry and dry_run match the CLI flags.
  • values is a JSON object merged over the path's contract and set a JSON array of key=value overrides, like --values and --set.
  • run_plugins is a JSON array of plugin names, each one the path lists. Nothing else runs. A dry_run lists each plugin and the binary it runs.
  • from refuses the intent inputs, such as interfaces, and pactify, fleet_roots and the cluster inputs.
  • pacto_create, pacto_edit and pacto_check serve stdio only. Over HTTP every caller would pull with the server's registry credentials, read its directories and write to its paths, so an HTTP server offers only pacto_schema from the contract tools.
  • pacto_fleet_entities with template: only lists golden paths.
  • declaration on pacto_fleet_entities and pacto_fleet_search takes inferred, which keeps only the services Pacto infers from Kubernetes workloads no contract describes, or declared, which leaves them out. Empty lists every service and marks the inferred ones declaration: inferred.
  • group on pacto_fleet_entities takes a group key, workload.group.key, and keeps the inferred services the cluster groups under it. An inferred service's workload.group says how the cluster groups it and where Pacto read that, workload.repositories lists the source repositories its Argo CD Application or Flux GitRepository names, and workload.repositoryUnknown says why none shows; see Groups and repositories. List rows carry group and repository.
  • pacto_fleet_graph lists runtime calls with an inferred service on one end in edges as inferred, and pacto_fleet_get and pacto_fleet_graph answer the key of a replaced inferred service with the service that replaced it and replacedFrom.
  • pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_explain and pacto_fleet_entity carry, for a service whose current revision carries a declaration or that replaced an inferred service through one, fields: each field of its current revision as declared, accepted (with by), attested or inferred, with source, asOf, completeness and, for a range left unknown, proposed, and replacesHidden, the replacements whose workload the caller may not see. replaces on pacto_fleet_get and pacto_fleet_entity lists the inferred services the service replaced, with link: inferred-from, revision, by and workload when a person's declaration names one. pacto_fleet_explain adds one REPLACES_INFERRED reason per replacement; see When a declaration replaces an inferred service.

pacto_create and pacto_edit return warnings for a value that validates but is likely wrong, such as an owner written as team/billing. pacto_schema returns the JSON Schema and, under agents, how to describe an AI agent as a service.

docs.title: Measure what Pacto does
docs.text: Pacto can record what it catches as unsigned statistics in a registry you name; pacto stats and the dashboard Metrics page total them, and nothing leaves your registry. This guide shows how to turn recording on, read the totals and keep the records small. The run record reference lists every field a record holds.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
A run record is a small JSON document. Pacto writes one for each pacto diff, pacto impact and pacto publish run in CI that reaches a result, one for each delivery operation the promoter concludes and, when you ask pacto fleet status for it, one coverage snapshot of the fleet. pacto impact event answers, pacto publish --plan and MCP calls record nothing. Recording is opt-in and best effort: a problem with recording prints one warning line, and the command's exit code and output stay the same.

A record holds no person's name, email address or token. The CI context fields (repository, ciRunUrl and environment) appear only when you list them in --stats-context, and an operation record holds the class of its actor, never a name.

docs.title: Where records go
docs.text:
Records go to the repository you name with --stats-registry or PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY, for example ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats. Pacto never picks one for you. Each service has one anchor in that repository, tagged pacto-stats-<sha256 of the service name>, and each record is an OCI referrer of that anchor, next to your bundles and never inside them. Every record stays in the registry you name. Pacto sends nothing to TrianaLab or any other party.

A coverage snapshot is the exception: pacto fleet status writes one only with --stats-registry or --stats-file on its own command line and ignores both environment variables on purpose, so a job that sets PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY for its other steps records no coverage by accident:

pacto fleet status --stats-registry ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats

Coverage records has the details.

Anyone with pull access to the repository can list every recorded service name with plain oras discover, so give it pull access that matches who may see the whole fleet.

docs.title: Turn it on in CI
docs.text:
Set the repository on a job that can push to it:

- run: pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/payments:1.2.0 . --stats-context repository
  env:
    PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY: ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats

A job without write access writes the record to a file with --stats-file run-record.json and uploads it as an artifact. A later job of the same trusted repository publishes it:

pacto stats publish --registry ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats run-record.json

The reference has the complete two-job workflow. Never publish files written by untrusted (fork) jobs.

docs.title: Turn it on in delivery
docs.text:
The promoter records every operation it concludes when the chart names a repository:

helm upgrade pacto-operator oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set delivery.stats.repository=ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats

Delivery run records covers the push credentials and why the repository must be private.

docs.title: Read the totals
docs.text:
pacto stats totals the records of a window. With --by owner it infers each service's owner from the fleet snapshot the fleet source flags build:

pacto stats --registry ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats --since 30d --by owner

asOf 2026-11-15T18:44:53Z  window 2026-10-16T18:44:53Z to 2026-11-15T18:44:53Z  records 112 read, 0 skipped (complete)  unsigned statistics; owner inferred as of 2026-11-15T19:44:53+01:00
OWNER     BREAKING CAUGHT  CONSUMERS PROTECTED  CLEAR  BLOCKED  UNVERIFIED
checkout  0 (0 runs)       0 (0 unknown)        4      0        0
orders    0 (0 runs)       0 (0 unknown)        0      0        0
payments  1 (2 runs)       1 (0 unknown)        3      1        0

Environments (alphabetical)
ENVIRONMENT  OPERATIONS  HELD        FAILED     ROLLED BACK  VERIFICATION FAILED  LEAD TIME p50  p90
prod         13          2/13 (15%)  0/13 (0%)  0/13 (0%)    0/13 (0%)            21h0m0s        22h0m0s
test         9           0/9 (0%)    0/9 (0%)   0/9 (0%)     0/9 (0%)             2h0m0s         2h0m0s

The read-only MCP tool pacto_stats gives the same answer to an agent. An MCP server reads the repository named with --stats-read-registry; over stdio, PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY and the tool's registry argument also work, and over HTTP only the flag turns pacto_stats on (MCP integration). Every answer carries its asOf, its completeness and how many records it read and skipped.

docs.title: Read the Metrics page
docs.text:
pacto dashboard --stats-registry draws the same answer on the Metrics page, plus promotion depth and lead time pooled over the environments that end a promotion chain. Only the dashboard computes these: pacto stats and pacto_stats give lead time per environment. Three headline tiles show breaking changes caught with the consumers they protected, release gates by their newest verdict (clear, blocked or unverified) and lead time to production at p50 with its p90. Five charts follow: what Pacto stopped, gate outcomes over time, delivery health by environment, lead time by environment and coverage over time. Each chart has a Show as table view, hovering or focusing a mark shows its exact numbers and every count links to its records.

An unknown, such as a rate with nothing to take it over, is hatched and never drawn as 0, and unverified gates are dotted. Up to eight environments get one small panel each; more turn delivery health into a heatmap you can filter and group by promotion depth, owner or domain, with owner and domain inferred from the fleet snapshot. A partial snapshot marks the whole answer partial, as pacto stats --by owner does.

docs.title: Run records are unsigned statistics
docs.text: Run records are unsigned statistics. Anyone with push access to the repository can add or change them, so nothing in Pacto that decides reads them: validation, diff, impact, publish and delivery gates work the same with recording on or off. Read the numbers as a trend of what Pacto caught, and use signed delivery records and evidence for anything you have to prove.

docs.title: Who sees which records
docs.text: The CLI and a stdio MCP server act as you and see every record. A signed-in dashboard and an HTTP MCP server started with --auth-issuer show the records of services the viewer may list Pactos for, and operation records only in namespaces where the viewer may list Operations. Records outside the view are left out of every number and never named: the answer says some records are outside your view and is marked partial. A dashboard shared without sign-in (--allow-anonymous) counts only the services of its fleet and no operation record. These restricted readers see no coverage history, only the current value computed from their view. Dashboard access has the details.

docs.title: Registries without native Referrers
docs.text: GHCR and released versions of the CNCF distribution registry have no native Referrers API. On those, run records fall back to the OCI referrers tag, an index of the anchor's records. The fallback has two caveats: two records of one service published at the same moment can drop one of them, and the index grows with every record, so prune it.

docs.title: Prune records
docs.text:
Pacto never deletes records. List a service's records with oras, pick the old ones by their dev.pacto.recorded-at annotation and delete them. ORAS 1.2 lists them under manifests and ORAS 1.3 under referrers, so the filter reads both:

set -o pipefail
repo=registry.example.com/acme/pacto-stats
anchor=pacto-stats-$(printf payments | shasum -a 256 | cut -d' ' -f1)
oras discover --format json "$repo:$anchor" |
  jq -r '((.manifests // []) + (.referrers // []))[] | select(.annotations["dev.pacto.recorded-at"] < "2026-01-01") | .digest' |
  while read -r digest; do oras manifest delete --force "$repo@$digest"; done

GHCR refuses a manifest delete through the registry API; delete a record there as a package version.

docs.title: Try it in the demos
docs.text:
• The browser demo opens Metrics with about 90 days of generated records that follow the payments story.
  • The Compose demo seeds CI records into its own registry.
  • The Kubernetes demo records its real publishes and promoter operations on top of a seeded history.

docs.title: The Pacto model
docs.text:
How Pacto decides whether a running service matches its contract. Three words carry the whole page:

  • A contract is what the service's authors say it is (pacto.yaml).
  • Evidence is what a tool saw in the running system, such as "a pod listens on port 8080".
  • A collector is the tool that gathers that evidence.

The engine compares the two and reports findings: one line per problem, each with a code such as INTERFACE_ABSENT. One rule governs it: a confirmed contradiction is an error, and a check Pacto could not make is Unknown. Most of what follows keeps those two apart.

docs.title: Declaration versus observation
docs.text:
The contract records intent: what a service is, whatever platform runs it. What it looks like at runtime is an observation, and it lives outside the contract. A contract carries only intent. Ports, scaling, images and other runtime settings belong to delivery and the integrations own them. Runtime facts travel separately, as an EvidenceSet produced by a collector, and the engine reasons over the two together.

flowchart TB
    A["Author intent<br/>pacto.yaml"] --> C["Contract"]
    R["Running environment"] --> COL["Collector"]
    COL --> E["EvidenceSet"]
    C --> EV["Evaluate"]
    E --> EV
    EV --> OUT["Findings + Coverage"]

docs.title: The engine: Evaluate(contract, evidence)
docs.text:
The heart of the system is a pure function, Evaluate:

Evaluate(contract.Contract, evidence.EvidenceSet) -> ([]finding.Finding, Coverage)

It keeps no state. Each observation carries an Outcome the collector set (Observed, Failed, Stale and so on), and the engine applies no timing, network or Kubernetes logic of its own. An assertion is one thing the contract claims, such as "the interface public-api is served". For each required assertion (an interface's availability, a capability, a dependency, a configuration, the workload or persistence), the engine looks for a matching observation and produces exactly one of three results:

Result When Finding Confirmed violation A matching observation has Outcome=Observed and its payload contradicts the contract. error, category RuntimeDrift, for example CONFIGURATION_ABSENT, CONFIGURATION_MISMATCH, INTERFACE_ABSENT, DEPENDENCY_UNREACHABLE. Uncertainty No usable observation exists: missing, Unsupported, Failed, Stale or Insufficient. A health check that answered and reports it is not healthy also lands here, since a failing endpoint does not contradict the contract. unknown, category Inconclusive, for example EVIDENCE_MISSING, COLLECTION_FAILED, HEALTH_FAILING. Satisfied A matching Observed observation is consistent with the contract. None.

A required assertion Pacto cannot observe never counts as a pass. Coverage is the count of what the engine could check: it reports how many required assertions were evaluated versus declared. Coverage leaves the aggregate compliance state unchanged, because a check Pacto could not make is uncertainty.

docs.title: Compliance model
docs.text:
The compliance model consumers derive from these findings has four substantive states, Compliant, NonCompliant, Unknown and Invalid, plus three informational ones:

State Meaning Warning A non-blocking finding. Reference The contract declares no workload, so there is nothing to run and nothing to observe. NotEvaluated The contract declares a workload but was never runtime-evaluated at all. This is what an offline OCI, cache or local source looks like, and what pacto doc, pacto fleet and the dashboard report for a bundle read off disk or out of a registry.

A workload that is being evaluated but has no usable evidence yet resolves to Unknown. The two answer different questions: Unknown means "we looked and could not tell" and NotEvaluated means "nothing has looked". The Kubernetes operator reports only Unknown. NotEvaluated is in the CRD enum for parity with the engine (see Kubernetes limitations).

docs.title: Collectors and the evidence boundary
docs.text:
A collector is any component that observes a real system and produces a valid EvidenceSet. That EvidenceSet is the stable extension boundary. A collector and a plugin extend Pacto in opposite directions: a plugin consumes a contract to generate an artifact, and a collector observes a system to produce evidence. You integrate a collector by producing an EvidenceSet. A collector is never installed as a plugin.

Pacto ships one general runtime collector and plugs it into each platform. The watcher observes TCP listeners and connection outcomes with eBPF and names the workload behind each socket: a pod, a container, a systemd unit, a pacto run session or a plain process. Its facts are platform neutral, and so are its health, metrics and protocol probes. It runs on Linux hosts that meet its requirements. Three front ends put it to work (see runtime conformance):

  • pacto run wraps one command and evaluates it locally.
  • pacto agent watches a host, binds workloads to contracts from Docker labels or a bindings file and evaluates them locally or sends signed evidence.
  • The Kubernetes operator (integrations/kubernetes) can deploy pacto agent on every node (opt-in: nodeAgent.enabled) and merges what it publishes with its own Kubernetes collector, which reads the API server, into one EvidenceSet.

Every path ends in the same Evaluate. The "custom collector" box below is a design extension point.

flowchart LR
    C["Pacto contract<br/>declared intent"]
    subgraph Collectors["Collectors: environment-specific"]
        W["Runtime watcher: eBPF + probes<br/><i>first-party, Linux</i>"]
        K["Kubernetes collector<br/><i>first-party, operator</i>"]
        X["Custom collector<br/><i>external integration</i>"]
    end
    W -- "pacto run / pacto agent" --> E["EvidenceSet<br/>observed facts"]
    W -- "node agent, merged by the operator" --> K
    K --> E
    X -.-> E
    C --> V["Evaluate"]
    E --> V
    V --> F["Findings + Coverage"]

In-process, a custom Go collector builds an EvidenceSet (pkg/evidence) and calls Evaluate (pkg/validation) directly. This is the compiled, run ExampleEvaluate in pkg/validation/collector_example_test.go:

// 1. The contract declares intent (loaded from a bundle in real use).
c := contract.Contract{
    Service:    contract.Service{Name: "orders", Version: "1.0.0"},
    Interfaces: []contract.Interface{{Name: "public-api", Type: "openapi", Ref: "interfaces/openapi.yaml"}},
}

// 2. A collector observes the environment and produces an EvidenceSet.
prov := evidence.Provenance{Collector: "example", DetectedAt: time.Unix(0, 0)}
ev := evidence.EvidenceSet{
    Subject:     evidence.SubjectRef{Kind: "service", Name: "orders"},
    ContractRef: "oci://example/orders:1.0.0",
    Source:      "example",
