Tally Partitions Buckets serviceCompliance matched services compliance states, rolled up from each service's targets, plus the staleCompliant subset targetCompliance matched operational targets compliance states as observed per target, plus the staleCompliant subset targetHealth matched operational targets available · degraded · unavailable · unknown · notObserved ownership matched services consistent · conflicting · unowned · unknown readiness matched contract revisions passing · belowThreshold · expired · notDeclared knowledge matched services that are no golden path described · withGaps · unknown, and gaps per kind

notDeclared is its own readiness bucket so that a missing assessment stays separate from a failing one. staleCompliant counts, of compliant, how many rest on stale evidence; it is a subset and is never subtracted from compliant. ownership.unowned counts only services whose read contracts declare no owner; a service whose contract Pacto cannot read counts in ownership.unknown.

docs.title: Operational health and knowledge
docs.text: Field Buckets Meaning operationalHealth (overview), health (owner and domain) available The revision declares a health check, a source evaluated it on fresh evidence and no finding names it. The dashboard and CLI call it Healthy unavailable The health check answered and reports it is failing (HEALTH_FAILING). Shown as Failing unknown Pacto cannot tell: no evaluation, stale or no evidence, an unresolved or quarantined target or another finding on the health capability notObserved The revision declares no health check degraded No source reports degradation yet, so it reads 0 knowledge described, withGaps, unknown Partitions services. A service with two gaps counts in two kinds and once in withGaps knowledge.gaps noSummary, noDomain, noInterfaceDocs, noReadiness, notDeployed, unverifiedCapability Services per gap kind. notDeployed counts only when every source reporting targets is complete knowledgeItems How many knowledge attention items the gaps and recent takeovers raise; the count on the overview tile coverage evaluated, required, reporting, notReporting Assertions summed over the targets that report coverage; notReporting counts targets whose source reported none staleCompliantTargets Of compliantTargets, how many rest on stale evidence

docs.title: Owner and domain summaries
docs.text:
Each row of the overview's byDomain carries services, targets, nonCompliant, failingHealth, unknown, stale, unowned, ownerUnknown, notDeployed and withGaps. Domains are ranked by non-compliant targets, then failing, unknown, unowned and services with gaps.

An owner or domain page's summary adds health, knowledge, readiness, notDeployed, placementUnknown (services with no visible target whose placement Pacto cannot see, never counted in notDeployed), unresolvedDependencies (declared dependencies that resolve to no known service) and undeclaredDependencies (observed calls no contract declares).

Owner and domain list rows carry unknown, stale, failingHealth and withGaps service counts beside nonCompliant, over the services an owner owns outright or every service of a domain. sort=health ranks them by non-compliant, failing, unknown, stale and gap services; sort=gaps puts the rows with the most services that leave knowledge out first.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text: Filter Values Lists gap (--gap) no-summary, no-domain, no-interface-docs, no-readiness, not-deployed, unverified-capability, unknown Services with that gap, or those whose knowledge Pacto cannot judge ownership (--ownership) adds unknown Services with no owner claim whose contract Pacto cannot read sourceHealth adds incomplete Sources that are partial, stale or unavailable; the overview's Incomplete sources entry point opens it sort (--sort) adds gaps Owners and domains with the most services that leave knowledge out first

docs.title: Attention categories
docs.text:
Attention items fall into these categories, worst first. The dashboard's sidebar badge counts only items above info.

Category Code Severity non-compliant NON_COMPLIANT error invalid INVALID_CONTRACT error health HEALTH_FAILING, a target whose own health check is failing warning provisioning PROVISIONING_FAILED, a provider reports a resource Failed error provisioning PROVISIONING_STALE, the last report about the current revision is stale warning unknown the cause: COLLECTION_FAILED, HEALTH_FAILING, EVIDENCE_STALE, OBSERVATION_UNSUPPORTED, EVIDENCE_INSUFFICIENT or EVIDENCE_MISSING, else UNKNOWN warning stale STALE_EVIDENCE warning unresolved UNRESOLVED_DEPENDENCY warning out-of-range DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED warning lifecycle DEPENDENCY_SERVICE_DEPRECATED, a provider the consumer's range reaches is deprecated warning lifecycle DEPENDENCY_SERVICE_SUNSET, that provider is past its sunset error lifecycle SUCCESSOR_OUT_OF_RANGE, the consumer's range excludes the provider's successor error undeclared DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED, a runtime call no contract declares warning undeclared UNCONTRACTED_CALLER, a caller with no contract info golden-path GOLDEN_PATH_DEPLOYED warning readiness MISSING_READINESS info knowledge the gap: NO_SUMMARY, NO_DOMAIN, NO_INTERFACE_DOCS, NOT_DEPLOYED or UNVERIFIED_CAPABILITY; or the cause of an unknown service: CONTRACT_UNREADABLE, INTERFACE_DOCS_UNREAD, SUMMARY_UNKNOWN, DOMAIN_UNKNOWN or PLACEMENT_UNKNOWN; or INFERRED_REPLACED, an inferred service a contract took over: a Pacto target's takeover shows for 24 hours, a declaration's hand-over stays while the declaration holds; or INFERRED_PROVIDER, services check a range against an inferred contract info unowned UNOWNED_SERVICE info

A revision with no readiness assessment raises a readiness item, so noReadiness raises no knowledge item. A service whose contract Pacto cannot read raises one knowledge item and no unowned item. The Overview tile "Undeclared runtime dependencies observed" opens both kinds of undeclared item.

nextAction names the operation that fixes an item and the tool that makes it, {"verb": "edit-contract", "tool": "pacto_edit"}, on DEPENDENCY_UNDECLARED, UNOWNED_SERVICE (when a contract could be read), INVALID_CONTRACT, MISSING_READINESS, DEPENDENCY_RANGE_UNSATISFIED, GOLDEN_PATH_DEPLOYED and a range that excludes a provider's successor, and {"verb": "declare", "tool": "pacto_declare"} on INFERRED_PROVIDER. Pacto infers it from the item's code, beside the nextStep prose. It grants nothing, and an unknown, stale, unresolved or non-compliant item carries none.

docs.title: Freshness
docs.text: pacto fleet, pacto mcp, pacto tui and pacto impact mark target evidence older than 24 hours as stale by default, like the dashboard. --freshness 0 skips the check, and every answer then carries the FRESHNESS_NOT_EVALUATED limitation, so a stale count of zero never reads as "nothing is stale". The limitation does not change completeness.

docs.title: The Pacto Operational Graph
docs.text:
The operational graph answers questions that span many services: what depends on payments-api, which revision runs in production-eu, is any of it failing its contract and how sure are we? It joins contracts, their published revisions and the places they run into one view that people, CLIs, platforms and agents can query.

pacto fleet search                                     # services found under .
pacto fleet graph payments-api --direction dependents  # who depends on it
pacto fleet status                                     # what needs attention

The graph is read-only. It collects results that other parts of Pacto produce.

docs.title: Three identities
docs.text:
The graph models three distinct things and keeps them separate: a name, a revision and a running instance answer different questions.

Identity What it is Example Logical service A stable name and owner. It has revisions and runs in targets. payments-api (owner: payments) Contract revision An immutable resolved revision. Identity is the service plus a content digest: the source's immutable digest, or one derived from the whole bundle when the source has none. A ref or a version is never an identity. Pacto omits a revision that it can neither pin nor hash. payments-api@sha256:… Operational target A concrete place a revision runs, generic as scope/kind/name. production-eu/customer-a → kubernetes-workload payments/payments-api

docs.title: How certainly a target is matched to a revision
docs.text:
A target can exist before Pacto knows which revision it runs, so every target records how the link was made.

Match What Pacto knows exact The target's content digest matches a revision's. Authoritative: this is the revision running there. inferred A unique correlation by mutable tag or version suffix. Probably right, but unproven. ambiguous Several revisions match that mutable reference. Pacto makes no link, and the target carries a REVISION_LINK_AMBIGUOUS limitation. unresolved Nothing matched, or the target's identity contradicts itself. No link, and a limitation on the target saying so.

The bottom two sit on the target itself, so a consumer can classify a link without parsing snapshot-level messages. The two read surfaces spell it differently, and the CLI's spelling has a trap:

  • Snapshot and pacto fleet get --target JSON carry revisionMatch, which is omitempty and only ever exact or inferred. An absent revisionMatch is the finding: it means ambiguous or unresolved. Read the target's limitations to learn which.
  • The entity-detail API (GET /api/fleet/entities/target?key=…, what the dashboard reads) carries linkState, always present, with all four values.

This inferred differs from the inferred relationship provenance below: one is how a target was matched to a revision, the other how an edge was derived.

docs.title: Relationships: declared, observed, inferred
docs.text:
Each edge carries a provenance discriminator that records where the fact came from:

  • declared: from a contract (dependencies[], and config/policy refs).
  • observed: seen in running traffic. Pacto keeps observed edges in their own adjacency index, so declared and observed answers stay separate.
  • inferred: an external system a source recognized in a service's configuration, such as the operator reading a workload's pod spec. The edge lists each source under inferredSources, with what it read (kind, where), the normalized host, confidence, the catalog entry and digest and observedAt. It is kept out of every index that impact and a gate read, so an inferred edge never clears a gate.
  • declared+observed: one edge backed by both. The neighborhood projection merges the two indexes for display and emits this combined value, so a consumer branching on provenance must handle all four.

A neighborhood edge reads inferred only when nothing declared or observed backs it; inferred: true marks the inferred evidence either way. An inferred-only edge appears in the Differences view and has no difference value.

The dashboard's Operational Graph draws each edge by what backs it: matched, expected but not observed, or observed but not expected.

docs.title: Sources and queries
docs.text: The graph is assembled from sources, each contributing what it can see right now: contracts in your registry, local folders, live Kubernetes, the Evidence Server and target-state files. It answers five kinds of question (search, get, graph, status and explain). The operational graph reference lists every source, the target-state file format, the query semantics and the canonical owner key.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
Every Pacto answer records how much of the world it saw. Each word below is a separate claim.

Word Claim complete Every source answered. Nothing is missing. empty Every source answered and there is genuinely nothing. This is complete knowledge of an empty result. partial At least one source was unavailable, stale or itself partial. What you see is a floor. stale Every source answered, but one of them last saw the world a while ago. Its records are real and may have moved on since. unavailable A source did not answer at all. Whatever it knows is missing from this answer entirely. unknown No completeness value arrived. This differs from empty.

Three of these travel on the wire, in every answer's meta.completeness: complete, partial and empty. The other three are a consumer's reading of the same envelope: stale and unavailable come from the per-source health reported alongside it, and unknown is what is left when no envelope arrived at all. The dashboard takes the worst of the six and gates every all-clear on that, so a source that is down shows even when the snapshot calls itself complete.

An unavailable source means missing data. A partial answer with zero rows is a set Pacto could not finish building.

docs.title: Organizational health and knowledge
docs.text:
Unknown is never a pass: Pacto reports what it cannot see as unknown and never counts it as healthy.

The dashboard overview, pacto fleet overview and the MCP tool pacto_fleet_overview return one answer to "how healthy is the organization and how much do we know?". Pacto computes no score from it. Each count opens the list of exactly what it counts, and every partition keeps its own unknown bucket.

docs.title: Three questions about a target
docs.text:
Each operational target answers three questions separately:

Question Answer Where Does it obey its contract? Compliant, NonCompliant, Unknown and the other compliance states compliantTargets and its siblings Is its own health check passing? Healthy, Failing, Unknown or Not observed operationalHealth How recently did we look? Fresh, stale or never observed evidence

A target is Failing when its declared health check answered and reports it is not healthy. The source records the finding HEALTH_FAILING, and compliance stays Unknown: a failing check neither satisfies nor contradicts the contract. A target is Unknown when Pacto cannot tell, for example because no evidence arrived or the evidence is stale. A target is Healthy only when its contract revision declares a health check, a source evaluated it on fresh evidence and no finding names it. Not observed means the revision declares no health check.

In the demo, the gift-cards target is Failing and its compliance is Unknown. The audit-log target is Compliant on evidence older than the freshness window, so it stays Compliant, counts in staleCompliantTargets and its health is Unknown. The dashboard draws stale Compliant targets hatched.

docs.title: What the contracts leave out
docs.text:
Knowledge partitions the services that are no golden path into Described, With gaps and Unknown. A service is Described only when Pacto read its current contract and the OpenAPI documents it names and nothing is missing. Pacto reads no gRPC or AsyncAPI document. The gaps are:

  • No summary: no revision declares service.summary;
  • No domain: the service has no business domain;
  • No interface document: an interface declares no document. A declared document Pacto could not read is unknown, never a gap;
  • No readiness assessment: the current revision carries none;
  • Runs nowhere: the service has no operational target. Pacto counts it only when at least one target source is configured, every target source is available and your view sees every target;
  • Unverified capability: the current revision declares an extension capability that no evaluator verifies.

A service whose contract or OpenAPI document Pacto cannot read, whose summaries or business domains conflict or whose placement Pacto cannot see is Unknown, and its attention item names the cause.

Ownership keeps two cases apart. No declared owner means Pacto read the contracts and none declares an owner. Owner unknown means Pacto cannot read the contract, so it cannot tell whether an owner is declared.

The tallies reference lists every field.

docs.title: Who consumes it
docs.text:
A human portal and an agent consume the same graph.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["Sources"]
        OCI["Contracts in OCI<br/>published revisions"]
        LOCAL["Local bundles<br/>revision being edited"]
        K8S["Live Kubernetes<br/>Pacto CRs: which revision runs where"]
        EVI["Evidence Server<br/>signed EvidenceSet reports"]
    end
    OTEL["OTel trace file<br/>offline analysis"]
    OCI --> OG
    LOCAL --> OG
    K8S --> OG
    EVI --> OG
    OTEL -->|--traces| OG
    OG["Operational Graph<br/><i>immutable read model</i>"]
    OTEL --> RECON["reconcile · impact<br/>declared vs observed"]
    OG --> RECON
    OG --> Q["Queries<br/>search · get · graph · status · explain"]
    Q --> DASH["Dashboard"]
    Q --> CLI["CLI<br/>pacto fleet …"]
    Q --> MCP["MCP fleet tools"]
    Q --> PLAT["Platforms"]
    Q --> AGENT["Agents"]
  • Dashboard: the visual front door. It builds one snapshot from every source it detects and serves the graph and change analysis through /api/fleet/*. The endpoints the UI reads (overview, entities, neighborhood and attention) carry their own schemaVersion, pacto.dev/fleet-product/v1, so a UI versions independently of the pacto.dev/fleet/v1 snapshot export above. The Operational Graph view offers three perspectives (Services, Revisions and Operational targets) and a Knowledge control (Expected · Observed · Differences). An operational target links to the dependency service it depends on. It draws no target-to-target mesh, because the snapshot has not observed that runtime routing. The service page gathers one service's owner, contract, dependencies, targets, delivery and signatures.
  • CLI (pacto fleet …): the five queries on the command line, plus overview for the organization in one answer, entities, entity and attention for owners, domains, offerings and what needs attention, neighborhood for the services around one service, versions for an offering's versions and reconcile and snapshot. Scriptable, deterministic output.
  • MCP fleet tools: pacto_fleet_search, pacto_fleet_get, pacto_fleet_graph, pacto_fleet_status, pacto_fleet_explain, pacto_fleet_overview, pacto_fleet_entities, pacto_fleet_entity, pacto_fleet_attention, pacto_fleet_neighborhood, pacto_fleet_versions and pacto_fleet_revision_document, plus pacto_impact and pacto_stats, give an agent read-only understanding of the operational system. See MCP integration for how they differ from authoring tools and generated service tools.

docs.title: A read model around many evaluations
docs.text:
Compliance is the pure Evaluate(Contract, EvidenceSet) function producing findings for one service in one environment (see the Pacto model). The graph is the read model around many such evaluations. It references each target's findings and coverage as the engine produced them.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Eval["Per-target evaluation (the engine, one at a time)"]
        C["Contract"] --> EV["Evaluate"]
        E["EvidenceSet"] --> EV
        EV --> F["Findings + Coverage"]
    end
    C -.-> OG
    F -.-> OG
    OG["Operational Graph<br/>composes many revisions + many targets"]
    OG --> ANS["Query answers<br/>with asOf · completeness · limitations"]

The graph also maintains a reverse-dependency index, which is what impact analysis traverses to answer "if this revision ships, which consumers are affected, directly and transitively".

docs.title: Observed dependencies and reconciliation
docs.text:
Declared intent is half the picture; the other half is what traffic does. The OTel observer (pacto otel observe <traces.json>) is an offline analyzer: it reads an exported OTLP/JSON trace file and derives the caller-to-callee edges its outbound spans prove. A missing span is no proof that a dependency is absent, so the observer reports only edges it saw. The callee of a span is the first of these attributes it carries: peer.service, rpc.service, server.address, net.peer.name, db.system, messaging.system and rpc.system. It can also emit signable EvidenceSets (pacto otel observe --evidence) so observed dependencies travel the same evidence protocol as any other report.

Those observed edges meet the declared graph in three places:

  • The snapshot itself: pacto fleet --traces <file> and pacto dashboard --traces resolve each raw observed endpoint name to a unique domain-qualified service and fold resolved edges in as observed relationships. A name no service carries goes through the external catalog: a catalog system value or host, or a host of three or more labels with a public registrable domain, becomes an observed edge to that external system. A name that matches more than one service, and a name that is neither a service nor an external system, stays unresolved and becomes an OBSERVED_IDENTITY_UNRESOLVED limitation, so observed traffic is always attributed to the right domain or to none. A service name always wins over an external one.
  • Reconciliation: pacto fleet reconcile --traces <file> labels each dependency matched, declared-not-observed (dormant or unseen in the window) or observed-not-declared (a shadow dependency the contract never mentions). Anything unresolvable goes into a separate unresolved category.
  • Impact: pacto impact --traces <file> feeds the same observed edges into the affected-consumer list; the confidence model has what they change there.

The backend computes reconciliation: every declared edge carries a state computed against the snapshot's observed edges. A snapshot with no observation data returns insufficient, so an empty Observed view never reads as "there is no traffic".

docs.title: The fleet is a view
docs.text: Pacto discovers the graph from the sources you already have. A contract has no kind: Fleet and no fleet: section, because a hand-maintained fleet list drifts the moment a team adds a service. The fleet is a view, computed on demand and versioned by its as-of time.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Operational graph reference: sources, the target-state file, query semantics and owner keys
  • Operational graph tallies: every count, knowledge-gap filter and attention category
  • The Pacto model: the engine, the compliance states and the boundaries the graph inherits
  • Impact analysis: the consumers a change affects, projected onto this graph
  • Fleet tools: the dashboard, pacto fleet and the terminal UI
  • MCP integration: the three MCP tool families

docs.title: Who may set a service owner
docs.text:
service.owner routes reviews: impact analysis, owner pages and the Backstage export name it. So declaring a service never claims it. A declaration that sets, changes or removes the owner is allowed only when its signer belongs to the current owner or is a default approver. Anyone else is refused before anything is pushed:

$ pacto declare invoices --registry ghcr.io/acme --yes
refused: service.owner is attested as team payments (CODEOWNERS:7 at a1b2c3, signed by github.com/acme/invoices/.github/workflows/ci.yml); only payments members or default approvers (platform-admins) may set it

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Pacto checks each owner change in this order and stops at the first match:

  1. The owner is unchanged: allowed.
  2. The signer is no person (an agent, a CI pipeline or a workload identity): refused with OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_PERSON, whoever it acts for.
  3. The signer is a member of the current owner, declared or attested: allowed.
  4. The signer matches a default approver: allowed.
  5. No verified owner policy was read: unknown, OWNER_POLICY_UNVERIFIED. Unknown is never allowed.
  6. Anyone else: refused with OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_ALLOWED.
Code Meaning OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_PERSON An agent, CI or workload signer never sets service.owner OWNER_SIGNER_NOT_ALLOWED The person is no member of the current owner and no default approver OWNER_POLICY_UNVERIFIED No verified owner policy was read, so who may set the owner is unknown OWNER_SIGNER_UNVERIFIED No signature of a published owner-setting version verified, or the fleet read no owner before it

A signer is a member of an owner when a rule of the policy's teams entry for the owner's team matches it, or when its subject is an email equal to the owner's DRI or to an email contact and its issuer is one of the policy's emailIssuers. With no emailIssuers, the issuers are https://accounts.google.com, https://github.com/login/oauth and https://login.microsoftonline.com. A signing certificate carries no groups, so without a team rule only the DRI and email contacts count. A current owner that is only declared via a target or inferred makes nobody a member.

docs.title: Agents and CI
docs.text: An agent never sets an owner. pacto_declare writes a draft carrying on_behalf_of, and its plan lists who may accept the owner change in mayAccept. on_behalf_of is recorded and grants nothing: the person it names signs with pacto declare --from-draft and is checked like anyone else.

docs.title: The current owner
docs.text: The reference for a change is the service's effective owner before it. Pacto walks the service's published versions in order and takes the owner of the last one whose owner was not refused or left unchecked: its declared owner, else its attested owner. The baseline a declaration names for itself is never the reference. A first owner has no current owner, so setting it takes a default approver. With no verified policy nobody can set it, and the service stays without an owner.

docs.title: Attested owners
docs.text:
An owner read from CODEOWNERS or catalog-info.yaml (the record's class: ownerFile) is inferred. It becomes attested when all of these hold:

  • the bundle carries a signature that verified, by a CI identity the publisher rule accepts;
  • the certificate names a source repository and the commit it was issued for;
  • that commit equals the record's inputs.commit.

The bundle, record included, is what the CI identity signed. A hand-edited marker, an unsigned or person-signed bundle, a refused CI identity, an empty commit and a commit mismatch each leave the owner inferred.

The first repository whose CI signs a service is trusted for attestation. When attested versions of one service were signed from two repositories, the service has no attested owner and reports OWNER_CONFLICT. A declared owner always outranks an attested one.

An attested owner routes reviews. It never clears a gate and never decides who may answer a delivery question: delivery reads the running contract's declared owner only.

docs.title: Owners the fleet ignores
docs.text:
The fleet judges every published version that changes the owner and either carries a declaration or has a signature other than accepted CI provenance. It drops the owner of a version the rule refused (OWNER_DECLARATION_REFUSED) and of a version it could not check (OWNER_DECLARATION_UNVERIFIED, which makes the answer partial). The fleet reads only the versions its sources name, so a change judged after a version it did not read reads as unverified. The operator marks a running bundle the same way with the OwnerVerified condition.

An unsigned version with no declaration keeps its owner, and so does one whose signatures name nobody, such as one signed with a key: removing the signature would make it unsigned. Whoever can write to the registry can already push any contract, so registry write access stays the trust boundary for these pushes.

docs.title: Where the policy comes from
docs.text: The owner policy is the operator chart's declare block; see Owner policy. The operator, the dashboard and pacto mcp --owner-policy over HTTP read it from its ConfigMap. pacto declare and pacto mcp over stdio read it from the signed target snapshots beside the registry, verified with the trust config in --delivery-trust (default $PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST). They use it only when every cluster's snapshot is complete, fresh, signed by a key scoped to that cluster and carries the same policy. Anything else (no trust config, a stale or unscoped snapshot, clusters that disagree) is no policy, and every owner change reads as OWNER_POLICY_UNVERIFIED. A local file is never accepted.

docs.title: Decide, unfreeze and roll back
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

This page is for the person Pacto asks to decide on a change. It covers everything you need to do it. If you set up Pacto for your team, read Pactify a service first.

Words in links are defined in the glossary. Commands below name a Stage by its service and its environment's namespace, so -n prod means "in prod". A change is a Kubernetes object of kind Operation.

docs.title: Why you were asked
docs.text:
Pacto holds a change and asks a person in these cases:

  • It would break a consumer. For example, payments 3.0.0 removes a field and the checkout contract accepts only payments 2.x. Pacto asks the team that owns checkout, because theirs is the service it would break. The same holds when checkout requires a guarantee from payments that the new version does not meet, wherever checkout runs and also when Pacto cannot see where it runs.
  • Its contract does not back the Stage's environment. The contract lists environments, but none named like the Stage's spec.environment, or that environment's values fail their configuration schemas. The service's team approves it, alongside any consumer team the change also waits for.
  • It could not check something. Monitoring had too little data, or no contract depends on the part that changed, so a service without a contract might call it. That check says Unknown.
  • The Stage is set to ask for every promote. This is approval.always, which pactify turns on. A person approves every promote, whatever the level.
  • The Stage is on advise. A person approves every promote that a person did not ask for; see the autonomy ladder.
  • The Stage is on auto for non-breaking and the change is breaking, possibly breaking or unclassified. Every consumer's contract accepts it, but this level ships only non-breaking changes on its own, so a person approves it.
  • The Stage requires records and the recorder cannot write them now. A person approves the promote or rollback to go ahead before its signed record exists. The change itself runs as usual.
  • Someone asked to raise the Stage's level. A raise lets Pacto do more on its own and keeps the running version. A person of the team that owns the service, other than the one who asked, approves it.
  • The version changes who owns the service (the team, or the DRI when no team is named). The team that owns the service now approves it, so the author of a version never picks who approves it. A version that only edits the owner's contacts does not wait. When the running contract cannot be read, no team is asked, and only break-glass can answer if the promoter, the part of delivery that runs each change, requires an owner team.
  • The version number is too small for the change. A breaking change published as a minor (1.9.0 after 1.8.0) would pass every ^1 range, so a person approves it. So does a version whose contract moved to another registry domain, because consumers declared against the old domain would not be counted.
  • A person or agent asked to roll back to a version a consumer has moved past. That consumer's team approves it first; see Cancel and roll back.

Pacto asks members of the owner team of each affected service, or the changed service's own team when none of them names one, and skips the person who asked. If an AI agent asked for you without naming you, leave that change to a teammate; the rule is in Who may approve.

docs.title: Look, then decide
docs.text:
Find the held change and read what Pacto asks:

kubectl get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod   # PHASE shows Held
pacto delivery explain -n prod <change>                       # what is asked and why

The question: line explain prints ends with what it asks for, for example Approve shipping it anyway? or Accept the unknown?. Give that answer, or reject.

Then give one answer:

Answer Use it when What happens approve The question says "Approve" and you accept it. Pacto asks that in every case in Why you were asked except a check that said Unknown Once every team asked has approved, the version goes ahead, or for a raise, the Stage moves up one level accept-unknown The question says "Accept the unknown": a check said Unknown and you accept the risk The version goes ahead and the record says "accepted". If the version already shipped and a later check said Unknown, only this or reject answers reject You do not want this version here If it has not shipped, the change ends and the Stage keeps the version it runs. If it already shipped, Pacto rolls it back to the version before. Someone can ask again later 
pacto delivery approve -n prod <change> --decision approve   # or accept-unknown, or reject

<change> is the name in the NAME column of the first command. All three answers go through approve; the --decision flag says which one.

A held change that nobody answers ends on its own after 24 hours. If it had not shipped, it ends as Expired and the Stage keeps the version it runs. If it had shipped and the question was about a later Unknown check, the Stage freezes instead, so a person looks at it. The person who asked can withdraw it at any time with pacto delivery cancel -n prod <change>.

In the dashboard (pacto dashboard), Delivery in the sidebar opens the Inbox, which lists the changes Waiting for your decision. Changes another team may answer too sit behind a Shared with other teams count, and frozen Stages and changes that could not finish behind their own counts. Open a change: the page leads with the question and two cards, If you approve and If you reject, each saying what happens and each with its own button. Write your note, then press Approve shipping (or Accept the unknown) or Reject. The checks, the affected services and the timeline are folded below, one click away.

docs.title: What you need to be allowed
docs.text:
Three things, all set up once by your cluster admin:

  1. Update rights on the workload. You may decide a change when you may update the Stage's workload, such as the checkout Deployment in payments. The built-in edit or admin role in that namespace gives it, and lets you create the Approval. If your admin narrowed answers to owner teams (teamGroupPrefix), your group must also be the owner team written in the contract of the service you are asked about: for a breaking change, the consumer that would break; otherwise, the service whose version or level is moving.
  2. A person's sign-in. A service account, any other system: user and a member of an agent group count as AI agents and can never approve. Every other sign-in is a person.
  3. A recent company login, if your admin asks for one. By default you decide with the sign-in you have. If your admin sets delivery.promoter.authFreshness (a recent sign-in to decide), the cluster must trust your company sign-in and you must have signed in within that time. Then pacto delivery approve prints an address, you sign in again in your browser and it sends your answer with that login, and the dashboard asks you to sign in again in the same way. Before the first time, set your company's sign-in address, which your admin gives you, in your shell: export PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://login.example.com.

Where a recent sign-in is required but the cluster cannot check it (where approving works), nobody can give any of the three answers, reject included. A held change then has three ways out: the person who asked cancels it and publishes a version that asks nothing, it ends after 24 hours, or someone in the break-glass group forces it (below).

docs.title: When a Stage is frozen
docs.text:
A frozen Stage shows true under FROZEN in kubectl get stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod, and its reason says why: What happens to a change lists when a failed version freezes a Stage instead of rolling back. A forced version (below) also freezes it. Fix the cause first, then let automation move it again:

pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type unfreeze --reason "fixed the config"

An unfreeze takes effect at once and needs nobody else, even though the command is propose. It also clears HOLD, so run it on a Stage that is on hold even when FROZEN shows false. It needs update rights on the Stage's workload but no fresh login: without them you are refused with CannotUpdateWorkload. With answers narrowed to owner teams, only the team that owns the service (the owner team in the contract running on the Stage) or break-glass may unfreeze it, and a person of another team is refused with NotYourTeam. In the dashboard, the Stages view has an Unfreeze button on each frozen Stage, shown only to the people the same rule lets unfreeze it.

docs.title: Roll back by hand
docs.text:
Pacto rolls a failed version back on its own. To remove a version that passed its checks, find the change that put it there and undo it:

pacto delivery blame -n prod --stage payments   # the "change:" line is the change to undo
pacto delivery undo -n prod <change>            # prints the exact rollback command; changes nothing

Run the command undo prints. If the Stage has moved on since, undo prints a normal change to the earlier version instead, and every check runs again. After a manual rollback, automation stops moving that Stage (the HOLD column shows true) until a person unfreezes it or asks for a new version, so your choice stays in place. In the dashboard, the History view has an Undo button on each change.

docs.title: Force a version (break-glass)
docs.text:
Someone in the break-glass group can force a version past every check. It shows in the history and freezes the Stage until a person unfreezes it. Use it only when nothing else works. <change> is the held change whose version you force:

to=$(kubectl -n prod get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io <change> -o jsonpath='{.spec.params.to}')
pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type override --to "$to" --reason "why"

docs.title: Pactify a service
docs.text:
To pactify a service is to give it a Pacto contract, pacto.yaml kept next to your code, and let Pacto check every new version before it runs. This guide takes a plain service to a contract, signed published versions and environments Pacto only watches, and shows how an environment moves past watching once it has earned it. Every command is on this page except the one-time cluster setup for approvals. To preview the result, press Play the delivery story in the live dashboard demo, which runs in your browser.

In the cluster, Flux does the deploying and Pacto tells it which version. Each environment starts on observe, the first level of the autonomy ladder: Pacto watches and moves nothing until a person raises it.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the pacto command, from Installation;
  • a service in a git repository, with a Dockerfile and the Kubernetes files that run it (a Deployment and a Service). Those files are what lands in the cluster. Leave the namespace out of them: each environment gets its own;
  • Docker with a builder that can write an image to a folder, as Pacto builds the image there and pushes it itself: docker buildx create --use --driver docker-container;
  • a container registry, and a login to it: pacto login registry.example -u <user> (or docker login). Any registry works for this page. The optional signed record of each change is stored next to what you publish, in a registry that serves OCI Referrers. Without records a Stage stops at advise; see What delivery needs;
  • a CI that hands out an OIDC token (GitHub Actions or GitLab CI), so Pacto signs keyless, or a cosign key pair if you sign with a key;
  • for step 4, a Kubernetes cluster (1.30 or later), kubectl and helm. People approve with a fresh company login, which needs a one-time cluster setup, maybe by you: the cluster trusts your identity provider. Until it works, nobody can approve; see where approving works.

Pacto writes the contract from your service.

If you only want the contract and its CI checks, run pacto init --describe-only: its next steps say how to validate the contract instead of how to publish it. Then go on to Put it in your repository: pacto ci --publish publishes it when publish.bundle is declared.

docs.title: 1. See what Pacto would add
docs.text:
From the root of your repository:

pacto init --delivery --plan

pacto init reads what is already there, such as the Dockerfile and the Kubernetes files (the full list), and fills in a contract from it. It reads your registry from the image name in your Deployment; pass --registry registry.example/acme if it cannot, or if the image is a bare name such as checkout: a Docker Hub official image only Docker can push to. --delivery adds the cluster files of step 4, so the first version you publish already carries them. With --plan it shows exactly what it would add and changes nothing. For a private registry, add --registry-secret registry-creds (step 4 creates that Secret). For a local registry that speaks plain HTTP, add --insecure-registry. --no-transparency-log applies with --from only: it writes transparencyLog: false under the golden path's publish.sign.

The plan lists the services yours depends on, what Pacto could not work out, marked Unknown, and a Next list of what to do after.

docs.title: 2. Write the contract
docs.text:
Add any flags you needed in step 1, such as --registry-secret:

pacto init --delivery --owner payments
pacto validate

--owner names the team that owns the service: the name of its group in your company login, whose members Pacto asks about this service (Decide, unfreeze and roll back). init writes pacto.yaml, the delivery/ folder and a .pactoignore, and never overwrites your edits. For an image registry.example/acme/my-service:1.0.0 and the files k8s/deployment.yaml and k8s/service.yaml, the contract is:

pactoVersion: "2.5"        # 2.5 holds compatibility: unknown
service:
  name: my-service         # no version: pacto ci --publish derives it
  owner:
    team: payments
workload: service           # from the Kubernetes workload kind
capabilities:               # from a readiness, liveness or startup probe
  - type: health
dependencies:               # one per service a URL in the environment names
  - name: billing
    ref: oci://registry.example/acme/contracts/billing   # where its contract would be published
    required: true                              # yours cannot run without it
    compatibility: unknown   # no range proposed: no contract or running version of billing was read
configurations:             # the environment, ConfigMaps included: keys and types, no values
  - name: env
    schema: configuration/schema.json
    required: true
  • The contract has no publish section and no service.version: pacto ci --publish derives both, building the image with the tool the folder shows and assembling the deploy artifact from your Kubernetes files. The image tag, 1.0.0 here, is named under Found as the version to declare for a first publish.
  • The configuration schema holds each key and its type, never a value, so it declares no defaults.
  • It marks a key writeOnly when its name holds password, passwd, secret, token, key, credential, private or dsn (any case), when it is read from a Secret or when its value is a URL with credentials.
  • Next steps name each manifest or ConfigMap that sets such a key to a literal value, because the bundle publishes that file.
  • A --cluster draft reads such a key from the Secret <workload>-env, which you create with kubectl create secret generic --from-env-file (details).

docs.title: What pactify recognizes
docs.text:
• init finds the vendor APIs, managed cloud services and legacy hosts the folder names and records them in the inferred record, never in pacto.yaml; see External dependencies. A --cluster draft lists them the same way.
  • A --cluster draft is completed by the same engine as a folder, and its pacto.inferred.yaml adds what the cluster showed, each value with when it was read and whether every node was observed (details).
  • On a folder that already holds a pactoVersion: "2.5" pacto.yaml, init completes the contract and never changes it: what the folder adds goes into the inferred record, published with the bundle, each value with its source.
  • For a new contract, init lists what the folder shows beyond the pacto.yaml it writes. pacto pack publishes that record only once pacto.yaml declares pactoVersion: "2.5", and init says so under Next when it writes an older version.

Fill in what the plan marked Unknown, above all the dependencies:

  • Replace each compatibility: unknown with the versions yours accepts, such as ^2.0.0 for any 2.x. With that service's contract in --fleet, init reads its bundle and proposes one.
  • Declare an OpenAPI document under interfaces (how): Pacto sees API changes only there. Every field is in Publish and Dependencies.
  • For private images, add imagePullSecrets: [{name: registry-creds}] under spec.template.spec in your Deployment.
  • With dependencies, run pacto lock . (Lockfile), and commit what init wrote, as What to commit lists.

docs.title: 3. Publish a version
docs.text:
In your build pipeline, on the merged commit, after your tests:

pacto ci              # what would be published, and the version; writes nothing
pacto ci --publish    # publish it

pacto ci --publish builds the image with the tool your folder uses, pushes it with your Kubernetes files and the contract to your registry and signs them so anyone can check they came from you. With no key configured, it signs keyless as the CI identity, which needs id-token: write on GitHub Actions or an id_tokens entry on GitLab, and prints that identity. To sign with a key instead, pass --sign-key with a key file outside the folder. The details are in Publish from CI.

Versions have three numbers, major.minor.patch, such as 2.4.1. With no service.version declared, the first publish is 1.0.0, and each later one raises the number the change needs: a change that breaks the services using yours raises the major. A declared version too small for the change is refused, and a published version is never overwritten; see Publish a version.

docs.title: 4. Connect the service to your cluster
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Install, once per cluster, Flux, the Pacto operator (it checks each running service against its contract) and delivery (it decides which version runs in each environment). One Helm chart installs both. With a private registry, give delivery a login in the operator's namespace and add --set delivery.promoter.registryCredentials.secretName=registry-creds to the delivery command below:

kubectl create namespace pacto-operator-system
kubectl -n pacto-operator-system create secret docker-registry registry-creds \
  --docker-server=registry.example --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token>

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

helm install pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.6.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --create-namespace

helm upgrade pacto-operator \
  oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --version 6.6.0 \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system \
  --reset-then-reuse-values --set delivery.enabled=true

Replace staff with your people's group; Install says why.

Delivery is opt-in: without it, Pacto never changes what runs. The chart's registry value publishes what runs for CI and keeps delivery off. Each environment is a namespace of the same name. A Stage promotes nothing until you set spec.verify.matchOIDCIdentity in its delivery/<env>.yaml to the identity pacto ci --publish printed. On GitLab CI, also set its issuer to your GitLab's address. Then apply the files:

for env in test prod; do
  kubectl create namespace $env
  # a private registry only:
  kubectl -n $env create secret docker-registry registry-creds \
    --docker-server=registry.example --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token>
done
kubectl apply -f delivery/test.yaml -f delivery/prod.yaml

registry-creds is the pull Secret your Deployment names and, with --registry-secret, the login Flux and the operator use. A read-only token is enough (on GitHub, read:packages); see Private registries.

Each delivery/<env>.yaml holds a Stage and the Flux pieces that watch your registry and apply what the Stage picks. delivery/pacto.yaml tells the operator to check the service; it ships inside every version, so you never apply it.

Each Stage starts at observe: it plans every new version and moves nothing, and the OCIRepository stays pinned to the tag you deploy (spec.ref.tag), so Flux applies what it did. With no version tag on the image, init writes no delivery/<env>.yaml.

  • --delivery also declares each --env under environments in pacto.yaml, with an empty values file environments/<env>.yaml, so pacto validate checks each environment's values.
  • It never rewrites an existing pacto.yaml: it names the environments it does not declare and the pacto_edit add_environments call that adds them.
kubectl get stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -A    # POINTER: the digest of the version each one runs
pacto delivery history -n test --stage my-service     # what happened in test
kubectl -n test describe stages.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io my-service  # if nothing moves: why, under Ready

docs.title: 5. Ship the next version
docs.text:
Make a change and merge it: pacto ci --publish publishes it with the next version the change needs, or with the service.version you declare. While the Stages observe, you deploy the new tag as before: set spec.ref.tag in delivery/<env>.yaml and apply it. Each Stage records what it would have done.

To leave observe, in this order:

  1. Keep deploying this way until 10 versions passed their checks (autonomy.proposeAfter lowers that, see the ladder). The Stage's status.proposal lists what is still missing.

  2. Remove spec.ref from the OCIRepository in delivery/test.yaml and apply it, so Flux stops setting the version, and label it so only Pacto may write its digest. Pacto then proposes advise:

    kubectl -n test label ocirepository my-service delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref=my-service

  3. Ask for the raise; another person who may update the workload approves it (see Why you were asked). Be quick: until the raise, nothing moves the version.

    pacto delivery propose --type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/autonomy --stage my-service -n test --to advise

Each level above that is one more approved operation. In prod, init also writes approval: always: true, so every promote there waits for a person: the contract check cannot see a consumer with no contract, or tell whether the version is healthy. Delete it from delivery/prod.yaml once a health check judges each version there (gates.verify.checks, see Delivery reference: health checks). A version that fails its checks after release is rolled back or freezes its Stage, as What happens to a change explains.

Each move is a change; one that waits for a person shows Held. To approve one, as a person who may update the workload (Decide, unfreeze and roll back has the details):

kubectl get operations.delivery.pacto.trianalab.io -n prod   # PHASE shows Held
pacto delivery approve -n prod <name> --decision approve

docs.title: Many services at once
docs.text:
pacto init takes several folders and ends with a summary table. --cluster drafts a contract for every workload no Pacto describes yet, from your current kubeconfig context, in <out>/<namespace>/<name>. Pass --namespace: without it, --cluster reads every namespace, system ones included:

pacto init --plan services/checkout services/payments
pacto init --cluster --namespace shop --out drafts --plan

With the Pacto node agent running, the Services a workload calls become dependencies. When the Pactos describing shop/payments report 2.3.1 and 2.4.0, the draft proposes ^2.3.0 in a comment and keeps compatibility: unknown until you declare a range; until then, impact cannot verify a BREAKING change. Without the agent, environment URLs name dependencies. Drafts are never published, and an invalid one fails the command. The MCP tool pacto_create with pactify: true takes paths, cluster and namespaces, and only plans unless dry_run is false. With cluster it also takes max_items, call_window and continue. Generate contracts from what you already have lists the permissions --cluster needs and walks through a whole folder of services.

docs.title: What Pacto reads from your folder
docs.text:
pacto init, pacto explain and pacto pack read these files at any depth of the service folder. Each value goes into the inferred record with its path:line, never into pacto.yaml.

Format Files What it records What it never reads When it cannot read it Dockerfile Dockerfile, Dockerfile.*, *.Dockerfile ports from EXPOSE, service.summary from the org.opencontainers.image.description label, a health check from a localhost URL in HEALTHCHECK the HEALTHCHECK command and the URL query DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED for a port set through a variable or a range OpenAPI, AsyncAPI and gRPC any .yaml, .yml, .json or .proto file that parses as one one interface per kind: api, events or grpc GraphQL (*.graphql, *.graphqls, *.gql), which has no Pacto interface type, and package tool files such as package-lock.json DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS when two files hold one kind, and no interface for that kind Helm chart Chart.yaml, Chart.lock, values.yaml, values-<env>.yaml and templates/*.yaml, up to two folders deep image, ports, configuration keys, environments and each locked dependency under inputs.chartDependencies a configuration value beyond the host it names; it never renders a template, downloads a dependency, opens a vendored charts/*.tgz or reads a subchart unpacked under charts/ DISCOVERY_CHART_DEPENDENCY_UNLOCKED for a dependency with no Chart.lock digest; DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED once per template with an expression it does not resolve Kubernetes manifests Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job and CronJob outside a chart's templates/, charts/ and crds/ folders image, container ports and environment key names an environment value beyond the host it names DISCOVERY_UNREADABLE for YAML that does not parse Kustomize kustomization.yaml and its local resources image from images, an environment per overlays/<env>/ remote resources and helmCharts DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED_FILE, naming a remote resource without its credentials Compose compose.yaml or docker-compose.yaml at the folder root image, container ports and environment keys of the service named like yours (the service.name in pacto.yaml, else the folder's name), else of the only one include, extends from another file and env_file; an environment value only for the host it names DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS when it lists several services and none is named like yours Owner files catalog-info.yaml in the folder; .github/CODEOWNERS, CODEOWNERS or docs/CODEOWNERS at the repository root, the last rule that matches pacto.yaml service.owner with the marker class: ownerFile, shown as "attested" by pacto init; from catalog-info.yaml also service.domain (spec.system) and dependencies (spec.dependsOn) spec.lifecycle. The owner is unverified until a signed commit is checked, so it never routes a decision or clears a gate DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED for a CODEOWNERS rule with email owners only Environments environments/<env>.yaml, Helm values files, overlays, and Argo CD Application and Flux Kustomization and HelmRelease objects in the folder environments[<env>].file; a GitOps object confirms it an Argo CD ApplicationSet, and the paths of a Flux object whose source is an OCI artifact, a bucket or a Helm repository, such as the delivery/ files pacto init writes DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED for an invalid environment name, or for a path outside the folder or one the folder does not hold (an Argo CD Application that deploys from another repository) Other formats helmfile.yaml, helmfile.yml, Tiltfile, *.jsonnet, *.libsonnet, *.cue nothing the whole file, a program or a template for another tool DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED_FILE
  • When two files give one value, the more direct one wins and the record lists the others under outranks: for a port EXPOSE, then a manifest or template, then Compose; for the owner catalog-info.yaml, then CODEOWNERS, then the workload's team label.
  • A file over 1 MiB is never read, and a link, a FIFO or a device is never opened.
  • A finding names the file and line, never a value. It changes no validation result and no gate, and the record keeps at most 100.
Finding Meaning DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED_FILE Pacto recognizes the file, or a part of it, and does not read it DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS several files or services fit, so none is recorded DISCOVERY_CHART_DEPENDENCY_UNLOCKED a chart dependency has no Chart.lock digest, so it is not read DISCOVERY_UNREADABLE the file is over 1 MiB, is not valid YAML, is not a regular file or has a : in its name DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED a template expression, an invalid environment name, a path outside the folder or missing from it, or a CODEOWNERS rule with email owners only DISCOVERY_TRUNCATED discovery stopped after 5000 files, so results are partial; always listed first

docs.title: External dependencies
docs.text:
pacto init, pacto explain and pacto pack record the systems a folder names outside the cluster:

  • Each vendor API, managed cloud service or legacy host becomes a dependencies[<name>] field of the inferred record, with every file and line that names it.
  • Pacto never writes one into pacto.yaml, and an inferred external never clears a gate. To declare one, copy its declare YAML into pacto.yaml and set the version you call.
Source What is read Confidence Workload environment, ConfigMaps included Each value that names a host, and each key name likely for a host, possible for a key name alone secretKeyRef and envFrom secretRef The Secret name and key names, never a value possible Helm values.yaml and values-<env>.yaml Every string value, read as data, and its key likely for a host, possible for a key name alone Compose environment Each value, as a map or a KEY=VALUE list likely for a host, possible for a key name alone Kustomize configMapGenerator literals and the envs files likely for a host, possible for a key name alone SDK manifests and lockfiles go.mod (direct requires), package.json (dependencies and optionalDependencies) with package-lock.json, requirements*.txt, poetry.lock (no dev packages), pom.xml (no test or provided scope) and gradle.lockfile (no test-only lines): each package name and its major version possible Terraform *.tf Each resource whose type the catalog lists: its id attribute and region when they are literals, and the region and account of its provider block possible Crossplane objects Each object whose <group>/<Kind> the catalog lists: its crossplane.io/external-name or name, spec.forProvider.region and connection Secret name likely when the workload reads that Secret, else possible
  • A library in a manifest or a resource in the folder proves no call, so those sources stay possible.
  • The SDK major is the client version the service uses. Without a lockfile or an exact range, Pacto leaves it out and never guesses it.
  • A managed resource gets the identity <provider>/<service>/<account>/<region>/<id> only when all four parts are literals in the folder. Otherwise it keeps the catalog identity, such as aws/sqs, and the record lists the parts it misses. A Terraform resource whose id attribute is not a literal is named by its label, and the record lists the id as missing.

docs.title: What Pacto never reads
docs.text:
• A URL keeps its host and port. The user name, password, path and query are stripped before anything stores it.
  • A value under a key named like a password, secret, token, key, credential, private key or DSN is never parsed, and a Secret's values are never read.
  • Compose env_file, .tfstate and .tfstate.backup files, a package-lock.json resolved URL, pom.xml repositories and every Terraform attribute other than the id, region and account are never read.
  • A catalog can never make Pacto read a secret attribute: a sensitive Terraform id attribute is refused when the catalog loads and again before the scan reads it.
  • A symlinked or ignored envs file is never followed.

docs.title: The plan line
docs.text:
init prints one line, then where each external comes from:

External dependencies: 2 (sqs:newsletter-signups, stripe), inferred
  dependencies[newsletter-signups]  external, from infra/main.tf:1 (aws_sqs_queue newsletter-signups, possible)
  dependencies[stripe]              external, from chart/values.yaml:9 (STRIPE_API_BASE) and requirements.txt:1 (stripe, possible)
  catalog default sha256:62a3fd52...
  • A possible external is also named under Unknown, such as infra/main.tf:1 suggests aws/sqs: nothing else in the folder confirms it.
  • Each file Pacto recognizes and does not read is a finding and is counted, so an unread input never reads as "calls nothing": External dependencies: none found in what was read, 2 sources not read, inferred. That covers yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, a Gradle build without gradle.lockfile, setup.py, Pipfile, Pipfile.lock, a pyproject.toml without poetry.lock, a Terraform module, *.tf.json, Terraform state, a symlinked envs file and an organization catalog Pacto cannot pull. A folder too large to read whole, or with more findings than a record keeps, is counted too.
  • A host outside the cluster that no catalog entry identifies is a DISCOVERY_UNRESOLVED finding; declare it in pacto.yaml if the service calls it.

docs.title: Choose the catalog
docs.text:
• The external catalog decides what each host, package, resource type or kind belongs to.
  • init classifies with the default catalog, plus an organization catalog pinned by digest with --external-catalog oci://REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST or PACTO_EXTERNAL_CATALOG. A tag is refused.
  • pacto pack, pacto push and pacto explain read PACTO_EXTERNAL_CATALOG too, so they classify alike.
  • The record lists each catalog digest under inputs.catalog, so a new catalog changes the record and nothing else.
  • When the organization catalog cannot be read, the default classifies alone and Unknown says so.
  • MCP pacto_create uses the catalog the server was started with.

docs.title: Packaging ignore
docs.text: Keep files out of the contract you publish. Put a .pactoignore file next to pacto.yaml, write patterns the way you would in .gitignore, and pacto pack and pacto push leave the matching files out. Use it for build output, editor files and anything secret, such as the sample config you inferred a schema from.

docs.title: Example .pactoignore
docs.text:
# Build artifacts
dist/
build/
*.log

# Editor files
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp

# Temporary files
tmp/
*.tmp

# Large binaries not needed in the bundle
data/*.bin

# Include specific exception
!data/config.bin

The final !data/config.bin re-includes one file that an earlier pattern excluded (negation).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
.pactoignore follows the same pattern matching rules as .gitignore:

Pattern Behavior # at start of line Comment (ignored) Blank lines Ignored * Match any number of characters except / ? Match a single character except / [abc] Character class: match a, b or c ** Match zero or more directories / at start Anchor to the contract root / at end Match directories only ! at start Negate the pattern (include matching files even if earlier patterns excluded them)

The last matching pattern wins: if a file matches several, the last one decides whether it is left out or kept.

docs.title: Default ignores
docs.text:
These patterns are always applied, even when no .pactoignore file exists:

  • .git/
  • .pactoignore
  • .DS_Store
  • pacto-plan.md, the plan pacto ci writes on GitLab CI

Note: pacto.lock is not in the default ignore list. When a lockfile is present it ships inside the bundle by default (see the lockfile). To keep it out of a pushed bundle, add an explicit pacto.lock line to .pactoignore.

docs.title: Immutable files
docs.text: pacto.yaml is never ignorable. Listing it in .pactoignore has no effect, because the bundle always includes the contract file.

docs.title: Referenced file validation
docs.text:
Ignoring a file that is referenced by the contract makes pacto validate, pacto pack and pacto push fail. You cannot ship a bundle missing a file it declares.

For example, if your contract references interfaces/openapi.yaml and your .pactoignore contains:

interfaces/openapi.yaml

Then pacto pack and pacto push exit with contract validation failed with N error(s) and nothing more. Under -v both add a debug line carrying the error count, never the file name. To see the message naming the file, run pacto validate: it prints FILE_NOT_FOUND (e.g. interface spec file "interfaces/openapi.yaml" not found in bundle). Neither command reports which ignore pattern excluded it.

The same rule applies to configurations[].schema, policies[].schema and any other file path declared in pacto.yaml.

docs.title: At the repository root
docs.text:
A .pactoignore at the repository root also hides folders from discovery. A directory pattern there, such as services/legacy/, keeps that folder out of pacto ci, pacto fleet --local and pacto dashboard --local. pacto ci names each folder it skips and the line that skipped it:

skipped: services/legacy (from .pactoignore:1)

Discovery also stops 8 levels below the root, and pacto ci and pacto migrate name each folder that limit cuts, as skipped: <folder> (from depth limit 8). Hidden folders, node_modules and vendor are skipped without a line.

Only folders are matched, so pacto.yaml is still always kept inside a bundle. When the repository root is itself a service, its bundle and discovery share this one file. A root .pactoignore that cannot be read stops these commands with an error.

docs.title: Commands affected
docs.text:
.pactoignore is applied by:

  • pacto pack: files matching ignore patterns are excluded from the tar.gz archive
  • pacto push: files matching ignore patterns are excluded from the OCI artifact
  • pacto init: files matching ignore patterns are not read when it drafts a contract from the folder, so none of them lands in the manifests artifact's build command
  • pacto ci and pacto fleet --local: folders matching a directory pattern of the root .pactoignore are not searched for services

Every command that loads a local bundle reads through the ignore filter, so ignored files are invisible to all of them. The commands that validate the bundle (validate, pack, push) hard-fail on a missing referenced file, while graph, diff, doc and explain do not see the file and produce incomplete output. Only pacto pack and pacto push additionally package the filtered file set into the shipped artifact.

docs.title: Pattern examples
docs.text:
• /docs/: anchored: matches docs/ at the contract root only
  • *.log: unanchored: matches build.log and output/build.log
  • tmp/: trailing slash matches only the directory tmp/
  • !README.md after *.md: re-includes README.md; place negations after the broader exclude

docs.title: Pacto for platform engineers
docs.text:
You run the platform other teams deploy to. Pactify a service connects one service to delivery. This page is for the rest of the job: reading any team's contract to see what its service needs to run, such as its kind of workload, whether it keeps data, its APIs, the services it calls and its settings.

How a service is deployed stays in its own Kubernetes files. With delivery, pacto publish ships those files with each version and Flux applies them; the contract only points at them (publish.deploy). The contract says what the service is. Provisioning runs in your platform's tools; Pacto validates the request and shows the result.

docs.title: Your workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R[OCI Registry] --> PL[pacto pull]
    PL --> E[pacto explain]
    PL --> DI[pacto diff]
    PL --> G[pacto graph]
    PL --> GEN[pacto generate]
    GEN --> K[Files a plugin writes]
    DI --> CI[CI Gate]

docs.title: 1. Pull a service contract
docs.text:
pacto pull oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

explain, diff, graph and generate accept oci:// references directly and cache what they download, so this pull step is optional.

A private repository needs credentials first: pacto login <registry>, or an already-authenticated gh for GHCR. Authentication gives the full resolution order.

docs.title: 2. Inspect it
docs.text:
pacto explain oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

See pacto explain for the output format.

docs.title: 3. Check for breaking changes
docs.text:
pacto diff oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.0.0 \
  oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0

It exits non-zero if breaking changes are detected. See Diff and change classification for the full reference and worked examples.

docs.title: 4. Resolve the dependency graph
docs.text:
$ pacto graph oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/payments-api:2.1.0
payments-api@2.1.0
├─ auth-service@2.3.0
│  └─ user-store@1.0.0
└─ notifications@1.0.0 (shared)

Pacto follows each dependency to its own contract in the registry, all the way down, and caches the results. Add --with-references to also show configuration and policy references, or --only-references to show only those.

docs.title: 5. Generate deployment artifacts
docs.text: If you would rather generate Kubernetes files from contracts than keep them by hand, pacto generate <name> runs a plugin program called pacto-plugin-<name> and writes the files it returns. The two official plugins generate parts of an existing contract: openapi-infer writes the OpenAPI document and schema-infer writes the configuration schema. Both need a pacto.yaml in the folder first. To generate deployment files, write your own plugin: a small program in any language that reads a contract as JSON and returns file contents. See Plugin development.

docs.title: Workload type
docs.text: workload Kubernetes resource Notes service Deployment or StatefulSet Based on state.type job Job Runs to completion scheduled CronJob Schedule defined externally

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
The values below, such as shared/persistent, are short for the state.persistence.scope and state.persistence.durability fields, as pacto explain shows them. They describe the service. The table shows one sensible way to map them on Kubernetes:

state.type state.persistence Infrastructure stateless local/ephemeral Deployment, no PVC, free to scale horizontally stateful local/persistent StatefulSet + PVC, stable identity per replica stateful local/ephemeral StatefulSet with emptyDir (stable identity, no durable storage) stateful shared/persistent Network-attached or shared storage hybrid local/persistent StatefulSet + PVC, tolerates cold starts hybrid local/ephemeral Deployment with emptyDir, warm caches improve performance

The contract leaves out upgrade strategy, shutdown timing, replica counts and autoscaling on purpose. Those stay in your Kubernetes files.

docs.title: Offerings and infrastructure
docs.text: Publish a contract for each kind of infrastructure you offer, with service.offering, a provisioning schema in configurations[], platform rules in policies[] and a service.lifecycle when a version is on its way out. Developers request a resource by referencing that contract from their own and writing values your schema checks. Your adapter reads the published consumer contract, provisions the resource and reports its state as signed evidence. See Provision infrastructure through contracts.

docs.title: Add your own capability
docs.text:
Any platform team can offer its own capability, such as an image scanner, a database service or an environment manager, as an ordinary provider contract. The demo's security-scanning offering, provided by platform-security, is the example:

  1. Choose a service.offering slug. The slug is open: any lowercase name works, such as security-scanning.
  2. Publish the provider contract with a configuration schema that consumers fill in. platform-security declares a scan configuration with level and failOn.
  3. Write an adapter that reads each consumer contract, does the work and reports what it provisioned as ResourceProvisioned evidence with pacto evidence provisioned.
  4. Give the adapter its own signing key and scope it to your provider repositories with allowedProviderRepos, so it can never mark another team's resource Ready. See Trust store and trust config.

To govern the slugs your organization uses, publish a policy whose schema restricts service.offering and reference it from every provider contract:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "service": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "offering": { "enum": ["postgresql", "security-scanning"] }
      }
    }
  }
}

policies:
  - name: offerings
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/acme/platform-offerings-policy:1.0.0

docs.title: What Pacto shows for your capability
docs.text:
The offering page and pacto fleet entity offering <slug> list your providers, their consumers and the adapters that reported on their requests. A request reads Unknown until a current report arrives. A report from an unsigned target-state file reads "Ready (unsigned)" and never counts as positive. unresolvedUses counts the declared references that may name your provider but did not resolve.

Delivery appliers and operation types are built in. Extension capabilities (capabilities[].type: extension) stay unverified, so report a scanner's verdict as provisioning or runtime evidence. Pacto skips a generated MCP tool of a provider bundle whose name starts with pacto_; see Bundle capabilities.

docs.title: Golden paths
docs.text: Publish a golden path for each kind of service your teams start often: a contract with service.template, the offerings it requires and the plugins it offers to run, signed with pacto publish. Developers create services from it with pacto init --from, and the fleet links each one back to its path. See Create a service from a golden path.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration and policy: the full reference
  • Composition patterns: root + component contracts, infrastructure contracts, published policy + schema bundles and the rest
  • Diff and change classification: what counts as breaking
  • Put it in your repository: using Pacto in pipelines
  • GitHub Actions integration: the reusable workflow
  • Fleet views: all your services at once (dashboard, pacto fleet, terminal UI)
  • Kubernetes operator: checks running services against their contracts, including what they actually do on the network
  • The operational graph: the fleet-wide read model
  • For developers: the other side of the same contract

docs.title: Platform offerings reference
docs.text: This page covers how the operational graph groups services by offering. Offering availability and lifecycle covers availability, deprecated providers, observed callers and impact, and the operational graph reference covers sources and queries.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A service's platform offering and summary are the service.offering and service.summary of its newest valid revision, by the rule business domains use. With no such revision the service takes the offering the operator read from each target's contract (status.contract.offering and status.contract.summary). When those operators report different offerings, the service has none and the graph raises an OFFERING_CONFLICT limitation. Different summaries leave the summary empty with no limitation.

Each distinct offering is an offering entity. The offering filter keeps the services that provide it. Only a query for the offering kind returns them.

An offering's detail lists its providers and its consumers:

  • each provider with its owner, summary, current revision, versions, interfaces, configuration and policies, at most 25 providers with the true total;
  • each consumer that reaches a provider through a dependency, a configuration reference or a policy reference, with the range status of a dependency, the provider's lifecycle and the provisioning status of each environment.

Each provider says where its membership comes from in offeringProvenance: declared when a contract revision declares the offering, observed when only the operators observing its targets report it.

The dashboard marks a provider owner that no revision Pacto read declares.

docs.title: The Offerings list
docs.text:
Each offering row of pacto fleet entities --kind offering, pacto_fleet_entities and the dashboard's Offerings list carries:

  • owner: the providers' owner, "2 owners claim it" when they disagree or "declared by contacts only" for one owner that names no team or DRI;
  • lifecycle: the worst lifecycle over the providers' current revisions, each the newest revision a target runs, else the newest readable one (supported, deprecated or sunset); unknown when a provider is observed only, the revision a target runs is unreadable or a provider is hidden from the viewer;
  • hiddenProviders: under a restricted view, the providers the viewer may not see, which owner, consumers and failedRequests leave out;
  • availability and availabilityProvenance: the offering's availability roll-up and where its worst environment comes from;
  • consumers: distinct declared consumers, and hiddenConsumers under a restricted view, where consumers and failedRequests are lower bounds;
  • failedRequests: distinct consumers with a Failed provisioning status;
  • targets: the providers' observed targets, or targetsUnknown: true with no count when a provider's targets are hidden or a target source is incomplete. Pacto prints "observed targets unknown", never 0.

The lifecycle filter (deprecated or sunset) and the failed filter narrow the list; --sort failed (the most consumers with a failed request first) and --sort consumers order it. The aggregate tallies every matched offering's provisioning statuses by phase in offeringPhases and offeringPhaseConsumers, and names the three offerings with the most failures in failedByOffering, where services counts the consumers whose request failed. The dashboard draws that tally as the phase track above the list.

docs.title: Consumers
docs.text:
The consumes filter keeps the services with a resolved dependency or configuration reference on a provider of an offering; the dashboard's View all consumers link, pacto fleet entities --consumes and the consumes argument of pacto_fleet_entities use it. With --phase, it keeps the consumers with a provisioning status of that offering in that phase, and --environment narrows those statuses to one environment, such as pacto fleet entities --kind service --consumes postgresql --phase failed --environment production. That answer carries a PROVISIONING_ENVIRONMENT_SCOPED limitation: consumers whose current revision does not declare the environment have no provisioning status there.

A service's detail lists the offerings it consumes (consumedOfferings) and, separately, inferred suggestions (inferredOfferings). A suggestion is an external or unresolved dependency whose name exactly matches an offering or a provider's name, ignoring case. Suggestions are never counted as consumption. A use of a provider that declares no offering joins consumedOfferings, with offering empty, once a provider reports on it. The service's hiddenProviders is a lower bound on the resources from providers you may not see. See Resources a service consumes.
