A golden path never consumes: the offerings its contract reaches are the requirements of the services created from it. Its detail lists them as requirements with the same entries a consumer's consumedOfferings carries, and the consumes filter and the offering's consumer list leave the path out. See the golden paths reference.

docs.title: Unresolved uses
docs.text: unresolvedUses counts declared dependency, configuration and policy references that may name a provider but did not resolve, so the consumer list leaves them out. The match is inferred. Each consumer counts once per reference type and repository, hidden services included. Above 0 the answer carries OFFERING_USES_UNRESOLVED and is partial.

docs.title: Consume snippet
docs.text:
Each provider carries a consume snippet to add to a contract, built from its newest readable revision, the one the offering page shows as current:

  • a dependencies entry when the provider declares a workload or an interface, with compatibility set to the widest caret range that admits the newest version: ^<major>.0.0, ^0.<minor>.0 for a 0.x version or the version itself for a prerelease. A version that is not semver gets an empty compatibility to fill in;
  • a configurations entry per required configuration, with ref pinned to the current version, a configuration selector when the provider declares more than one and a values skeleton of the schema's required properties. Each property gets the first candidate the schema accepts: its default, its first enum value, the minimum of a number or the empty value of its type. A property no candidate satisfies is left out of values, written as a comment line such as # storageGi: required integer, set a value and named in missingValues;
  • a policies entry named after the provider when the provider declares a policy or ships policy/schema.json, and neither entry above applies.

The snippet carries the same entries twice: as YAML in yaml and as structured contract entries in entries (dependency, configurations and policy), so an agent can add them without parsing YAML. The dependency ref is the provider's registry repository without a tag or digest. A deprecated current revision adds a comment saying so. A provider that is not published to a registry has no snippet.

docs.title: Provider versions
docs.text: pacto fleet versions <offering>, pacto_fleet_versions and the offering page list each provider's versions, newest first, with whether a target runs each one and the service lifecycle it declares. With a range, such as ^16.0.0, each version carries rangeStatus (satisfied, unsatisfied or unknown) and each provider names its latestCompatible version, checked the way a dependency's range is checked. The list comes from the contract revisions the snapshot holds, and its completeness is fleet: the registry may publish other versions. An OCI-sourced fleet lists what the registry holds, and pacto lock resolves a range against the registry.

docs.title: Provisioning status
docs.text:
A provider adapter reports the state of a resource a consumer asked for as ResourceProvisioned evidence: a signed EvidenceSet through an Evidence Server, or an unsigned report in a v2 target-state file. Pacto joins reports onto the offering's uses at query time, one status per environment, with the provider, external reference, producer, signing key, source, report time and verified, true only for signed reports. Every environment the consumer's current revision declares has a status. A use whose consumer points more than one configuration or dependency at the provider has one status per entry, named in entry. Only a signed Ready is positive: badges and tallies show any other Ready as "Ready (unsigned)" in the info tone, and phases.readyUnsigned counts them.

A status reads a phase only from a current report. It reads Unknown, with a reason and the phase the newest report gave in reportedPhase, when:

  • no provider has reported for that use;
  • the newest report is older than the freshness window, or 24 hours when --freshness is 0;
  • the report's outcome is not Observed;
  • the newest report is about another revision of the consumer, so a provider switch never inherits the old provider's Ready;
  • two current reports, fresh and about the current consumer revision, from different producers or sources disagree, which also raises a PROVISIONING_CONFLICT limitation and lists their phases in conflict.

Reports are ordered by the time the Evidence Server accepted them, and reports from a file by their observedAt. A report dated more than five minutes after it was accepted, or after the snapshot time for a file, is rejected. Reports that name no revision in the snapshot, or a use that revision does not resolve, are dropped and counted in one PROVISIONING_UNMATCHED limitation, and a snapshot keeps at most 10000 reports (PROVISIONING_TRUNCATED).

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text:
An offering's adapters lists up to 10 programs that report on its requests, by slug, producer and signature, from current reports, else the newest. Adapters are observed, from visible consumers' reports only.

Field Meaning provider The adapter slug the reports carry, free text the adapter picks. A report with no slug reads "unnamed adapter" producer, verified The producer that sent the reports and whether they were signed environments, phases The environments its reports cover and the phase of each request, as the badge shows it if its own current report agrees, else Unknown disagrees Requests where its report disagrees with another adapter's, so the status is Unknown lastReportedAt When its newest report was observed total, count, truncated Every adapter that reports, how many items lists and whether the list stops short of total items The adapters, signed first, then by slug (an empty slug last) and producer conflicting Requests whose adapters disagree; each of those adapters is listed unattributed Requests no adapter reported on

docs.title: Offerings under a restricted view
docs.text:
A viewer restricted to some namespaces sees a provider that has no Kubernetes target, with its owner, offering and versions, when its contract declares the offering and every Kubernetes source is available. All of that provider's targets are removed from the view and its versions omit inUse. Any provider with a target in a namespace the viewer cannot read omits inUse too. With a Kubernetes source unavailable or partial, the absence of a target proves nothing, so the provider stays hidden.

A consumer the viewer cannot see is never named: the offering counts them in hiddenConsumers, and its provisioning statuses, external references and namespace stay hidden. A PROVISIONING_CONFLICT reflects only the reports the viewer can see, and PROVISIONING_TRUNCATED counts only the dropped reports about visible consumers. A visible consumer whose configuration reference resolves to a hidden provider has the reference validated again without it, so the reference reads CONFIG_REF_UNVERIFIED and no finding carries what the hidden provider declares.

Availability, observed callers and offering impact count what a restricted view hides; see Under a restricted view.

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text:
A plugin turns a contract into files: Helm charts, Terraform, Kubernetes manifests, a README. It is a separate program, written in any language. pacto generate <name> sends it the contract as JSON on stdin, and the plugin answers with a list of files on stdout. The Bash example below is a complete, working plugin.

A plugin is also one seam for infrastructure adapters: it can turn a consumer contract that references an infrastructure contract into the files your provisioning tool applies. See Provision infrastructure through contracts.

A golden path names the plugins it offers under service.template.plugins. pacto init --from runs only the ones you name with --run-plugins, over a temporary copy of the new service's files, and adds the files they return. See Create a service from a golden path.

docs.title: Official plugins
docs.text:
Plugin Description pacto-plugin-schema-infer Infers a JSON Schema from sample configuration files (JSON, YAML, TOML) pacto-plugin-openapi-infer Extracts OpenAPI 3.1 specs from source code (FastAPI, Huma)

Both read files you already have and write contract inputs, so you can skip writing a schema by hand. Pacto ships no deployment-artifact plugin. To use pacto generate helm, write or install a pacto-plugin-helm yourself. Without a pacto-plugin-helm on your PATH it exits 1 with plugin "helm" not found (looked for pacto-plugin-helm in $PATH and ~/.config/pacto/plugins/).

See Installation for how to install them. Refer to each plugin's README for usage:

  • pacto-plugin-schema-infer
  • pacto-plugin-openapi-infer

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Pacto loads the contract, finds the plugin program (pacto-plugin-<name>), writes a request to its stdin, reads the response from its stdout and writes the files. A plugin gets a copy of the contract and cannot change it. Pacto stops a plugin after 60 seconds or 64 MB of output.

docs.title: Plugin discovery
docs.text: Pacto searches for pacto-plugin-<name> in $PATH, then ~/.config/pacto/plugins/. Not found is an error: pacto generate helm without pacto-plugin-helm exits 1.

docs.title: Request (stdin)
docs.text:
Pacto writes a JSON object to the plugin's stdin:

{
  "protocolVersion": "1",
  "contract": {
    "pactoVersion": "2.0",
    "service": {
      "name": "my-service",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    },
    "interfaces": [...],
    "workload": "service",
    "state": {...},
    ...
  },
  "bundleDir": "my-service",
  "outputDir": "helm-output",
  "options": {
    "namespace": "production"
  }
}
Field Type Description protocolVersion string Always "1" contract object The full parsed contract bundleDir string Path to the bundle (may be relative) outputDir string Path for output files (may be relative) options object Optional. User-provided key-value options from --option key=value

docs.title: Response (stdout)
docs.text:
The plugin writes a JSON object to stdout:

{
  "files": [
    {
      "path": "deployment.yaml",
      "content": "apiVersion: apps/v1\nkind: Deployment\n..."
    },
    {
      "path": "service.yaml",
      "content": "apiVersion: v1\nkind: Service\n..."
    }
  ],
  "message": "Generated Kubernetes manifests for my-service"
}
Field Type Description files array List of generated files files[].path string Relative path within output directory files[].content string File content message string Optional message

files[].path must be relative. Absolute paths and .. are rejected. On error, write to stderr and exit non-zero.

docs.title: Example: Minimal plugin in Bash
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# pacto-plugin-readme: generates a README from a Pacto contract

set -euo pipefail

# Read the full JSON request from stdin
REQUEST=$(cat)

# Extract fields using jq
NAME=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.service.name')
VERSION=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.service.version')
WORKLOAD=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.workload // "n/a"')
STATE=$(echo "$REQUEST" | jq -r '.contract.state.type // "n/a"')

# Generate a README
CONTENT="# ${NAME}

**Version:** ${VERSION}
**Workload:** ${WORKLOAD}
**State:** ${STATE}

This file was auto-generated by pacto-plugin-readme.
"

# Write the response JSON to stdout
jq -n \
  --arg path "README.md" \
  --arg content "$CONTENT" \
  --arg msg "Generated README for ${NAME}" \
  '{files: [{path: $path, content: $content}], message: $msg}'

Make it executable and place it in your $PATH:

chmod +x pacto-plugin-readme
mv pacto-plugin-readme /usr/local/bin/
pacto generate readme my-service

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Read only from bundleDir. Do not access files outside the bundle.
  • Write only to stdout. Do not write files directly; return them in the response. Pacto handles file creation.
  • Follow the protocol. Return clean relative paths, write errors to stderr and exit non-zero on failure.
  • Be deterministic. Given the same input, produce the same output.
  • Handle missing optional fields. Only pactoVersion and service are required, so a contract may omit workload, state, configurations, dependencies or capabilities.

docs.title: Provider reports
docs.text: A provider adapter tells Pacto about the resources a consumer's contract asks for: their phase with the ResourceProvisioned observation kind and their usage and cost with ResourceUsage. Both arrive as signed EvidenceSets, and each needs a key granted that kind by name. Every provider is optional: with no report a resource reads Unknown and its usage reads not reported.

docs.title: Provisioning reports
docs.text:
A provider adapter reports the state of a resource with the ResourceProvisioned observation kind. The report is about the consumer's contract revision, and its observation subject is the consumer's configuration or dependency that asked for the resource. Decoding rejects any key beyond these four:

Key Meaning provider A lowercase slug of at most 63 bytes naming the provider. Pacto keeps no list of providers. externalRef Optional. An opaque handle of the resource at the provider, at most 253 printable bytes. Viewers of the consumer see it; a URL with credentials is rejected. phase Requested, Provisioning, Ready, Failed or Deleting. environment Optional. The consumer environment the resource serves, a lowercase slug.

Any other outcome carries no payload; the observation's subject.environment names its environment. pacto evidence provisioned writes the EvidenceSet; sign and send it like any other:

pacto evidence provisioned \
  --contract oci://registry.example.com/acme/orders@sha256:<digest> \
  --configuration database --environment production \
  --provider my-platform --phase Ready \
  --external-ref databases/orders-production > report.json

The subject defaults to <repository>/<environment or default>/<kind>/<name>, one per resource: the server keeps the latest report per producer and subject.

The server accepts a provisioning report only when:

  • its key lists ResourceProvisioned in allowedObservationKinds;
  • the EvidenceSet carries only ResourceProvisioned observations;
  • its subject starts with the consumer's repository path, so the key's allowedSubjects globs scope which consumers it reports for;
  • each observation names a configuration reference or a dependency the consumer declares, in an environment it declares;
  • when its key sets allowedProviderRepos, that configuration reference or dependency is an oci:// ref to a provider repository under one of them;
  • it is dated no more than five minutes after the server accepted it.

The server evaluates no compliance findings for a provisioning report and lists it under provisioning on the targets endpoint, never as a target. The operational graph joins it onto the offering's uses. A v2 target-state file carries the same reports unsigned, for tests and demos.

docs.title: Usage reports
docs.text:
A provider adapter reports how much of a resource a consumer uses, and what it costs, with the ResourceUsage observation kind. Its subject is the consumer's configuration or dependency, as in a provisioning report. Decoding rejects any key beyond these five:

Key Meaning provider A lowercase slug of at most 63 bytes naming the provider. externalRef Optional. The resource's handle at the provider, with the provisioning report's rules. environment Optional. The consumer environment the resource serves, a lowercase slug. metrics Up to 16 of {name, value, unit}: a lowercase slug, a number from 0 to 10^18 and an optional unit of at most 16 printable bytes. cost Optional. {amount, currency, period}: a decimal string such as 212.40, an ISO 4217 code and an ISO 8601 period of one unit (D, W, M or Y) from P1D to P1Y, so P30D or P1M but never P1M15D.

A report carries at least one metric or a cost. pacto evidence usage writes the EvidenceSet:

pacto evidence usage \
  --contract oci://registry.example.com/acme/orders@sha256:<digest> \
  --configuration database --environment production --provider my-platform \
  --metric storage-used=31:Gi --cost 212.40:USD:P30D > usage.json

The subject defaults to <repository>/<environment or default>/usage/<kind>/<name>. The server keeps the latest report per producer and subject, so only usage subjects hold the usage segment and a usage report never replaces a provisioning report. Otherwise the provisioning rules above apply, with ResourceUsage in place of ResourceProvisioned.

The targets endpoint lists usage under usage with schema pacto.dev/evidence-source/v4 (v5 when the response also names a cluster), written only when it holds usage, so a v3 reader keeps working. The operational graph shows a figure as reported only when one signed, fresh report about the newest consumer revision that uses the resource, named as revision, is contradicted by no other producer. An unsigned, stale or foreign report reads unknown, with its figures apart as reported; disagreeing reports read unknown, name the producers under conflict and give no figures. Pacto never sums or converts a cost, and usage never changes a service's compliance. A v2 target-state file carries usage reports unsigned, so they always read unknown.

docs.title: Provision infrastructure through contracts
docs.text:
A platform team publishes a contract for each kind of infrastructure it offers, such as a PostgreSQL database. A developer who needs one references that contract from the service's own contract and writes the values the provider lets them control. The consumer contract is the request. Pacto validates it against the provider's published schema, and your platform's tools provision the resource. Pacto then shows what those tools report back.

This guide follows the PostgreSQL offering of the demo from both sides.

docs.title: Publish an infrastructure contract
docs.text:
An infrastructure contract describes what consumers may ask for:

pactoVersion: "2.4"
service:
  name: postgresql
  version: 16.1.0
  offering: postgresql
  summary: Primary relational database for transactional data
  owner:
    team: infra-data
  lifecycle:
    deprecated: "2026-11-01"
    sunset: "2027-06-30"
    successor: oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/postgresql:17.0.0
workload: service
configurations:
  - name: provisioning
    schema: configuration/provisioning.schema.json
    required: true
policies:
  - name: database-standards
    schema: policy/schema.json
  • configurations[] holds the provisioning schema: the fields a consumer controls, their types, ranges and defaults. In the demo a consumer chooses size and storageGi and may turn on highAvailability and backups.
  • policies[] holds the platform rules every consumer contract must meet.
  • service.lifecycle announces a deprecation, a sunset date and a successor. Consumers are warned with DEPENDENCY_SERVICE_DEPRECATED and DEPENDENCY_SERVICE_SUNSET.
  • service.offering and service.summary list the contract on the dashboard's Offerings page, in pacto fleet search --offering postgresql and in pacto_fleet_search.

Publish each version with pacto push or pacto publish. Each published version is the platform interface consumers pin.

docs.title: Consume it
docs.text:
Developers find the offering on the Offerings page or with pacto fleet versions postgresql --range '^16.0.0' and pacto_fleet_versions. Each version shows its lifecycle and whether it satisfies the range. The list comes from the contract revisions the fleet holds, and the registry may publish others. The Offerings page also gives a snippet to copy, built from the version it shows as current.

A consumer uses both forms:

pactoVersion: "2.4"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/postgresql
    required: true
    compatibility: ^16.0.0
configurations:
  - name: database
    ref: oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/postgresql:16.1.0
    configuration: provisioning
    required: true
    values:
      size: medium
      storageGi: 50
environments:
  - name: production
    file: environments/production.yaml

The dependency carries the version range and puts the consumer in impact answers. The configuration reference carries the request. configuration selects one of the provider's configurations and may be omitted when the provider declares exactly one. Inline values are the defaults, and each environment file merges its own values on top:

# environments/production.yaml
database:
  highAvailability: true
  backups:
    retentionDays: 14

pacto validate fetches the referenced contract and checks the inline values and every environment's merged values against the selected schema. When the reference cannot be fetched, validation fails with CONFIG_REF_UNRESOLVED, so values are never accepted unchecked. pacto lock pins the reference to a digest in pacto.lock, which the fleet needs to resolve the reference.

docs.title: Request provisioning
docs.text:
Publish the consumer contract. That published revision is the request: it names the provider version, the selected configuration and the values for each environment. An adapter in your platform reads it and provisions the resource. Pacto itself provisions nothing and keeps no provider-specific code.

The request takes three steps: edit the contract, publish it and promote it. pacto_edit with add_configuration_refs returns them before anything else runs:

  • impact: who the edit affects, read from the session's fleet snapshot, with completeness and asOf. Without a snapshot it is absent, and the first step says who the edit affects is not known.
  • chain: each remaining step with its tool and its CLI command (pacto impact, pacto publish --plan, pacto publish, pacto delivery plan). A step this session does not serve leaves tool empty.
  • executor: who acts on the published revision, here the provider's adapter.

docs.title: Write an adapter
docs.text:
An adapter is any program that turns a published consumer contract into a resource: a CI job, a controller or a script. It:

  1. Maps the offering slug, postgresql, to your implementation. The mapping lives in the adapter; the contract carries no provider hints.
  2. Reads the consumer's values for each environment from pacto explain <consumer> --output-format json. Each entry of configurations carries environmentValues: the inline values with that environment's file merged on top. Objects merge key by key, and a null removes its key.
  3. Provisions the resource with your platform's tools.
  4. Reports the result:
pacto evidence provisioned \
  --contract oci://ghcr.io/acme/orders@sha256:<digest> \
  --configuration database --environment production \
  --provider my-platform --phase Ready \
  --external-ref databases/orders-production > report.json
pacto evidence sign report.json --key adapter.key --key-id adapter-2026 \
  --producer platform-adapter --sequence 42 > envelope.json
pacto evidence send envelope.json \
  --url https://evidence.example.com/api/evidence/v1/envelopes

--phase is one of Requested, Provisioning, Ready, Failed or Deleting. Use --dependency instead of --configuration when the resource answers a dependency. The subject defaults to the full repository path, the environment (or default), the kind and the name, such as ghcr.io/acme/orders/production/configuration/database. Keep one subject per resource so each resource keeps its own latest report.

Give the adapter its own key. A key may report ResourceProvisioned only when its trust entry lists it, so a team's runtime key cannot mark its own database Ready. allowedProviderRepos scopes the key to the provider repositories the adapter serves, so it cannot mark another team's resource Ready:

apiVersion: pacto.dev/evidence-trust/v1
keys:
  - keyId: adapter-2026
    producerId: platform-adapter
    publicKeyFile: platform-adapter__adapter-2026.pub
    allowedObservationKinds: [ResourceProvisioned]
    allowedContractRepos: [ghcr.io/acme]
    allowedProviderRepos: [ghcr.io/acme/platform/postgresql]

The Evidence Server stores each report on the consumer revision it is about, so that revision must be one of its --subject values. Its targets endpoint lists consumer contracts, producers and external references: keep it behind the same network and auth boundary as the dashboard. See Evidence for the trust store and the Evidence Server.

On Kubernetes, put that trust config in the operator's trust Secret next to the public keys and set evidence.trust.configKey to its key; see Provisioning reports. Without it, the operator's Evidence Server trusts each public key for runtime evidence only and rejects ResourceProvisioned reports.

Plugins are another seam: pacto generate hands a contract to a program that writes files, such as the manifests your provisioning tool applies.

docs.title: Follow provisioning status
docs.text:
The dashboard's Offerings page, pacto fleet entity offering postgresql and pacto_fleet_entity show each consumer's provisioning status per environment, with its producer, source and report time. Every environment the consumer declares has a status, and a consumer that points two entries at one provider gets a status for each. Unknown means Pacto cannot say; it is neither failure nor success. The status is Unknown when:

  • no provider has reported for that use;
  • the newest report is older than the freshness window, 24 hours by default;
  • the provider reported an outcome other than Observed;
  • the newest report is for an older revision of the consumer;
  • two producers with current reports disagree, which also adds a PROVISIONING_CONFLICT limitation.

Reports from a target-state file show as unsigned. A viewer restricted to some namespaces sees a provider with no Kubernetes target, its owner and versions, and none of its targets. Consumers the viewer may not read appear only as a count, with their provisioning status hidden, and a conflict reflects only the reports the viewer can see.

docs.title: Resources a service consumes
docs.text:
The service page's Resources section, pacto fleet entity service <key> and pacto_fleet_entity list every resource a service consumes, one row per provider and kind of use. A use of a provider that declares no offering appears once a provider reports on it. Each row carries:

Field Shows Provenance provider, offering The provider, linked, and its offering or none declared providerOwner, providerAvailability Who owns the provider and whether it answers where it runs, apart from this resource's phase declared, observed requested The configuration entry, provider revision and values the service asks for, on the configuration-reference row only declared provisioning The phase per environment, with the adapter, signed or unsigned and the report time observed consumption Usage and cost per environment: reported with the provider's figures, unknown with a reason, or not-reported observed

The CLI prints the same facts in its Resources block. A provider adapter reports usage and cost with usage reports. Only one signed, fresh report about the newest revision that uses the resource (revision) reads reported. Any other reads unknown: an untrusted report's figures sit under reported, disagreeing producers under conflict. For live utilization, ask Mira: with Mira configured, the dashboard links the service to it, and the MCP instructions point at Mira's query_metric.

A resource's phase is its lifecycle, never the service's health: a Failed resource leaves the service's compliance unchanged. It raises an item in the provisioning attention category instead: PROVISIONING_FAILED when a provider reports Failed and PROVISIONING_STALE when the last report about the current revision is older than the freshness window. A resource that no provider ever reported on stays Unknown and raises nothing.

A restricted viewer never sees a provider it may not read. The service's hiddenProviders says at least that many resources come from such providers, counted from the service's own contract and reports, and an environment they may provision in reads Unknown. A Failed or stale report about such a provider raises attention without naming the adapter or external reference; its usage and cost stay out.

docs.title: Use the resource
docs.text:
Each status also shows the provider's external reference for that environment, such as databases/orders-production, and links the resource to the consuming service. The adapter delivers the connection details as a ConfigMap or Secret. On Kubernetes, the consumer's Pacto CR binds that object to the configuration with spec.target.configBindings:

spec:
  target:
    configBindings:
      - configuration: database
        kind: Secret
        name: orders-database

The operator then checks that the object exists. It never reads Secret values. See Configuration and policy.

docs.title: Update or retire
docs.text:
To change a request, edit its values and publish the consumer contract again; pacto_edit sets environment values with set_environment_values. To retire it, remove the configuration reference with remove_configuration_refs and publish. Both edits return the same impact, chain and executor, also with dry_run.

Resize or delete runs in the provider's tools. pacto_edit refuses a request the provider's schema rejects, and pacto validate and push fail on it.

When the platform team ships a new provider version, pacto impact and pacto_impact list every consumer by dependency and by configuration reference. Impact checks a reference consumer's values against the new schema, also when it declares a dependency, so a breaking change never clears on its behalf and values the new schema rejects block it where the consumer runs. Pacto shows the declared lifecycle and the provider's latest report.

docs.title: Publish from CI with pacto ci --publish
docs.text:
On a merged commit, pacto ci --publish builds, signs and publishes every changed service of a repository, providers before the services that depend on them. It runs the engine pacto publish runs, one service at a time, so a single-folder pacto publish behaves like one row of it.

pacto ci                    # the plan: what changed and the version each would publish
pacto ci --publish          # on the merged commit: publish every changed service

A contract needs neither service.version nor a publish section. When it declares them, Pacto uses them as written; when it leaves them out, Pacto derives them from the folder and the registry and records each derived value in the inferred record with its source. Pacto never writes them into pacto.yaml.

docs.title: What Pacto derives
docs.text:
Value Derived from Recorded as service.version The newest verified version in the bundle repository and the change since it field service.version, source registry:<repo>@sha256:<digest> How the image is built The one build tool the folder shows field publish.build, source <file>:<line> What deploys the service The folder's Kustomization, Helm chart or manifests field publish.deploy, source <file>:<line> An image built elsewhere --image or a workload image pinned by digest field publish.build, source flag:--image or <manifest>:<line> The repositories The registry pacto ci resolved, and the service name bundle <registry>/<name> (or <registry>/contracts/<name> when the image already lives at <registry>/<name>), image <registry>/images/<name> unless the workload's image is under the registry, deploy <registry>/deploy/<name>

A service that depends on one with a derived section sets the dependency's ref to that bundle repository, such as oci://ghcr.io/acme/contracts/ledger when the ledger image lives at ghcr.io/acme/ledger.

docs.title: The derived version
docs.text:
The baseline is the highest final release in the bundle repository whose signature verifies against the publisher identity. Pacto compares the folder with it, using the same classification as pacto diff:

The bundle repository holds Pacto publishes No version 1.0.0 A baseline, and the folder has not changed nothing: the row reads unchanged A baseline and a NON_BREAKING change the next patch, such as 1.4.2 to 1.4.3 A baseline and a POTENTIAL_BREAKING change the next minor, such as 1.4.2 to 1.5.0 A baseline and a BREAKING change the next major (before 1.0, the next minor) A higher tag whose signature does not verify the version above it, with the note ignored <version>: no signature by the publisher identity Tags and none verifies nothing: the service fails with no verifiable baseline in <repo> No version, while the other bundle repository of the layout holds some nothing: the service fails with bundle repository moved: <repo> holds versions A release candidate above the baseline that the derived version does not satisfy nothing: declare service.version to publish a candidate line

A declared service.version publishes as written, and one too small for the change still fails, as with pacto publish. Its row reads unchanged only when the bundle at that version is signed by the publisher identity and its deploy artifact is there.

docs.title: How the image is built
docs.text:
Pacto runs each program directly, never through a shell, in the service folder.

Tool Found by What Pacto runs Skaffold skaffold.yaml with one artifact skaffold build --push=false, then docker image save ko .ko.yaml ko build --push=false --bare --sbom=none --oci-layout-path=... Jib pom.xml or build.gradle[.kts] naming the Jib plugin ./mvnw or mvn jib:buildTar; ./gradlew or gradle jibBuildTar buildpacks project.toml pack build, then docker image save Dockerfile one Dockerfile docker buildx build into an OCI layout

Skaffold wins when the folder holds it, because it drives the others. Any other pair is a finding that asks for --image or a publish section, such as finding: services/api: both ko (.ko.yaml) and Dockerfile found; pass --image or declare publish. A folder with no build tool needs --image too. pacto publish --plan checks that each program and docker (for Skaffold and buildpacks) is installed before anything is built.

--image <service>=<repo>@sha256:<digest>, or a workload image already pinned by digest, skips the build. The deploy artifact pins that digest, and Pacto writes, signs and copies nothing in the image's repository.

docs.title: What the deploy artifact holds
docs.text:
Pacto assembles the deploy artifact itself from one deploy source per folder; two sources are a finding that asks for a publish section. It reads the folder through the root .pactoignore and pins the image by digest.

Source What ships Plain manifests Each file under its folder path, each image: of the built repository set to <repo>@<digest> Kustomization The kustomization no other one names, and only the files its resources, patches, components and configMapGenerator name, at their folder paths, each kustomization with an images: entry for the digest. A kustomization in a subfolder, such as k8s/, keeps that path, so the applier reads the artifact from it Helm chart The chart packaged as a .tgz, filtered by .helmignore, with version and appVersion set to the service version and the image digest in values.yaml. The chart is the deploy artifact delivery/pacto.yaml Ships with the version filled in: as pacto-resource.yaml beside the manifests, also added to the root kustomization's resources, or as the chart's templates/pacto-resource.yaml

Pacto leaves out, with a plan note:

  • every file holding a kind: Secret;
  • a kustomization with a secretGenerator, and the files and env files it names;
  • a chart's per-environment values-<env>.yaml files;
  • files listed in .pactoignore.

A symbolic link, or a Kustomization path outside the folder, fails the service. Every file Pacto would ship is scanned for sensitive literal values, such as a password in a ConfigMap or a chart's values: a hit fails that service and names the file. A values key that only names a Secret, such as existingSecret: my-secret, can be a hit too; move it to a values-<env>.yaml file, which never ships.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
The contract Pacto signs with Declares no publish.sign, or no publish section keyless, as the identity the CI's OIDC token names Declares sign.key or sign.kms that key Declares sign.keyless with identity and issuer keyless, verified against that identity Declares no publish section, with --sign-key <file> that key; add --no-transparency-log to keep its signatures out of the public log

The identity read from the token:

CI Token Identity GitHub Actions permissions: id-token: write https://github.com/ + job_workflow_ref. When that names a reusable workflow of another repository, such as pacto-actions, an earlier version verifies when that workflow at any commit, or a workflow of your repository, signed it on the repository and branch the token names GitLab CI an id_tokens entry named SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN with aud: sigstore https:// + ci_config_ref_uri Other SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN the token's email claim, else declare publish.sign.identity

The row prints the identity it signed as. Pacto verifies each new signature against it before any tag is written. --sign-key, --image and --registry apply only to a contract that declares no publish section, and --no-transparency-log needs --sign-key.

docs.title: What it refuses
docs.text:
• A pull or merge request pipeline: refused: pull request pipelines do not publish; publish runs on the merged commit, before any token is asked for or anything is built.
  • A stale checkout: superseded: <service> <version> was published from <revision>, which this checkout does not contain. In a shallow clone without that commit, Pacto compares the commit times; a baseline published before this check says fetch more history to check and the publish goes on.
  • A contract behind the current pactoVersion publishes as the current version when that keeps its meaning, else as written, with a plan line (see Older contracts). One kept behind that declares no publish section or no version fails that service and asks to set the current pactoVersion.

docs.title: Tags, races and order
docs.text:
• Pacto reads each tag before writing it and reads it back after, and reads every tag of the service once more after the deploy tag. A tag another run wrote in between fails that service.
  • A run that loses a derived version to a concurrent run plans again, up to 3 times: payments 1.5.0 published by another run; re-planned and (attempt 2/3). A declared version, or a tag signed by another identity, is never planned again.
  • A registry has no conditional tag write, so two runs writing in the same instant after the final read can still overwrite. Close that window with tag immutability (ECR, GAR, ACR or Harbor) or a CI concurrency: group that runs one publish per repository at a time.
  • A service that fails blocks the services of the run that depend on it. So does a BREAKING change whose new version a consumer's range does not accept; a compatibility: unknown range never counts as accepting. A dependency cycle publishes in name order.

docs.title: Reproducible builds
docs.text: Two runs over the same commit publish byte-identical bundles, charts and manifests. Image builders get SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH: the environment value, else the commit time of HEAD. Without either, the row says not reproducible: no commit time (set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH). Skaffold and buildpacks build through the Docker daemon, so their images are as reproducible as the tool makes them.

docs.title: Output, exit codes and records
docs.text:
Output Content Table One row per service: published, unchanged, failed, blocked or refused, the version and the signing identity --output-format json The plan with each row's state, identity and images Job summary $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY on GitHub, pacto-plan.md on GitLab Images record A signed referrer of each bundle listing every image the deploy pins, with its digest and whether Pacto built it Run record One per published, failed, blocked or refused service; a blocked service is a refusal with reason dependency

The exit status is 0 when every changed service is published or already published, else 1. A run that finds no pacto.yaml, or skips a folder it cannot read, exits 1. To publish one folder by hand, pacto publish takes the same --image, --registry, --sign-key and --no-transparency-log flags; see Publish a version.

docs.title: Publish a breaking change
docs.text: A breaking change needs a new major version (1.4.2 becomes 2.0.0): pacto publish refuses a breaking change with a smaller version. Do not remove fields to get past the check. Raising pactoVersion never hides a breaking change: pacto ci publishes an older contract as the current version only when that keeps its meaning. Announce the break in breaks and each consumer owner accepts it with pacto accept; the gate clears once every consumer accepted. See Ship a breaking change.

docs.title: Publish a version
docs.text:
This page describes pacto publish. To take a new service to its first release, follow Pactify a service. In CI, publish every changed service of a repository with pacto ci --publish, which runs the same engine; After a merge: publish sets it up.

pacto publish publishes what a contract's publish section declares: the contract bundle, the service's images and the manifests or chart an applier deploys, all tagged with the service version. Pacto derives a publish section or a service.version the contract leaves out from the folder and the registry, as pacto ci --publish describes. Pacto pushes, signs and checks.

pacto publish --plan    # what is missing, and what would refuse it; writes nothing
pacto publish           # publish it

publish needs contract format 2.1, which earlier Pacto releases cannot read. Before your first publish, make sure the services that depend on yours run a Pacto and operator that read 2.1: see publish.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Pacto runs no tests. It refuses to publish when one of its own checks fails:

  • the contract is invalid, or uses a local reference or breaks its pacto.lock;
  • the contract does not declare service.name (PUBLISH_NEEDS_SERVICE_NAME). A name Pacto inferred from the folder is never published. An undeclared service.version is derived from the newest verified version in the registry (the rule), while pacto pack and pacto push refuse it (PUBLISH_NEEDS_SERVICE_VERSION);
  • a provider does not meet what a required dependency requires (GUARANTEE_UNMET). Pacto fetches each provider that a dependency declares requires for, as pacto validate does, and --plan shows the unmet guarantee as the failed validation check. An unmet guarantee of an optional dependency and a provider Pacto cannot fetch (GUARANTEE_UNVERIFIED) are warnings: the validation check passes and names them;
  • a configuration reference that a check depends on cannot be fetched (CONFIG_REF_UNRESOLVED), as with an unreachable policy reference, or the values fail the referenced schema. pacto push refuses the same way. A "2.0" to "2.3" reference with no values anywhere only warns; see Resolution and versions;
  • the signing key file would end up inside the bundle, or the signer does not open: a missing key file, a wrong COSIGN_PASSWORD, an unreachable KMS key or, for keyless signing, no OIDC token refuses the plan, before anything is built;
  • there is no source revision (run it in a git checkout, or pass --revision). Pacto reads the commit from .git itself, worktrees and packed refs included;
  • the git checkout has uncommitted changes to tracked files, so the commit stamped and signed on every artifact would not hold what was built. Publish from a clean checkout. This check runs git status; --revision skips it, since you then name the revision yourself. Untracked files are not checked;
  • a dockerfile build has no usable docker buildx builder, a command build's program is not an executable here, or a build tool Pacto detected is not installed;
  • two artifacts, or an artifact and the bundle, share one repository;
  • an SBOM is declared on a dockerfile build, which writes none, or sits in the contract directory without a .pactoignore line (--plan names it);
  • the version is too small for the change.

The signer, the clean checkout and the builders are checked only for what is still to write: a builder for each artifact not yet published, the signer and git status when anything is. Running publish again for a version already published (to --propose it, say) needs none of them.

A version too small for the change is also kept as a signed refusal in the contract bundle repository, signed with the publish key, so the dashboard's Published view shows it with the bump it needed. The refusal record leaves the outcome unchanged: if the registry rejects the record, publish reports that beside the refusal.

A release candidate's fixes ship as the version it was a candidate for: after 2.0.0-rc.1, 2.0.0-rc.2 and 2.0.0 are accepted whatever changed. The change since the last final release must still fit the version: after 1.0.0 and 1.1.0-rc.1, a breaking change cannot ship as 1.1.0. The version rule compares the contract with the highest version already published below it, using the same classification as pacto diff:

Change since the last version Smallest version allowed Breaking a new major version (before 1.0, a new minor) Potentially breaking: Pacto cannot tell a new minor version Not breaking any higher version

pacto diff prints the same rule as Required bump.

docs.title: Never overwritten
docs.text:
For every artifact the plan says what the registry holds for its tag:

State Meaning Publish does absent The tag does not exist builds, pushes and tags it identical The tag holds exactly what Pacto computed (the bundle) nothing adopt Its version and revision annotations match this publish reuses it if it is signed by the configured identity; refuses otherwise conflict The tag holds something else refuses; nothing is overwritten unreadable The registry could not be read refuses; unreadable is never absent

Annotations are not signed, so anyone who can push can write them. Pacto therefore never signs what it adopts: a tag it wrote was signed before it was tagged, and one without that signature is someone else's.

A run that stopped halfway finishes when you run it again from the same commit: the plan adopts what the first run pushed and writes only what is missing. Run it from another commit and every tag the first run wrote is a conflict, so that version is spent: publish a higher service.version.

The deploy artifact is tagged last: once its tag exists, everything it points at exists and is signed. The other tags, the bundle's included, may already exist when a run stops, but no Stage takes a version without its deploy artifact. Each tag is read again just before it is written, which narrows the window in which two runs racing on one version could both write. A registry has no compare-and-swap on tags, so the window stays open: give each version one publisher.

docs.title: What gets published
docs.text:
Each build gets PACTO_OUT, PACTO_VERSION, PACTO_REVISION and, for every artifact built before it, PACTO_DIGEST_<NAME> and PACTO_REF_<NAME>, so a manifests build can pin the image it deploys by digest. Pacto then:

  1. pushes each artifact by digest, with org.opencontainers.image.version and org.opencontainers.image.revision on its manifest, and in CI org.opencontainers.image.source: $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY on GitHub Actions, $CI_PROJECT_URL on GitLab CI. The contract bundle carries none, so its digest stays the same wherever it is built;
  2. annotates the deploy artifact, the manifests or chart any applier deploys, with delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/contract, which names the digest-pinned contract bundle;
  3. attaches the SBOM file the build wrote to each image that declares one, and signs it, unless one signed by the configured identity is already there. Pacto never makes an SBOM, and refuses a file older than the build;
  4. signs every digest, unless a valid signature by the configured key, KMS key or keyless identity is already there, then verifies the new signature against that identity. A keyless signature carries whatever identity the CI token had, so a mismatch fails here, before any tag is written, so Pacto never publishes a version no Stage would take;
  5. pushes the bundle, attaches to it a signed record of every image the deploy pins (application/vnd.pacto.images.v1+json: each image's repository, digest and whether Pacto built it), and writes the tags.

The bundled pacto.yaml always declares pactoVersion. When the contract leaves it out, pacto pack, pacto push and pacto publish write the newest version the CLI supports into it. pacto ci also raises an older pactoVersion in the bundle when that keeps the contract's meaning (see Older contracts). Readers rely on it: a bundle pulled from a registry, or an inline contract in a Pacto resource, without pactoVersion, service.name or service.version is rejected. The operational graph reports it as SOURCE_RECORD_INVALID and the operator as ContractUndeclared.

It needs docker buildx with a builder that can write an OCI layout (the docker-container driver can) for dockerfile builds, and git to check that the checkout is clean unless you pass --revision. It needs no syft or cosign. With no declared build, it runs the build tool the folder shows (Skaffold, ko, Jib, buildpacks or a Dockerfile) directly, never through a shell, and assembles the deploy artifact itself; see How the image is built. publish.artifacts[].build is deprecated in pactoVersion: "2.5". Registry credentials and plain-HTTP registries come from the same settings as pacto push.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
Pacto signs with the Sigstore library and needs no cosign binary. Each signature is a Sigstore bundle attached to the digest as a referrer, the way cosign 3 writes one, so cosign verify and Flux's spec.verify both check it.

sign What signs Notes none, or no publish section A short-lived certificate for the CI identity the OIDC token names The identity rule and GitLab's id_tokens are in Signing. --sign-key signs a derived section with a key key: cosign.key A PEM private key file A cosign key is decrypted with COSIGN_PASSWORD kms: awskms:///alias/ci A KMS key awskms://, gcpkms://, azurekms:// or hashivault://, with that cloud's usual credentials. The key must be ECDSA P-256, Ed25519 or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256: Pacto refuses RSA-PSS and SHA-384 or SHA-512 keys. The released pacto binaries leave cloud KMS out to stay small: build one with go install -tags kms github.com/trianalab/pacto/v4/cmd/pacto@<version>, or one provider's tag (kms_aws, kms_gcp, kms_azure, kms_hashivault). The error names the build to use keyless: true A short-lived certificate from public-good Fulcio The OIDC token comes from SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN or GitHub Actions (id-token: write)

A signature goes to the public transparency log unless transparencyLog: false. Keyless signing needs the log: its certificate lives ten minutes, so it verifies only at the time the log saw it, and Pacto refuses keyless with transparencyLog: false. Pacto verifies a keyless signature against the identity and issuer you configure, or the ones the token names when you configure none, under the trusted root Sigstore publishes through TUF. publish.sign only says how publish signs: who may publish a service is the installation's decision, checked against a publisher rule, a person's pin or a signed policy (which publishers Pacto accepts). An operator signature never declares a contract (run.pacto.contract.provenance: inferred). The repository a keyless CI certificate attests must match the artifact's org.opencontainers.image.source. The dashboard and pacto_fleet_get show whether a published version's signature verifies; see Bundle signatures and referrers.

docs.title: The organization index entry
docs.text:
Every published version also writes one entry to the organization index, <registry>/pacto-index:<hash>-<version>. It exposes the service name, version, bundle digest, every dependency reference and the publisher it claims. An entry is never overwritten. A failed write warns and the publish still succeeds; publishing the current version again writes a missing entry.

  • --index names another <registry>/pacto-index, with no tag or digest, and --index none writes none.
  • pacto push under a tag other than the version writes none.

docs.title: In CI and from agents
docs.text:
CI calls pacto ci --publish as one step after the tests pass, on the merged commit. An agent calls pacto publish through MCP: pacto mcp --publish adds pacto_publish_plan and pacto_publish beside the authoring tools, over stdio only.

  • Carry-forward. pacto ci --publish reads the signed acceptances attached to the version before and re-reads the ones its inferred record cites. It pins each counted range into the published pacto.yaml, unless the repository's pacto.yaml declares that field, and cites every carried record in inputs.acceptances. A record that no longer verifies stops carrying. A plain pacto publish carries none.

docs.title: Declare a running service
docs.text:
pacto declare <workload> --registry <registry> publishes a contract for a running workload, without a repository or a build.

  • Source. It drafts the contract from the cluster with your kubeconfig credentials, as pacto init --cluster does, or reads --dir, a folder that command wrote.
  • Plan. Without --yes it prints the plan and writes nothing; the plan ends with its intent digest, and --intent <digest> refuses a run whose plan changed since you reviewed it.
  • Contract only. The bundle holds pacto.yaml, the files it references and pacto.inferred.yaml. Nothing is built and no deploy tag is written: the plan reads deploy: none, or the deploy artifact of the published baseline, which keeps pointing at the baseline.
  • Version. A first declaration is 0.1.0. With a published baseline the version is the baseline raised by the change, as pacto ci derives it, and an unchanged declaration publishes nothing. A baseline below pactoVersion: "2.5" is refused until you run pacto migrate.
  • Who signs. Only your interactive Sigstore login, in a browser or with --device, publishes a declared version. A key, an ambient OIDC token such as SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN, a CI token or a workload identity writes the next draft-<n> tag instead. The plan warns that a keyless signature records your email in the public Rekor log.
  • Ranges. A range the cluster read proposes stays unknown until you name its dependency with --accept. The record lists each accepted range.
  • Owner. Setting, changing or removing service.owner takes a person who belongs to the current owner, declared or attested, or a default approver; anyone else is refused before anything is pushed. An owner read from the workload's team label stays inferred. An unsigned version pushed without pacto declare keeps its owner: registry write access is the trust boundary for unsigned pushes. See Who may set a service owner.
  • Drafts. pacto declare <workload> --from-draft draft-<n> --yes accepts a draft an agent or CI wrote: the workload is read again under your credentials, every declared change the read and the baseline do not back is flagged and you sign.
  • Verify. pacto pull --verify-identity <email> --verify-issuer <issuer> pulls a bundle only when that person signed it; --verify-key checks a key instead. The record's declaration block is in the inferred record.
  • What the fleet shows after you declare. Once a registry read verifies your signature and the installation signer rule allows you, the fleet shows one service: the inferred service the declaration names is handed over to the declared one, and each field says whether it is declared, accepted by you or inferred. A Pacto target that runs as the workload wins. See When a declaration replaces an inferred service.

docs.title: Hand-off to delivery
docs.text:
With Pacto delivery installed, a Stage that watches the deploy artifact's repository (candidates.registry), or whose candidate OCIRepository follows it, sees each new version without an extra step, and --propose <namespace>/<stage> proposes it on a Stage that does not promote by itself. A Stage promotes only versions published this way: the registry watch or Flux checks the signature and the promoter checks the contract annotation. So --propose first waits until the Stage records the version as published, which happens once the watch or Flux reads the new tag and accepts its signer. It waits up to --propose-timeout (10 minutes by default), then gives up and says so.

A CI service account is an agent to Pacto delivery, so its --propose must also name the person who asked for the change with --on-behalf-of, as the Kubernetes username the cluster authenticates them as, any OIDC prefix included. A pull request author's Git login is a different name: map it to that username first, or the person's own approval goes unrecognised. That person may not approve the change, and the name is asserted, never verified (agents).

To take a version back out of an environment, see Roll back by hand.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: In this tutorial you write a contract, check it and use it to catch a breaking change. It takes about five minutes. A contract is one file, pacto.yaml. Everything here runs on your machine, with no account and no registry.

docs.title: 1. Install Pacto
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TrianaLab/pacto/main/scripts/get-pacto.sh | bash

Installation covers the other ways to install and what to do if the script fails.

docs.title: 2. Create a contract
docs.text:
Run this from an empty directory and stay there through step 5; step 6 moves inside my-service.

pacto init my-service --owner orders

This writes four files: pacto.yaml (the contract), interfaces/openapi.yaml (a placeholder API spec), configuration/schema.json (a placeholder config schema) and .pactoignore (which keeps a signing key out of the bundle). --owner names the team that owns the service. The argument is the folder to write into, and its last part becomes service.name, so pacto init fleet/checkout writes a contract for checkout in fleet/checkout. Run pacto init in a folder that already holds a service and it reads the Dockerfile and Kubernetes files instead: see Pactify a service.

Edit my-service/pacto.yaml and set service.version: 1.0.0. Then replace my-service/interfaces/openapi.yaml with an API that has required response fields:

openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  title: my-service
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /orders/{id}:
    get:
      summary: Get an order
      responses:
        "200":
          description: OK
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [id, total]
                properties:
                  id:
                    type: string
                  total:
                    type: number

docs.title: 3. Validate
docs.text:
$ pacto validate my-service
my-service is valid

Validation checks three things: the file's shape, that fields agree with each other (a field that names an interface must name one the contract declares, for example) and your policies, the rules your platform team may set for every contract. See the Contract Reference for the full rules.

docs.title: 4. Add consumers
docs.text:
Two services depend on my-service, each with a different compatibility range. Copy the folder twice and declare the dependencies:

cp -r my-service checkout
cp -r my-service reporting

In checkout/pacto.yaml, set service.name: checkout and replace the dependencies: block that pacto init wrote as comments with:

dependencies:
  - name: my-service
    ref: ../my-service
    required: true
    compatibility: "^1.0.0"

In reporting/pacto.yaml, set service.name: reporting and use a wider range:

dependencies:
  - name: my-service
    ref: ../my-service
    required: true
    compatibility: ">=1.0.0"

checkout accepts ^1.0.0 (1.x only), reporting accepts >=1.0.0 (1.x and above). Step 7 shows what that difference changes.

docs.title: 5. Introduce a breaking change
docs.text:
Copy my-service to v2 and delete the total field from the response schema:

cp -r my-service v2

In v2/pacto.yaml, set service.version: 2.0.0. In v2/interfaces/openapi.yaml, remove total from required and from properties so the schema becomes:

schema:
  type: object
  required: [id]
  properties:
    id:
      type: string

docs.title: 6. Diff the two versions
docs.text:
Move into my-service and compare the original contract against v2:

$ cd my-service
$ pacto diff . ../v2
Classification: BREAKING
Required bump: major
Changes (3):
  [NON_BREAKING] service.version (modified): service.version modified [1.0.0 -> 2.0.0]
  [BREAKING] openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.total (removed): openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.properties.total removed [- map[type:number]]
  [BREAKING] openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.required[total] (removed): openapi.paths[/orders/{id}].methods[GET].responses[200].content.application/json.schema.required total removed [- total]
breaking changes detected
$ echo $?
1

The classification is BREAKING, so the next published version must be a new major version, and the exit code is 1. That is the CI gate: pacto diff exits non-zero when the change is breaking for anyone who may use the service (pacto impact below says which consumers), so a branch-protection rule that requires passing checks blocks the merge.

docs.title: 7. Find the affected consumers
docs.text:
pacto impact takes that diff, finds every service that depends on my-service and tells you which ones break:

$ pacto impact . ../v2 --local ..
Impact: my-service 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0
Classification: BREAKING
Breaking changes: 2
Potentially breaking changes: 0
Ranges: 2 declared and 0 accepted of 2 dependency edges (100%)
Affected consumers (2):
  checkout                     direct     confidence=contractual  compat=incompatible owner=orders
    path: checkout > my-service  provenance: declared  via: dependency
  reporting                    direct     confidence=contractual  compat=compatible   owner=orders
    path: reporting > my-service  provenance: declared  via: dependency
    note: the range >=1.0.0 has no upper bound, so compatible only means the range >=1.0.0 accepts 2.0.0; this change is BREAKING, so check that reporting does not use what it removes or changes
By outcome: 1 incompatible, 0 unknown, 1 compatible
Most affected owners: my-team 2 (1 incompatible)
Release gate: unverified
unverified: the change is BREAKING and 2 consumers depend on my-service, but none is shown to be both incompatible and running. Review each consumer, and add a source that knows where services run (for example --target-state) to tell deployed impact apart

checkout and reporting declare the same edge to the same service and get opposite verdicts. checkout pins ^1.0.0 (1.x only) and breaks. reporting accepts >=1.0.0 (any major), so its range still matches. The note says what that match does not prove: that reporting avoids what the change removes. Pacto tells the two apart because each contract carries its compatibility range.

The exit code is 2: the gate is unverified. The bundles say nothing about where the consumers run, so Pacto neither blocks the change nor calls it safe. Release gate and exit status explains the three outcomes.

owner=orders is the team you passed to pacto init. confidence=contractual means the answer comes from the declared ranges alone, without a runtime observation of the call. direct means each consumer declares my-service itself.

docs.title: Optional: publish to a registry
docs.text:
The steps above need no registry. To see the full round trip, start a local registry and push the contract:

docker run -d --rm -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5000 --name pacto-registry registry:3
pacto push oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto -p .

Port 5001 because macOS binds 5000 for AirPlay. 127.0.0.1: because the registry accepts anonymous writes.

Read it back without pulling:

pacto explain oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto:1.0.0

Or pull the bundle:

pacto pull oci://localhost:5001/demo/my-service-pacto:1.0.0 -o pulled

Clean up:

docker rm -f pacto-registry

For a real registry like GHCR, you need pacto login with a personal access token. See Installation for the supply-chain guarantees and Put it in your repository for what to commit.

docs.title: Run record reference
docs.text: A run record is a small JSON document that pacto diff, pacto impact and pacto publish can leave behind in CI to count what Pacto catches. Measure what Pacto does shows how to turn recording on and read the totals. Records are unsigned statistics, never evidence: nothing in Pacto that validates, diffs, analyzes impact, publishes or delivers reads them. Only pacto stats, the read-only MCP tool pacto_stats and the dashboard's Metrics page read them back, to total them. Recording is opt-in and best effort. A problem with recording prints one warning line on stderr, and the exit code and stdout stay the same as a run without recording. MCP tools never record. pacto impact event answers (--unavailable, --removed and --regressed) and pacto publish --plan record nothing, and neither does a run that could not produce a result.

docs.title: Turn recording on
docs.text:
Flag Environment variable What it does --stats-registry PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY publishes the record to this repository, for example ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats --stats-file PACTO_STATS_FILE writes the record to this file, for a later pacto stats publish --stats-context none adds the context fields it names

A flag takes precedence over its environment variable. The repository is never defaulted, and these settings are never read from pacto.yaml. Credentials and insecure registries come from the same settings every other registry command uses (PACTO_INSECURE_REGISTRIES lists registries reached over plain HTTP). An empty flag, such as --stats-file=, turns its environment variable off for that command. A file holds one record. --stats-file:

  • replaces the record a file already holds, with a warning;
  • writes an empty file like a missing one;
  • refuses to overwrite a file that holds something other than a run record.

PACTO_STATS_FILE applies to every recording command in the job, so give each command its own file with --stats-file when a job runs more than one.

pacto ci:

  • writes one record per checked service, run.payments.json for --stats-file run.json;
  • never publishes a record, since it only plans.

Recording prints one of these lines on stderr:

  • pacto: run record published to <repo>@<digest> (unsigned statistics)
  • pacto: run record written to <path>
  • pacto: warning: run record not published: <reason>
  • pacto: warning: run record not written: <reason>
  • pacto: warning: replaced the run record of <kind> <service> in <path>

A diff or impact run whose bundle digest cannot be computed records nothing and says run record not written: could not compute the bundle digest.

pacto stats publish <file...> publishes record files to --registry (or PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY). It tries every file, prints the kind, service and id of each record it publishes, and exits 1 when any file could not be read, parsed or published. It rejects a record whose id does not match its kind, service and revisions.

docs.title: Who can read records
docs.text:
Anyone with pull access to the stats repository can list every recorded service name and its consumer counts with plain oras discover. That listing bypasses the restricted views of the dashboard and the fleet tools. Use a dedicated repository whose pull access matches who may see the whole fleet. A bundle repository is a poor fit, because its readers are usually every consumer of the service.

The job that runs pacto stats publish vouches for the contents of each file with its own credentials. The id check stops a forged id, and nothing stops a forged service name or count. Publish only files written by trusted jobs, and never publish files from untrusted (fork) jobs into a repository others read.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Each service has one anchor in the stats repository, and each record is an OCI referrer of that anchor. Records sit next to bundles and never inside them.

Part Value Anchor artifact type application/vnd.pacto.stats.v1 Anchor layer application/vnd.pacto.stats.v1+json, holding {"stats":"<service>"} Anchor tag pacto-stats-<hex sha256 of the service name> Record artifact type application/vnd.pacto.run.v1 Record layer application/vnd.pacto.run.v1+json, holding the encoded record (at most 64 KiB) Record annotation dev.pacto.recorded-at: the record's recordedAt, an unsigned ordering hint

The tag keeps a registry that collects untagged manifests from deleting the anchor. The pacto-stats- prefix keeps Pacto's anchors apart from other tools' tags in a shared repository. Publishing the same record again changes nothing.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Every record has version, id, kind, service, pactoVersion and recordedAt, and every record other than a coverage record has outcome. The other keys appear only where the table says.

Key Type Present Holds Personal data version string always pacto.trianalab.io/run-record/v1 none id string always sha256: and the hex SHA-256 of kind, service, oldRevision and newRevision joined by vertical bars: the distinct-change key, so reruns of one change share it. On an operation record, the operation's Kubernetes UID none kind string always diff, impact or publish, operation for an operation record or coverage for a coverage record none service string always the contract's service.name; for diff and impact, the name in the new revision, so a renamed service records under its new name none oldRevision string when known diff and impact: the old bundle's digest. publish: the highest published version below this one none newRevision string when known diff and impact: the new bundle's digest. publish: the version being published none bundleDigest string publish, when it did not fail the digest of the published bundle none deployDigest string publish, when it did not fail the digest of the published deploy artifact none images array of strings publish, when it did not fail and deploys an image each image the published bundle deploys, as <repository>@<digest>, the same list as its signed images record none classification string when computed NON_BREAKING, POTENTIAL_BREAKING or BREAKING none gate object impact, refused publish the gate the run reached none gate.verdict string with gate impact: clear, blocked or unverified. publish: refused none gate.reason string with gate impact: a gate code. publish: the first failed check (version, sign, refs, sbom, revision, validation or publish), else conflict or unreadable none consumers object impact consumer counts of the change none consumers.incompatible integer with consumers consumers whose declared range or required guarantee rejects the new version, running or not none consumers.unknown integer with consumers consumers the evidence could not classify none consumers.compatible integer with consumers consumers whose declared range accepts the new version; a BREAKING change can still break them none consumers.unclassified integer with consumers consumers with no recognised verdict none consumers.blocking integer with consumers consumers that hold the gate: incompatible and running on a known target none completeness string impact complete, partial or empty: how complete the snapshot behind the counts was none asOf string impact the snapshot's time, RFC 3339 in UTC at full precision, equal to the asOf of the impact answer none outcome string except on a coverage record diff and impact: passed, failed or unverified. publish: published, unchanged, refused or failed none pactoVersion string always the Pacto release that wrote the record, for example 4.6.0 or dev. It is distinct from the contract's pactoVersion none recordedAt string always when the record was written, RFC 3339 in UTC to the second none repository string when named see context fields only when listed in --stats-context ciRunUrl string when named see context fields only when listed in --stats-context environment string when named see context fields; on an operation record, the environment its Stage delivers to only when listed in --stats-context; on an operation record, its Stage's environment

The four consumer counts incompatible, unknown, compatible and unclassified split the consumers with no overlap, so a reader never has to subtract one count from another. The counts come from declared ranges and guarantees; none of them is observed runtime behaviour. An unknown consumer is never counted as safe. blocking is a subset of incompatible. Read the counts together with completeness and asOf: a count from a partial snapshot is a lower bound.

A bundle digest is the digest of the content compared. With --old-set, --new-set, --old-values or --new-values, that content is the overridden bundle, so its digest names no published bundle.

A record never holds a person's name, an email address, a token or any environment variable it does not name here.

docs.title: Operation records
docs.text:
The delivery promoter writes an operation record for each delivery operation it concludes. Its id is the operation's Kubernetes UID: a record published twice is two referrers with one id, which readers count once. Its outcome is the operation's outcome: Succeeded, Failed, Errored, Cancelled, Expired, Rejected, Superseded or Witnessed. An operation record never holds the CI-only keys above (oldRevision through asOf, repository and ciRunUrl), and a CI record never holds the keys below.

Key Type Present Holds Personal data type string always the last segment of the operation type, such as promote or rollback none verification string when set Verified, AcceptedUnknown or Unverified none reason string when it is a plain code the outcome's machine code, such as PlanStale none actorClass string when set controller, agent, human or break-glass, never a name the class, never a name delegated boolean when true the operation named a person it acted for (onBehalfOf with a user); the person is never recorded whether a person was named, never who heldFor string when the operation was held the time from its last hold until it applied or, when it never applied, concluded, as a Go duration such as 14m0s; it includes the waits after a person answered, on the Stage lock, a freeze and the apply none serviceDomain string when the Stage's service has one the domain of the Stage's service none stage object always the Stage the operation ran on none stage.namespace string always the Stage's namespace none stage.name string always the Stage's name none stage.cluster string always the cluster's id: its kube-system namespace UID none to string pointer operations, when a digest the digest the operation moves to none from string pointer operations, when a digest the digest the operation moves from none contract string when a gate cited one the contract digest a gate cited none gates array when gates ran one entry per gate result, in order none gates.gate string with gates the gate id none gates.phase string with gates pre or verify none gates.result string with gates Pass, Fail or Unknown none startedAt string when admitted when the operation was admitted, RFC 3339 none finishedAt string always when the operation concluded, RFC 3339 none

service is the service the Stage declares. An operation record holds no actor, approver, note, message, citation or correlation id.

docs.title: Coverage records
docs.text:
pacto fleet status writes a coverage record of the fleet snapshot it read:

  • only when --stats-registry or --stats-file is on its command line; it ignores PACTO_STATS_REGISTRY and PACTO_STATS_FILE;
  • best effort, like the other commands: a failure prints a warning and leaves the exit code unchanged;
  • fleet-wide: its service is always _fleet, a name no contract can declare. A run with --namespace writes none, and every scheduled run should read the same sources, since readers take the newest record whatever read it;
  • with an id over coverage, _fleet, an empty old revision and the snapshot's snapshotAsOf, so one snapshot recorded twice counts once;
  • with no outcome, CI-only key, environment or operation key;
  • read as a level: readers take the newest coverage record in a window and never sum them;
  • hidden from a reader that may see only part of the fleet, and the answer says so with COVERAGE_OUTSIDE_YOUR_VIEW.
Key Type Present Holds Personal data coverage object always the snapshot's coverage counters none coverage.services integer always services that are no golden path none coverage.uncontracted integer always callers the fleet observed with no contract none coverage.knowledge object when the snapshot carried a knowledge tally absent means unknown, never 0 none coverage.knowledge.services integer with knowledge services the tally partitions: described + withGaps + unknown none coverage.knowledge.described integer with knowledge services whose contract and interface documents leave nothing out none coverage.knowledge.withGaps integer with knowledge services with at least one knowledge gap none coverage.knowledge.unknown integer with knowledge services whose knowledge Pacto cannot judge none coverage.knowledge.notDeployed integer with knowledge services with gaps that run nowhere; unknown services are never counted here. The observed services are knowledge.services minus knowledge.unknown minus knowledge.notDeployed, with unknown services shown beside them none coverage.links object always operational targets by how they link to a contract none coverage.links.exact integer always targets linked exactly none coverage.links.inferred integer always targets linked by inference none coverage.links.ambiguous integer always targets that match more than one contract none coverage.links.unresolved integer always targets that match no contract none coverage.snapshotAsOf string always the snapshot's time, RFC 3339 in UTC; never after recordedAt none coverage.completeness string always complete or partial; an empty snapshot is recorded as partial none

docs.title: Impact gate codes
docs.text: Code Verdict CONSUMERS_INCOMPATIBLE blocked POLICY_REFERRERS_FAIL_RUNNING blocked POLICY_UNKNOWN_RANGE blocked POLICY_UNCONTRACTED blocked POLICY_REFERRERS_FAIL_UNPLACED unverified POLICY_UNCHECKED unverified INFERRED_POSSIBLE_BREAK unverified SERVICE_NOT_IN_FLEET unverified SERVICE_NAME_INFERRED unverified ANSWER_PARTIAL unverified CONSUMERS_UNCHECKED unverified INFERRED_PROVIDER unverified RUNNING_UNREAD unverified FIRST_VERSION_UNCHECKED unverified NOT_BREAKING clear POTENTIAL_BREAKING clear NO_CONSUMERS clear BREAKING_ACCEPTED clear FIRST_VERSION_ACCEPTED clear

docs.title: Context fields
docs.text:
--stats-context takes a comma-separated list of names. A bare name reads its value from the CI environment, and name=value gives the value explicitly. A name that is not listed stays out of the record. When a name appears twice, the last one wins. --stats-context has no environment variable, so pass it on each command. It has no effect unless --stats-registry or --stats-file is set.

Name Record key Value of a bare name repository repository GITHUB_REPOSITORY, else CI_PROJECT_PATH run-url ciRunUrl $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID, else CI_JOB_URL environment environment none: write environment=<name>
