  --exchange-client-id pacto-mcp

Every request must carry a bearer token for the resource; the server publishes where to get one at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. It exchanges each caller's token at the identity provider (RFC 8693) for one the apiserver accepts and asks the apiserver who the caller is on every request. Everyone gets the read tools, an agent also propose and cancel, nobody an approve tool. Put agent clients in pacto:agents (or your agent group): signed in through OIDC, they otherwise count as people. Without token exchange the server refuses --delivery over HTTP. With --fleet it needs token exchange too, names each caller the same way and answers as the dashboard does. The exchanged token is the agent's own, so on_behalf_of still comes from the tool's arguments. One server serves both:

PACTO_MCP_EXCHANGE_CLIENT_SECRET=... pacto mcp --fleet --k8s --delivery -t http \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --auth-issuer https://idp.example.com \
  --resource https://pacto-mcp.example.com/mcp --exchange-client-id pacto-mcp

Both servers log every refused token, sign-in and signed-in request as a warning with the issuer, audience or client, the reason and where it came from (X-Request-Id too, when a proxy sets it), never the token. With --verbose the MCP server also logs each caller's class and whether it got the write tools, and a line per tool call.

docs.title: Delivery reference: eval providers
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

An eval provider is a suite runner: it runs one of the checks the version ships, such as an AI agent's eval suite. The Stage check names it in suite:

spec:
  gates:
    verify:
      checks:
        - name: quality
          provider: evals
          suite: evals
          suiteDigest: sha256:...   # optional
          params:
            minPassRate: "0.95"

Without suite the runner runs the only check the version ships. A version that does not ship the named check, or with no suite ships no check or more than one, is held before it ships (the pacto.suites gate): a person accepts it or it does not ship.

suiteDigest pins the sha256 of the suite the version ships, which covers every file in the suite's directory (see Checks): a version with another suite is held the same way, and its eval is Unknown. A suite must be self-contained in its directory.

docs.title: The runner's answer
docs.text:
The promoter posts the same {"input": ..., "params": ...} as to an HTTP provider, the input also naming the contract the version ships and the suite in it: "contract": "oci://...@sha256:...", "suite": {"name": "evals", "path": "evals/suite.yaml", "digest": "sha256:..."}. The runner runs that suite on the version under check and answers with a Sigstore bundle: a DSSE envelope over a statement it signs.

{
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1",
  "subject": [{"name": "pay-agent", "digest": {"sha256": "..."}}],
  "predicateType": "delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/eval/v1",
  "predicate": {
    "operation": "<the input's operationUID>",
    "challenge": "<the input's challenge>",
    "suite": "sha256:...",
    "run": "https://evals.example/runs/7",
    "passed": 48,
    "total": 50,
    "observedModel": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
    "message": "two refunds wrong"
  }
}

docs.title: Trusted runners
docs.text:
operation and challenge echo the input's: the challenge is new for every check, so an old answer cannot be replayed. suite is the sha256 of the suite it ran and observedModel (optional) the model it saw answer. The provider lists the runners it trusts in signers, each a public key or a keyless identity:

delivery:
  gates:
    providers:
      - name: evals
        type: eval
        url: https://evals.internal
        signers:
          - name: evals-ci
            publicKey: |
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              ...
          - name: evals-keyless
            identity: https://github.com/acme/evals/.github/workflows/run.yaml@refs/heads/main
            issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
            trustedRoot: '{"mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.trustedroot+json;version=0.1", ...}'

The Stage sets the pass bar:

Param Default Meaning minPassRate 1 The share of cases that must pass, above 0 and up to 1. Fewer fails

These answers count as Unknown:

  • an answer no listed signer signed
  • an answer about another version or another suite
  • an answer for another operation or another challenge
  • a suite whose sha256 is not the Stage's suiteDigest
  • no cases, or no run to cite
  • a version whose contract cannot be read or does not ship the suite

The verdict cites the contract, the suite, the run and the runner (runner), and keeps the signed answer (runnerBundle) for record verify.

docs.title: Which model answered
docs.text:
When the runner reports an observedModel that no external dependency version of the version under check names, the check fails and says both. Pacto takes the runner's signed word for it; nothing else checks it. A Stage check can require the runner to say:

        - name: quality
          provider: evals
          suite: evals
          requireObservedModel: true

Then no observedModel, or no dependency version to compare it with, is Unknown.

docs.title: Delivery reference: health checks
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Beyond the Pacto contract check, a Stage can check a version's errors and response times in your monitoring, an AI agent's evals and that the service calls only what its contract declares (its claims). Every check answers Pass, Fail or Unknown and cites what it read, so anyone can run it again. An Unknown check holds the change for a person, who can accept the unknown.

The Pacto resource ships inside every version and names its own target, so pacto.contract and pacto.runtime count only a Pacto that evaluated the workload the Stage says the service runs: spec.workload (kind and name in the Stage's namespace), or the Deployment named spec.service.name when it is empty. A Pacto that checked another workload, a decoy a version shipped for example, is Unknown. pacto init --delivery writes spec.workload.

docs.title: Add checks to a Stage
docs.text:
List the checks under spec.gates.verify.checks. Each names a provider:

apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: prod
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}
  startLevel: advise
  gates:
    verify:
      window: 5m
      recheck: 1m
      checks:
        - name: health
          provider: mira
          params: {minSpans: "50", maxErrorRatio: "0.02", soak: "3m"}
        - name: claims
          provider: pacto.runtime

The checks run on the time since Flux applied the version, all at once, and one that takes longer than a minute is Unknown. The promoter works on delivery.promoter.workers (4 by default) operations and Stages at a time, so a slow provider does not hold up the others. Any Fail rolls it back, all Pass verifies it and anything else waits; when window runs out a person is asked to accept the unknown or reject the version. While that question waits, the checks run again every recheck: a Fail still rolls the version back and all Pass verifies it without the person.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
pacto.runtime is built in. Every other provider is configured in the operator chart's delivery section, so a Stage or an agent can name a provider and only the chart sets the host it calls:

delivery:
  gates:
    providers:
      - {name: mira, type: mira, url: "https://mira.observability:4318"}

The URL must be https. A verdict ends up in a signed record, so an answer forged on the way could get a Pass signed. Plain http works only on loopback, or with allowPlainHTTP: true on a test cluster. The promoter never follows a redirect: a provider that answers one gets Unknown.

A provider inside the cluster often has a certificate from an internal CA. Put that CA's PEM certificates in a ConfigMap in delivery.namespace and name it, so the promoter trusts it on top of the public roots:

delivery:
  gates:
    caBundle: {configMap: internal-ca, key: ca.crt}

docs.title: Mira
docs.text:
A mira provider counts the service's spans in Mira by service.name, one span kind at a time: server spans by default, so one span per request served. Its params:

Param Default Meaning spanKind server The spans counted: server, consumer, producer, client, internal, unspecified or any minSpans 20 Fewer spans than this is Unknown maxErrorRatio 0.05 A larger share of failed spans fails soak 1m A clean result passes only after this long latencyThreshold off Spans slower than this count as slow maxLatencyRatio 0.05 A larger share of slow spans fails where none Extra Mira terms as JSON, for example the namespace matchVersion false Count only spans whose service.version is the contract's service.version

By default the provider counts every span of the service in the window, so while a rollout is still replacing pods the old version's spans count too: they can hide a breach or fail a clean version. The window starts when Flux or Argo CD reports the version applied, not when the rollout finished. Set matchVersion: "true" to judge only the version under check, once the service sets the service.version resource attribute to its contract's service.version (for example through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES). Without a contract version to match, the check is Unknown.

A read that fails or stops short is Unknown. Mira's query API has no count, so the provider pages through the spans and stops at 200,000 per query. A window holding more is judged on its newest soak only, and the message says so; if even that holds more, the check is Unknown, so narrow it with where. The citation holds the exact queries with absolute time bounds, so posting them to Mira again reads the same spans.

docs.title: What a verdict can prove
docs.text:
Mira and http verdicts are unsigned and, by default, self-reported. Mira counts the spans the service sends about itself, keyed on the service.name and service.version the sender sets. The version under check, or any pod that can reach the OTLP endpoint, can leave out its errors or send clean spans to force a Pass, or send failed ones to force a Fail and a rollback. An http provider's answer is believed as it arrives over https. To make a verdict worth more:

  • accept telemetry only from authenticated senders at the collector;
  • add a where on attributes the collector sets, not the sender, such as the k8s.pod.uid or k8s.namespace.name the k8sattributes processor adds;
  • count the spans of the service's callers (spanKind: client on the caller's side) instead of the service's own.

docs.title: HTTP providers
docs.text: An http provider is the plug-in format for any other tool. The promoter posts {"input": ..., "params": ...}, where the input names the operation, the Stage, the service, the digests under check and the time window. The tool answers {"subject": "sha256:...", "result": "Pass|Fail|Unknown", "message": "...", "citation": {...}}, where subject is the digest it judged. An answer that names no subject, or a version other than the one under check, is Unknown.

docs.title: Eval providers
docs.text: An eval provider runs an AI agent's eval suite that the version ships. See Delivery reference: eval providers.

docs.title: Claims against the running service
docs.text: pacto.runtime uses the node agent. It fails a version the kernel saw calling a Pacto-managed service its contract never declares, or not listening on a port it declares. It reads the Pacto evaluation of exactly this version and passes only when status.evaluatedRevision.kernelCoverage is Complete and the version has run for soak (a Go duration, default 1m); otherwise the answer is Unknown. A Pass means only that the node agent saw neither of those two things: right after a rollout the version may not have handled traffic yet, which is what the soak is for. A contradiction the kernel saw fails at once.

docs.title: After release
docs.text: After release the checks run again every recheck (default 1m) on the last window. A confirmed Fail marks the version failed and raises one rollback citing the check. The Stage freezes instead when that cause already had its rollback, when there is nothing to roll back to or when a person or an agent chose the running version (a rollback, or a promote during auto-hold). It also freezes, naming the operation, when an operation Pacto did not raise holds the name of the rollback or freeze it raises (<operation>-rollback, <operation>-freeze). Unknown after release never rolls back, and a result about a version the Stage stopped running is dropped. The newest result is in status.lastCheck, which also says when the operation that shipped the running version is gone. The Stage's Watched condition is True while that result passed. It turns False with reason RecheckUnknown while nothing watches the running version (a provider down, too many spans, no coverage) and RecheckFailed after a Fail. The promoter emits an Event when it turns False, and the pacto_delivery_stage_watched gauge drops to 0, so you can alert on it.

docs.title: Where the re-check shows
docs.text: pacto delivery status, pacto_delivery_status and the dashboard's service page show that result as lastCheck, with each verdict and its citation, and read Watched only while the result is about the running version; see status, progress and lifecycle. A pacto.contract verdict cites, for each Pacto it judged, <pacto>.target (its fleet target key), <pacto>.contractStatus, <pacto>.evaluatedAt and <pacto>.findings (the codes of its error and warning findings, at most 10), so it links to the compliance findings behind it.

docs.title: Explain
docs.text:
pacto delivery explain -n prod <operation>

explain shows where an operation is and every verdict with its citation and how to run it again. --cause-verdict on propose cites a verdict as its cause, for example on a frozen Stage; the promoter runs it again and refuses a cause that comes back with another result.

docs.title: Delivery reference: approvals
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

People decide in the dashboard and agents reach Pacto over the network, each under their own Kubernetes identity (agents). The dashboard and the MCP server pass the caller's own token on, so the apiserver decides what the caller may do and its audit log names the person. There is no impersonation.

docs.title: The cluster trusts your identity provider
docs.text:
A person decides with the sign-in they have. If you also ask for a recent sign-in to decide, approving needs the login time, read by the apiserver itself. Structured authentication maps the OIDC auth_time claim to userInfo.extra["delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time"], only for tokens issued to the two clients that make a person log in again: the dashboard and pacto delivery approve's own client, pacto-approve. A client-credentials or exchanged token never has it, and neither does a kubeconfig login (pacto-cli): any process in your shell, an agent included, can reuse that one.

apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuthenticationConfiguration
jwt:
- issuer: {url: https://idp.example.com, audiences: [pacto-dashboard, pacto-cli], audienceMatchPolicy: MatchAny}
  claimMappings:
    username: {expression: "'https://idp.example.com#' + claims.sub"}
    groups: {claim: groups, prefix: ""}
    extra:
    - key: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time
      valueExpression: >-
        has(claims.auth_time) && has(claims.azp) && claims.azp in ['pacto-dashboard', 'pacto-approve']
        ? string(int(claims.auth_time)) : ''

The identity provider must put azp on these tokens. Dex sets it only on a token with two audiences, so give the dashboard and pacto delivery approve the extra scope audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli and make pacto-cli trust pacto-dashboard and pacto-approve. Register pacto-approve as a public client (PKCE, no secret) whose redirect is the loopback address http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback, and use it for nothing else. Without that trust, people decide from the terminal with their own kubeconfig.

docs.title: Where approving works
docs.text:
Only a recent sign-in needs the login time. The apiserver must load this file (flag --authentication-config), and its claimMappings must be able to set extra. That is in your hands wherever you set the apiserver's flags, as with kind, kubeadm or k3s; Pacto's own tests run it on kind. Managed clusters mostly decide it for you:

Cluster Can it map delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time? kind, kubeadm, k3s and others where you set apiserver flags Yes, tested on kind AKS Not verified: structured authentication is in preview EKS, GKE Not verified

To check a cluster, sign in again and run kubectl auth whoami -o yaml. If extra holds no delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/auth-time, nobody can approve there with a recent sign-in required. Delivery still promotes every change that needs no decision. People can still freeze, unfreeze, roll back and cancel. The dashboard and the CLI still read everything. What you need to be allowed lists the three ways a held change still ends.

docs.title: Who counts as a person, an agent or a team
docs.text:
Delivery tells people from agents by how they sign in. A ServiceAccount, any other system: user and an unauthenticated request are agents. Every other signed-in identity, such as an OIDC or client certificate user, is a person. These values, all optional, mark automation and narrow who may answer:

delivery:
  identities:
    agentGroups: [pacto:agents]          # agents propose, never approve or unfreeze
    breakGlassGroups: [pacto:break-glass]
    teamGroupPrefix: null                # set it, even to "", to let only owner teams answer
    requireOwnerTeam: false              # true: a question naming no team is answered by nobody

The chart renders the admission policies from these values and publishes them in the ConfigMap pacto-delivery-identities in delivery.namespace, which every signed-in user may read. The promoter runs with that ConfigMap and restarts when it changes. pacto delivery, pacto mcp --delivery and the dashboard read it too, from --delivery-namespace (default pacto-delivery; the chart points its own dashboard at delivery.namespace), so what they offer matches what admission and the promoter decide.

docs.title: When a client cannot read the policy
docs.text: The client still classifies you with the defaults above for display, but its status, offers, undo offers and "why not yet" fixes then offer nothing and name the error. When the ConfigMap is not found, the error suggests passing --delivery-namespace with the namespace the chart's delivery.namespace names. Admission and the promoter still decide.

docs.title: Owner teams and agent groups
docs.text:
A held question goes to the teams that own the affected services. Unless teamGroupPrefix is set, that only routes it, and whoever may decide answers. Once set, only owner team members answer: team T is the group T with "", or the prefix followed by T. A system: group is never a team. With requireOwnerTeam: true, a question whose services declare no owner is answered by nobody but break-glass, as its plan says.

Automation that signs in through OIDC counts as a person until you put it in agentGroups. So does a bot that completes a pacto-approve login with stored credentials: the public client gives it a login time. humanGroups is deprecated: when set, anyone outside its groups is an agent.

docs.title: Who may decide
docs.text:
A person may decide a held change when they may update the Stage's workload. When it counts an Approval, the promoter asks the apiserver a SubjectAccessReview with the Approval's user and groups, such as update deployments/checkout in payments. The same review decides a person's unfreeze and acknowledge. With delivery on, the chart aggregates delivery reads into the built-in view, edit and admin roles, and creating Approvals and Operations into edit and admin, so edit or admin in the namespace is enough. A custom role without edit also needs the pacto-operator-delivery-approver ClusterRole.

Agents never decide. Without update rights the refusal is CannotUpdateWorkload. A review that fails, or a workload kind with no known resource, is ApproverUnverified, never allowed.

Records keep how each actor was classified and, for each approval, the access phrase, which review answered it and when. Older records show "not recorded".

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
To keep the earlier team rules, set both values before you upgrade:

delivery:
  identities:
    teamGroupPrefix: ""
    requireOwnerTeam: true
  • An upgrade that takes the new chart's defaults turns team narrowing off unless you set teamGroupPrefix yourself, and the ownerless protection unless you set requireOwnerTeam: a values file through Argo CD or a Flux HelmRelease, helm upgrade -f and --reset-then-reuse-values. The promoter then emits a TeamNarrowingOff Event on each Operation it holds.
  • An upgrade that reuses the earlier release's values whole keeps the earlier defaults, and so keeps narrowing.
  • Approvers need update on the Stage's workload, with or without narrowing.
  • allowEmptyHumanGroups is ignored. Other system: users are agents.
  • Records gain actor.classifiedBy and, on each approval, classifiedBy, access, accessSource and accessAt. Signed records are read strictly, so upgrade a promoter that follows another cluster's records (upstreamTrust) no later than the recording cluster.

docs.title: The dashboard's delivery settings
docs.text:
The delivery views need dashboard sign-in. For approvals, add the extra scope audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli (see above). The delivery settings sit under dashboard.delivery:

dashboard:
  auth:
    oidc:
      extraScopes: [audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli]
  delivery:
    namespace: ""      # where the identity policy is; empty means delivery.namespace when delivery.enabled
    trust: {configMap: delivery-trust, key: trust.yaml}   # verifies History
    miraURL: http://mira.observability:4318

trust is the trust config the CLI reads (trust and key rotation). The dashboard's ServiceAccount gains nothing in delivery and cannot impersonate. A dashboard on loopback without sign-in shows the pacto delivery approve command instead of deciding: any process on your machine could decide as you.

docs.title: Follow delivery in the dashboard
docs.text: The Delivery tab (what it shows) appears only where the cluster serves the delivery API and the dashboard holds your own credentials. Every action shows the plan first, and the fresh plan if anything moved since. When you may not list delivery objects across the cluster, the views say they may be incomplete.

docs.title: Approve from the dashboard
docs.text: A held change asks one question of the teams that own the affected services. Whoever may decide answers it, and only owner team members when team narrowing is on. A person decides with the sign-in they have. The dashboard and pacto delivery approve check a decision with the promoter's own rule, asking with your own credentials, before they record it, and refuse one it would not count, saying why. Agents are refused, ServiceAccount tokens included; a person's token decides where its login time allows.

docs.title: A recent sign-in to decide
docs.text: Set delivery.promoter.authFreshness to a duration such as 15m to make deciding need a recent sign-in. The promoter then ignores an approval given more than that long after its author's login, and every Stage publishes the setting in status.authFreshness for the dashboard and pacto delivery approve to follow. Once a login is older than two thirds of it, the dashboard says so next to the decision buttons, and a decision opens a dialog that sends the person to sign in again (prompt=login), keeping their choice and note for one more click. A token with no login time cannot approve.

docs.title: Approve from the terminal
docs.text:
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve

It decides as your kubeconfig signs you in. Where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in or cannot be read, it never sends your kubeconfig's credentials:

export PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://idp.example.com
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve \
  --oidc-extra-scopes audience:server:client_id:pacto-cli --oidc-redirect-port 8001

It prints an address with prompt=login and max_age=0, waits up to ten minutes on the loopback port for you to log in again in your browser, refuses a token whose auth_time is older than the command, and sends the Approval with that token alone. The token is not stored. --oidc-client-id defaults to pacto-approve; a confidential client's secret comes from PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. Without --oidc-redirect-port it picks a free port, which suits a provider that allows any loopback port (RFC 8252).

  • Where the installation accepts signed approvals, it signs your decision keyless into the registry instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• An agent holding a person's credentials, session or refresh token is that person to the cluster, and by default it can approve as them. A recent sign-in raises the bar; it does not close the gap. pacto delivery approve asks for the login with prompt=login, but the cluster cannot see what a login asked for: a process that drives your browser could run the pacto-approve login itself and ride your identity provider's session, and it gets a login time only as old as your last real login there. An identity provider that ignores prompt=login widens this.
  • Run agents under their own identity. An agent that runs pacto with a person's kubeconfig is that person: it can approve as them, and it needs no --on-behalf-of. Set delivery.promoter.authFreshness so that an approval needs a recent sign-in, which a kubeconfig login never carries.
  • A stolen dashboard session can take that person's actions until it ends. With a recent sign-in required, it approves only in the first two thirds of delivery.promoter.authFreshness after they signed in again.
  • The SubjectAccessReview names the Approval's user and groups, not its extra. An authorizer that narrows by extra, such as token scopes, answers for the user without them.
  • Sessions live in the dashboard's memory: it runs as one replica and a restart signs everyone out (sessions).
  • A change's timeline shows only the Operation's own times, not Kubernetes events. Published versions are those your Stages know, and refused publishes are listed as the registry holds them, without checking their signatures.

docs.title: Delivery reference: plan, propose and approve
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

How a change is planned, proposed and approved, for Pacto delivery. Setting up a Stage is in Delivery reference: setup and gates. To see first where each Stage stands and why a version cannot move yet, run pacto delivery status --service <service> --why; see status, progress and lifecycle.

pacto delivery candidates -n prod --stage payments
pacto delivery plan -n prod --stage payments --to 3.0.0
pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --to 3.0.0 --intent-digest sha256:...
pacto delivery approve -n prod <operation> --decision approve

candidates lists the versions a Stage may take, with their digests. --to takes a version, a tag or a digest; a version or a tag must name exactly one candidate, or Pacto refuses it and says why. The operation records the digest.

approve decides as your kubeconfig signs you in. Where the Stage asks for a recent sign-in, it makes you log in again in your browser through its own pacto-approve client instead, so it needs the issuer the cluster trusts (--oidc-issuer-url or PACTO_DELIVERY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL). Where the installation accepts signed approvals, it signs your decision keyless after a fresh login and pushes it to the registry, and --intent <record reference> approves with no kubeconfig. See approve from the terminal.

docs.title: What a plan says
docs.text: plan predicts each gate's verdict and the one question a person would be asked. Its next lines say which teams must sign, that an agent cannot answer and that an operation nobody decides before its approval deadline (24 hours unless the Stage's deadlines.approval says otherwise) concludes Expired. A Rejected plan asks nobody anything; its failing verdict says what to do first. A promote held for a person on a frozen Stage also lists the StageFrozen conflict, and next says that even once approved it waits until a person unfreezes the Stage. propose with the plan's intent digest refuses with PlanStale if anything moved since. The digest also binds the reason and the on-behalf-of person, so pass the same ones you planned with: when they explain the difference, PlanStale names them.

docs.title: Confirm a new publisher
docs.text: Only the promoter raises an Operation of type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/trust, named <stage>-trust-<10 hex> after the signer, when a Stage that watches the registry finds a CI signer no rule, pin or policy covers. Its spec.params.publisher holds the signer's issuer, subject and repository, and its plan holds for a person. Approve it like any held operation. It changes no pointer: a confirmed signer becomes a pin, and its versions still pass every gate. See confirm a new signer.

docs.title: Cancel and roll back
docs.text:
cancel works until the pointer moves; after that, propose --type rollback --undoes <operation>. A rollback runs no gates, so only a person or break-glass may roll back a rollback or an override: an agent proposes a promote of that version instead, which the gates judge. One check applies to a rollback a person or agent raises: when a consumer's range does not accept the version it returns to (checkout moved to ^3 and the rollback goes back to 2.x), that consumer's team approves it first. Nothing Pacto cannot see holds a rollback, and the promoter's own rollbacks never wait. An agent may cancel only an operation it proposed; a rollback or freeze the promoter raised, or anyone else's operation, is cancelled by a person or break-glass. Once an operation has moved the pointer nobody deletes it, not even break-glass: re-checks, rollbacks and history cite it. Only the promoter (after delivery.recorder.operationTTL, and never the one the Stage runs) and the namespace controller remove it. With the recorder off, history names any seq whose Operation is gone. Names ending in -rollback, -freeze or -stepdown, and <stage>-auto- or <stage>-witnessed- names, are the promoter's own: admission refuses them to everyone else, so nobody can take the name of a rollback before the promoter raises it.

pacto mcp --delivery gives agents the tools Which tools exist lists, with propose and cancel only when the apiserver says the caller is an agent.

docs.title: When another service must move first
docs.text:
When a promote breaks a consumer, the plan names a version of that consumer to ship first: one that accepts both the running and the new provider version, fits the other services there, is newer than what runs and was offered by its upstream Stage. It shows in plan, explain, status.plan.order and the dashboard's Update these first. While a change waits, the promoter plans again, so a consumer that moved stops being asked and one newly broken is asked. Pacto never promotes the other service itself.

Only consumers in the same environment count. A Pacto's delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/environment label places it; without one, it is where a Stage's Kustomization applies (targetNamespace), even if you deployed it there for another environment, so label it then. A Pacto that cannot be placed counts everywhere and, as a consumer, asks a person.

docs.title: Who may do what
docs.text:
Identity May May not Agent (its service account or pacto:agents) propose, read and cancel its own operations approve, freeze, unfreeze, write status, edit the pointer Person propose, read and cancel any operation, approve a question when they may update the workload (and, with team narrowing, are in a team asked), freeze, unfreeze write status (beyond clearing a Stage's upstreamSeen) Break-glass (pacto:break-glass) override and edit spec.ref.digest Promoter write status and raise its own operations sign or push Recorder write the record fields and finalizer, an Approval's status.record, spec.record and spec.signedAt; sign and push records anything else

Admission requires an Approval's spec.by and spec.groups to match the requesting user, and a spec.authTime to match its login time. The promoter does not count a login older than delivery.promoter.authFreshness when you set one, an approval from the operation's own actor or whoever it acts for, one from someone who may not update the Stage's workload, one from outside the teams asked when team narrowing is on, one given before the question was last asked, an accepted unknown where an approval is needed or an approval once the version shipped. The operation's status.message says why an Approval does not count. Once given, an Approval's spec cannot change; the promoter makes its operation its owner, so deleting the operation deletes its Approvals. A break-glass edit of the pointer is never undone: it is recorded as a witnessed override and the Stage freezes.

With the recorder on, an Approval counts only once its signed record exists and verifies. The recorder signs an Approval made in the cluster on behalf of its author; an approval a person signed keyless counts once the promoter verifies its record itself, dated by the signature's verified time.

docs.title: Delivery reference: appliers and several clusters
docs.text:
Pacto delivery never applies a version itself. It moves the version through the manager that already applies the service's workloads: a Flux Kustomization, a Flux HelmRelease or an Argo CD Application. This page covers how the promoter finds that manager, the HelmRelease and Argo CD set-ups, and a Stage that follows a Stage in another cluster.

Experimental

HelmRelease, Argo CD and several clusters are experimental, within an Alpha component: they may change more than the rest of delivery. Every pull request that changes delivery runs each of them live once; Flux Kustomizations run in every delivery scenario.

docs.title: Which manager applies a Stage
docs.text:
The promoter reads, and never writes, the workloads each Pacto in the Stage's namespace reports for the service, and names the manager of each one. The first match wins:

  1. An argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id annotation that names this object: Argo CD, with the Application from the id.
  2. helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/name and /namespace labels: a Flux HelmRelease.
  3. kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/name and /namespace labels: a Flux Kustomization.
  4. meta.helm.sh/release-name and /release-namespace annotations: a plain Helm release.
  5. An app.kubernetes.io/instance label written by an argocd field manager: Argo CD.
  6. A controller owner reference, kapp, Rancher Fleet, Spinnaker, Skaffold, Terraform or Pulumi: a manager Pacto does not support.
  7. A field manager, label or annotation the chart's fingerprints.managers names: external: <product>. It weighs like the first four marks, so it and another one read as ambiguous. See Fingerprints.

Marks of two different managers read as ambiguous. The Stage records the result in status.applier, with the evidence, asOf and completeness, and compares it with its spec.applyRef:

State Means A promote Adopted The Stage's applier manages every workload goes ahead Unmanaged No Pacto reports a workload yet, or the workload it reports does not exist yet goes ahead Conflict Another manager or another object owns a workload, a plain Helm release owns it, or the workloads disagree is refused; Ready is False with ApplierConflict Unknown A workload carries no mark of the Stage's applier, an unsupported, external or ambiguous manager owns it, Pacto could not read it, a Pacto is not reconciled yet or evaluated another workload than the Stage runs, or a Kustomization in another namespace does not apply from the Stage's OCIRepository is refused; Ready is False with ApplierUnknown

Nobody can accept a Conflict or an Unknown: Pacto never writes a pointer another manager may overwrite, and moving a workload is yours to do.

  • pacto delivery status, pacto_delivery_status and the dashboard print one line, such as applier: Argo CD (Application payments, tracking annotation) (as of 2026-11-15T09:59:00Z), with the reason when the Stage does not adopt it and a warning when the promoter stopped checking.
  • pacto delivery plan keeps what the promoter observed apart from what the Stage declares.
  • The Stage's spec.applyRef names the applier; a contract never names one.
  • An external: <product> workload is gate-only: the verdict reads external: <product> manages <workload> (<evidence>): Pacto runs the gates and writes no pointer.

docs.title: Apply through a Flux HelmRelease
docs.text:
A Stage can apply through a Flux HelmRelease whose spec.chartRef names an OCIRepository. The promoter writes the chart digest to that repository's spec.ref.digest, and a move counts as applied once the HelmRelease is Ready at that digest. A failed release of the digest fails the promote and starts the usual rollback.

apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: OCIRepository
metadata:
  name: payments-chart
  namespace: prod
  labels: {delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref: payments}
spec:
  url: oci://registry/charts/payments
  interval: 1m
---
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: prod
  labels: {delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref: payments}
spec:
  interval: 1m
  serviceAccountName: payments-deployer
  chartRef: {kind: OCIRepository, name: payments-chart}
---
apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {kind: HelmRelease, name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}
  • Both objects carry the apply-ref label set to the Stage's name, and the chart repository lives in the Stage's namespace. A chartRef to another namespace reads ApplierUnreadable, and the promoter never writes to it.
  • A HelmRelease that takes its chart from spec.chart, a HelmChart, reads ApplierNotChartRef: a HelmChart pins a version, never a digest.
  • values, valuesFrom or postRenderers set the Stage's Mediated condition False (ApplierOverrides), and no serviceAccountName sets it False (ApplierUnscoped). The message names the fields, never their values.
  • An admission policy keeps the chart source, values, service account and suspend of a labelled HelmRelease to break-glass.
  • The chart grants HelmRelease read when Flux access is on and the cluster serves helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2 HelmRelease.

docs.title: Apply through Argo CD
docs.text:
A Stage can point at an Argo CD Application instead of a Flux OCIRepository. The chart grants the promoter access by itself: under the default delivery.argocd.enabled: auto it does when the cluster serves Argo CD Applications at install or upgrade, so install Argo CD first or run helm upgrade after. Set true or false to decide regardless of the API.

This gives the promoter patch on Argo CD Applications and adds an admission policy. On a labelled Application only the promoter or break-glass may change spec.source.targetRevision.

The Application must:

  • live in the Stage's namespace. Argo CD calls this Applications in any namespace. Add the namespace to application.namespaces and to the project's sourceNamespaces. An Application of the same name in the Argo CD namespace is a different object, so its workloads read Conflict.
  • have one OCI source (spec.source.repoURL: oci://…), not spec.sources, and set no Kustomize images, patches or components, Helm parameters, values or value files, or plugin. Otherwise the Stage's Mediated condition is False: something besides the digest decides what runs.
  • sync on its own (syncPolicy.automated), because the promoter never runs a sync.
  • carry the delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref label, set to the Stage's name. Without it the Stage has Ready False with the reason ApplierUnlabelled.
  • start with targetRevision empty or at the digest the Stage runs. Any other value is a write the promoter did not make, so the first promote freezes the Stage.

The Stage is not Ready while the Application breaks one of these, and the reason names which: ApplierUnreadable (missing, the promoter may not read it, or its CRD is not installed, such as Argo CD in a Flux-only cluster), ApplierUnlabelled, ApplierMultiSource, ApplierNotOCI or ApplierNotAutomated. A Flux OCIRepository the Stage applies through needs the same label, so ApplierUnreadable and ApplierUnlabelled apply to it too.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments
  namespace: prod
  labels: {delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/apply-ref: payments}
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: oci://registry/deploy/payments
    path: .
  destination: {server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: prod}
  syncPolicy: {automated: {}}
---
apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {kind: Application, name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamStage: {name: payments, namespace: test}

docs.title: How a promote applies
docs.text:
The promoter sets spec.source.targetRevision to the new digest and asks Argo CD to refresh. The move counts as applied once the Application is Synced and Healthy at that digest; status.sync.revision alone is not proof, since it moves on refresh while the old version still runs. A sync of the digest that ends Failed or Error, or Degraded health after that sync, fails the promote and starts the usual rollback.

Argo CD does not check signatures. The candidate source checks them, and the promoter only ever writes a digest, so Argo CD fetches exactly the checked bytes. Admission keeps the rest of spec.source, spec.sources and the label to break-glass, so nobody else changes what those bytes become. The first Stage of a service admits a new version through spec.candidates.registry, where the promoter lists the service's version tags and verifies each signature against the installation's publisher rule (delivery.publishers), or through a Flux OCIRepository with spec.verify. A cluster that runs only Argo CD uses candidates.registry and needs no Flux. Stages after it can take versions from that Stage, in the same cluster or through its records. An Argo CD Stage places no consumers, so label the Pactos it runs with delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/environment.

docs.title: Follow a Stage in another cluster
docs.text:
A Stage in one cluster can take its versions from a Stage in another cluster, such as prod in one cluster following staging in another. The clusters do not talk to each other. The downstream promoter reads the upstream Stage's signed records from the registry.

You need:

  1. The recorder running in the upstream cluster (see Signed records).
  2. The upstream recorder's public key in the downstream promoter's trust config, bound to the upstream stream:
promoter:
  upstreamTrust: |
    keys:
      - name: staging-recorder
        publicKey: |
          -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
          ...
          -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
        streams: ["8d1e…/staging/*"]
  1. The downstream Stage naming the upstream stream and the repository that holds its records. The stream is the upstream Stage's status.stream.id.
apiVersion: delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/v1alpha1
kind: Stage
metadata: {name: payments, namespace: prod}
spec:
  service: {name: payments}
  environment: prod
  applyRef: {name: payments}
  candidates:
    upstreamRecords:
      repository: registry/delivery/streams
      stream: 8d1e…/staging/payments

docs.title: What the follower takes
docs.text: The promoter rebuilds from the records what the upstream verified: a promote that Succeeded, Verified and passed the published gate there is offered here, and a failure the follower has read is never taken: a version that failed there, or was rolled back after release. That includes a version that fails a check after release when the promoter cannot roll it back there (a person or agent chose it, or its rollback is used up): the promoter freezes that Stage with a freeze operation whose record names the failed version. Its own gates, approvals and checks still run. The digest must also exist in the Stage's own apply repository: use the same repository or a mirror that keeps digests. pacto delivery plan reads these records only with --trust and the upstream recorder's key.

docs.title: When the records cannot be trusted
docs.text:
The promoter offers nothing when it cannot check the history: without delivery.promoter.upstreamTrust the Stage is not Ready (UpstreamUntrusted). A gap, a fork or an unreadable registry make it not Ready (UpstreamUnreadable, saying why) until a read succeeds, and refuse a promote as NotPublished. A record no trusted key signed is skipped, since anyone with push access could attach one. A trusted record that stops verifying leaves a gap.

What the follower cannot see, it cannot refuse. It detects records removed from before status.upstreamSeen, but not a record hidden after it was written and before the follower first read it, nor one signed with a key upstreamTrust does not list, which is skipped like a forgery. A version that failed upstream through such a record can still be taken. So rotate the recorder's key in every follower first (list the new key beside the old one in upstreamTrust), then upstream. The Stage's Ready message counts the referrers on the upstream anchor it could not verify, so a skipped record does not go unsaid.

docs.title: When records were removed or rewritten
docs.text:
The Stage remembers the newest upstream record it read in status.upstreamSeen. A later read that ends before it, or holds another record at its seq however far the stream has grown since, is refused the same way: records were removed or rewritten, and one of them could be a failure. Every pacto.published verdict on such a Stage cites the record it relied on as upstreamHead and upstreamSeq, so an auditor can replay the stream up to it.

Sometimes the cut is intended: the upstream stream was recreated, or a StreamConflict repair removed its newest record. Nothing clears the mark on its own, so the follower stays not Ready until a person does. Once an auditor confirms the cut, clear it, with the right to patch stages/status. Admission lets that right do nothing else: only the promoter writes the rest of a Stage's or an Operation's status, so the write must remove upstreamSeen and change nothing more. The next read, within 30 seconds, sets it again:

kubectl patch stage <stage> -n <namespace> --subresource=status --type=merge \
  -p '{"status":{"upstreamSeen":null}}'

The promoter reads the upstream registry at most every 30 seconds for auto-promotion, and afresh when it plans a promote. It fetches and verifies each record once.

docs.title: Freezes
docs.text: A freeze is local, in one cluster or across two. Freezing the upstream Stage does not stop a follower from taking a version the upstream already verified: freeze the follower too. When the promoter freezes a Stage because a check failed after release, its record names the failed version, so followers never take that version.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A Stage sees the upstream's history only as far as its records reach the registry, so a failure not yet recorded is not seen.
  • A cut is noticed only against a record the Stage already read. A Stage that starts following a stream whose newest records were already removed cannot tell.

docs.title: Delivery reference: record keys
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

docs.title: Trust and key rotation
docs.text:
Readers and the recorder check every signature against a trust config. To rotate, sign with the new key and keep the old one listed:

delivery:
  recorder:
    trust: |
      keys:
        - name: old-recorder
          publicKey: |
            -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
            ...
            -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
          streams: ["*/prod/*"]

streams are patterns over stream ids (<cluster>/<namespace>/<stage>), so a dev key cannot sign prod history. A keyless entry names identity, issuer and the required trustedRoot. The recorder's own key is always trusted. List the old key before the recorder signs with a new one, also when a KMS alias moves. Otherwise the old records stop verifying and the Stage freezes. Pass the same file (or the recorder's PEM public key) to the CLI with --trust or PACTO_DELIVERY_TRUST, and to pacto mcp --delivery and pacto dashboard with --delivery-trust. A dashboard the operator deploys reads it from the ConfigMap in the operator namespace that dashboard.delivery.trust names, as in {configMap: delivery-trust, key: trust.yaml}. Without it, records are read unchecked and every answer says it is partial.

docs.title: Revoke a key
docs.text:
When a key leaks, rotate the recorder to a new key first. Then keep the old key listed with untilRecord, the id of the last record it signed on that stream, and untilSeq, that record's seq. The old key then verifies only that record and those it chains from, so history stays readable. Anything else it signs is skipped as untrusted, whether a record after untilSeq or a forgery backdated to a seq it already used. So a forgery neither extends nor forks the stream and the Stage does not freeze:

keys:
  - name: leaked
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...
      -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
    streams: ["<cluster>/prod/payments"]
    untilSeq: 41
    untilRecord: 3f9c...e1 # the record at seq 41

Seqs count per stream, so give a key that signed several streams one entry per stream. The last seq and record of each are in the Stage's status.stream.recordedSeq and status.stream.head, or in pacto delivery record verify. Set both fields or neither. A read of one version's records, not the whole stream, cannot walk the chain, so it shows what the old key signed as not verified. Followers need the same trust config: one that does not trust the new key sees the stream end at the last record it can verify.

Removing the key instead makes its records unverifiable: the recorder stops on the missing head and every follower sees a hole.

docs.title: Delivery reference: signed records and history
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

The recorder writes a signed record of every operation that ends, refusals included, into your registry next to the versions it touched. Off by default. Only the recorder can sign and push records. With it on, history, blame and undo read the records in place of the Operations left in the cluster.

docs.title: What a record is
docs.text:
An in-toto statement of predicate type delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/operation/v1: what was asked, by whom and for whom, the Stage policy, every check result with its proof, every approval and the outcome. It holds references, never secrets. It is a sigstore bundle attached as an OCI referrer to the version moved to, the one moved from, the new contract and the Stage's stream anchor, or a write-once tag. guarded: true says the admission policies checked who asked and who approved. The promoter admits an operation only while its admission policies guard the cluster, so every record it writes carries it. A record from an earlier promoter that ran without them lacks it, and its names are only what their writers claimed.

An eval verdict carries two signatures:

  • the eval runner's, on its own answer, kept in citation.runnerBundle (eval providers), with the runner named in citation.runner
  • the recorder's, on the whole record around it

docs.title: Streams, stand-ins and gaps
docs.text:
Each Stage has one stream: records are numbered (seq) and each names the one before (parent). An unrecordable record stands in for an operation that failed a check before signing (a value that looks like a secret, an approval no longer bound); status.record.refused says why. It keeps none of what the operation did, so record verify reports it as a problem, and a Stage in another cluster that follows the stream offers nothing from then on: the stand-in could be the failure that marks a version failed. The follower's Ready message names the stand-in's record id. A person checks what the operation did upstream, then acknowledges that one stand-in on the follower:

pacto delivery propose -n prod --stage payments --type acknowledge \
  --record sha256:... --reason "checked upstream: the rollback failed nothing"

The acknowledge takes effect at once and is recorded like any other operation, with who asked, the record id and the reason. The follower then skips that stand-in and offers versions again; any other stand-in still stops it. Only break-glass or a person who may update the follower's workload (and, with team narrowing, of the service's team) may acknowledge, with a reason. When nothing runs on the follower yet, or what runs names no team or cannot be read, only break-glass may acknowledge, whatever requireOwnerTeam says. Break-glass can still move the follower with an override instead. A gap record marks a number no operation holds. A record can be late, never skipped: an Operation keeps its delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/record finalizer until the registry lists its record.

docs.title: Approval and intent records
docs.text: • Each stream also holds an intent record for every admitted Operation and an approval record for every decision, outside the operation chain. See signed approvals.

docs.title: Identity pins
docs.text:
• When a person confirms a new publisher (confirm a new signer), the recorder signs a delivery.pacto.trianalab.io/identity-pin/v1 statement before the trust operation's own record: the service, the signer's issuer, exact subject and repository, who confirmed it, the approval record of that decision, the operation, the namespace of the Stage it was confirmed on and the time.
  • It lives on the service's own stream pins/<domain or ->/<name> in the streams repository (the domain path-escaped, so ghcr.io/acme reads ghcr.io%2Facme), as a referrer or a write-once tag like every record, so anyone who reads the registry reads it.
  • A pin counts only for the Stages of the namespace it names, and only when the approval record it cites answers an operation in that namespace, so a confirmation in one namespace never decides for a Stage of the same service in another.
  • The promoter and clients use the newest pin of a namespace by signed time, so confirming a changed signer stops trusting the one it replaced. They use only a pin that verifies under the recorder's pin key and cites an approval record that verifies and names the same identity. Any other pin is listed as unreadable with why.
  • To let another cluster's recorder sign pins for these services, give its key in delivery.recorder.trust an explicit pins/ stream pattern, such as pins/*/* for every service. A pin stream has three segments, so pins/* matches none. A key with no streams signs no pin.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The recorder detects how your registry stores records, so any registry works:

delivery:
  recorder:
    enabled: true
    streamsRepository: registry.example/pacto/streams  # default: <registry>/pacto-streams
    registryCredentials:
      secretName: recorder-push       # a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret
    signing:
      ed25519:
        secretName: recorder-key      # holds key.pem, a PKCS#8 Ed25519 key
      allowOperatorReadableKey: true  # the operator can read this Secret too

The push Secret needs write access to the streams, deploy and contract repositories. Create a test key with openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out key.pem. The operator reads every Secret, so the chart refuses such a key without allowOperatorReadableKey and a recorder sharing the promoter's ServiceAccount.

In production, sign with a KMS key (delivery.recorder.signing.kms: awskms:///alias/pacto; ECDSA P-256, Ed25519 or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256; AWS, GCP, Azure and Vault) or keyless (delivery.recorder.signing.keyless: certificate identity and issuer, a Fulcio, a required timestamp authority and a trustedRoot). Workload identity goes in delivery.recorder.serviceAccount.annotations. The recorder checks a probe record at startup, so a wrong key stops it first.

docs.title: Registries and their mode
docs.text:
Registry Referrers mode Listing Source of the row zot native _catalog Conformance test CNCF distribution (registry:2, registry:3) write-once-tags _catalog Conformance test GHCR write-once-tags tags anonymously, _catalog with credentials Probe of ghcr.io Harbor, ECR, ACR, Docker Hub native where the registry serves the Referrers API detected at run time Registry documentation GAR and any other registry detected at run time detected at run time None
  • Read the mode of a running Stage with kubectl get stage <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.stream.registryMode}'.
  • Before you install, pacto fleet providers --oci <ref> prints one Registry <host> row per registry it reads.

docs.title: Write-once tags
docs.text:
Without the Referrers API, each record is a tag in the streams repository:

  • The tag is stream-<hash of the stream>-<seq>-<first 12 hex of the record digest>. The recorder writes it once, never moves it, and the tag names the record by content. Approval and intent records carry approval or intent in place of the seq.
  • A person's signed approval is a tag of the same form in the approvals repository, under the Stage's anchor tag.
  • The recorder never tags an apply or contract repository. A record keeps its referrer on a version or contract only where that registry serves the Referrers API. When the recorder cannot probe that registry, the write fails with RegistryUnavailable and is retried.
  • Records are signed and verified the same way in both modes, and every reader reads both forms, so a stream keeps its history when its registry gains the Referrers API.
  • Registries offer no conditional tag create. Tag names are content-addressed, so two writers never race for one tag, and a taken tag that names another record is refused.
  • Anyone with push access can add, move or delete a tag, as they can attach a referrer. Every loss fails safe. A tag no trusted key signed is ignored and a deleted record breaks the chain from status.stream.head, which readers report. A person's signed approval record that was deleted does not count, so the person approves again. A record the recorder signed for an Approval made in the cluster counts once written; if it is deleted later, the operation record names a record id nobody can read. A reader resolves each tag once, so a moved tag is reported as unreadable the next time a new reader (a CLI call or a restarted process) resolves it.
  • Tag-immutability rules (Harbor, ECR, ACR and GAR) can enforce write-once on the streams repository.
  • pacto delivery plan reads only this Stage's records for what a version did elsewhere, so that answer stays partial.
  • A Stage recorded native never moves to tags on its own. If its registry stops serving the Referrers API, RecordStoreReady turns False with reason RegistryUnavailable and the message the registry served the Referrers API for this stream and no longer does. The records admission policy refuses changing a recorded native mode for every requester, the recorder included.

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
Each Stage gets a RecordStoreReady condition:

Reason Meaning ReferrersSupported Records are being written as native referrers WriteOnceTags Records are being written as write-once tags: the registry serves no Referrers API RegistryUnavailable The registry did not answer; it tries again SignerUnavailable The signer (KMS key, keyless token, Fulcio or timestamp authority) failed; it tries again StreamConflict Two trusted records with one number, a broken chain or a missing head (the one the Stage names). The recorder stops and the Stage freezes

A record signed by no key trusted for its stream is not part of its history: the recorder and followers skip it, and the condition names the first one. Anyone who can push can attach a referrer, so an untrusted one never freezes a Stage.

Pacto never resolves a StreamConflict for you. Find the bad record with pacto delivery record verify, delete its referrer manifest (or its tag) from the streams repository, wait for RecordStoreReady to turn True, then unfreeze. After an etcd restore the recorder continues from the newest record.

docs.title: Require records
docs.text:
By default automation keeps moving a Stage while the recorder cannot write, and records catch up later. To stop that, set records.required:

spec:
  records:
    required: true

Then every promote or rollback an agent or the promoter raises waits for a person's approval while RecordStoreReady is not True, or while more than five of the Stage's operations wait for a record. People, break-glass and freezes are not held. With delivery.recorder.monitoring.enabled, the chart scrapes the recorder and ships a PrometheusRule. PactoDeliveryRecordsPending fires when a stream has waited 15 minutes for a record, and PactoDeliveryRecorderDown when no recorder answers a scrape.

docs.title: Trust, key rotation and revocation
docs.text: Readers and the recorder check every signature against a trust config. How to write it, rotate the recorder's key and revoke a leaked one is in Delivery reference: record keys.

docs.title: History, blame and undo
docs.text:
pacto delivery history -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub
pacto delivery history --all --trust recorder.pub
pacto delivery history --all --correlation-id inc-4211 --since 24h
pacto delivery blame -n prod --stage payments
pacto delivery undo -n prod <operation>

Every answer says when it was read (asOf), its source (records, or status when only the cluster's Operations could be read) and its completeness: complete only when every record verifies and the chain is whole. problems lists what the records show is wrong, and unreadable what could not be read. On a partial answer a missing change may still have happened. --all walks every Stage you can list, up to 500 in two minutes.

--cause keeps the changes whose cause (reason, operation or cited verdict) names a text, ignoring case, and --correlation-id those with exactly that id; both narrow the timeline too. Each line shows when it was applied, its cause and its correlation id. A line with record - is read from the Operation's status, so those three are not signed, and the output says so. pacto delivery record get reads one record by its id; see status, progress and lifecycle.

A service's changes and history explains --at and the IMPACT and REVISION (DERIVED) columns.

blame names the change that moved the Stage to what it runs: who asked, who approved, what each check said. No change on a partial history means unknown, never nobody. undo proposes nothing; it returns the plan and the command that would undo an operation. pacto delivery plan also lists what the new version's records say happened on other Stages, so a version that failed in test shows when you plan it for prod.

docs.title: Correlation ids and the person an agent acts for
docs.text:
Records sign correlationID and onBehalfOf as the Operation's intent said them:

  • A plan or a proposal takes a correlation id from --correlation-id, correlation_id or the dashboard's "Ticket or incident id" field. The automatic rollback, freeze and step-down the promoter raises after a change inherit its id.
  • The admission policy accepts a spec.correlationID of at most 128 printable ASCII characters, so every reader prints it as written.
  • onBehalfOf is asserted, never verified; an agent must set it when it proposes (agents).
  • The intent digest binds the cause a proposal cites, never the correlation id: a new id never makes a reviewed plan stale.

docs.title: Upgrade: cause in the intent digest
docs.text:
• Proposals that cite a cause (--cause-verdict, cause_verdict) need the CLI, the dashboard and the operator at the same release, in both directions. Across releases the client and the promoter compute different digests, and the promoter finishes the Operation Rejected with PlanStale. Planning again with the same client gives the same digest, so upgrade the side that is behind.
  • Proposals without a cause and Operations held before the upgrade are unaffected.

docs.title: Verify records
docs.text:
pacto delivery record verify -n prod --stage payments --trust recorder.pub

It checks every signature and the whole chain, exits non-zero if anything is wrong and prints a command that checks one record without Pacto, with oras and cosign. record verify --all checks every stream.

Eval runners:

  • A record with an eval runner's signed answer verifies only when the trust config also lists that runner's key with role: runner. A keyless runner takes identity, issuer and trustedRoot.
  • The output names who ran each exam.
  • An eval verdict that says Pass or Fail fails the check when it keeps no runner-signed answer, when the answer is for another operation or version, or when the signed counts and the Stage's minPassRate give another result.
  • providers on a runner key lists the gate providers whose verdicts a runner must sign, so you decide which verdicts are exams.
  • A runner key verifies only runner answers, and a recorder key only records.
  • To check a runner's signature with cosign, see Verify a record.
keys:
  - name: recorder
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...
  - name: evals-ci
    role: runner
    providers: [evals]
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...

  seq 4    operation     sha256:9c1f... promote-pay-agent-1-1-0
           evals: the exam was run and signed by evals-ci

Check one record without Pacto gives the oras and cosign commands for a recorder key file.

For a keyless recorder it uses these flags instead of --key recorder.pub, with the entry's trustedRoot saved as trusted_root.json:

--trusted-root trusted_root.json --certificate-identity <identity> \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer <issuer> --use-signed-timestamps \
  --insecure-ignore-sct

--insecure-ignore-sct appears only when the trusted root lists no certificate transparency log, as in many private Sigstores: then a certificate carries no SCT and cosign needs the flag. The TSA timestamp is still checked.

docs.title: Target snapshot
docs.text:
• Where: with the chart's top-level registry value set, the operator publishes the cluster's signed target snapshot to <registry>/pacto-targets:cluster-<uid> at start and every 5 minutes, whether or not delivery runs. <uid> is the kube-system namespace UID. With no registry it publishes none. The recorder publishes no snapshot.
  • What: every target source the installation accepted, each with its own asOf and completeness: the cluster's Pacto resources (their status), workloads no Pacto targets (as inferred services, without env values, probes or pod data) and, with evidence.enabled, the targets the Evidence Server accepted from any producer, pacto agent included. A section the operator reads only in part is published as partial with the others.
  • Signature: the installation key signs it, and it names the operator ServiceAccount as its publisher. The operator creates that key once, in the Secret <fullname>-installation-key, so the snapshot key stays apart from the recorder's delivery key. It is a plain manifest with no subject, so it needs no Referrers API on any registry. The tag moves on each publish; readers treat an asOf older than 15 minutes as stale, so a tag moved back to an older snapshot reads stale.
  • RBAC: the operator's existing reads of pactos and workloads cover it. With controller.watchNamespaces, it reads only those namespaces and publishes the snapshot as partial.
  • Push: the operator's workload identity or the registryPullSecret Secret needs push to <registry>/pacto-targets. A snapshot over 8 MiB is logged and not pushed, so readers see the previous one turn stale.
  • Read audience: pull on pacto-targets reads every namespace's Pacto status and workload shape regardless of Kubernetes RBAC and, with evidence.enabled, every target, provisioning and usage record (cost included) the Evidence Server accepted, usually for every CI job of the organization. Give that repository its own read ACL.
  • Retention: each publish writes a new manifest and Pacto deletes none. Expire untagged manifests with the registry's rule: GHCR untagged version cleanup, an ECR lifecycle policy on untagged images, or Harbor or zot retention.
  • Readers: CI verifies a snapshot only under a trust entry scoped to the cluster's UID. A bare PEM or an entry with no streams trusts every cluster, which another cluster's operator could sign for, so it reads the snapshot as unscoped and partial. Add one entry per cluster, with the public key in public.b64 of the <fullname>-installation-key Secret (the helm upgrade notes print the entry). Where consumers come from shows the CI side.
keys:
  - name: installation-6f1e2a90
    streams: ["6f1e2a90-5b7d-4c1e-8a3f-2d6b0e9c7a41/pacto-targets/snapshot"]
    publicKey: |
      -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
      ...
      -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

docs.title: Retention and events
docs.text:
A recorded Operation is deleted after delivery.recorder.operationTTL (a week), except the one a Stage runs. Nothing in Pacto deletes a record, but registry retention rules can, leaving history partial: keep the streams repository and the referrers out of them. With delivery.recorder.cdeventsSink set, the recorder posts a CDEvent for every record, best effort. It also posts one when a Stage is created or deleted:

Event Sent when time environment.created the promoter first gives the Stage its stream id the Stage's creationTimestamp environment.deleted the Stage is deleted after it got its stream id its deletionTimestamp; absent when the deleted Stage has none, with customData.observedAt holding when the recorder saw the delete (CDEvents requires context.timestamp, so it holds that time too)

About these two events:

  • The CloudEvent id is <stage uid>/created or <stage uid>/deleted, so a sink can deduplicate.
  • The subject id is the Stage's stream id, unique per Stage, and its content.name is the environment (the CDEvents environment content holds only name and uri, so service and domain go in customData).
  • customData carries service, domain, stage, stageUID, createdAt and, on a delete with no deletionTimestamp, observedAt.
  • A recorder restart sends neither again. A Stage whose status was reset sends environment.created again with its original createdAt.
  • Each event names one Stage; other Stages for the same environment are unaffected.
  • Every event's data follows the CDEvents v0.5.1 schemas. Any event whose occurrence time is unknown has no CloudEvent time, and its context.timestamp and customData.observedAt hold when the recorder saw it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The recorder notices a tampered record only when it next records on that Stage; record verify checks any time.
  • Deleting a Stage while a change runs leaves that change unrecorded. Wait for its changes to conclude first.
  • A follower in another cluster notices records removed from a stream's tail only against the newest record it already read (details).
  • No record goes to a transparency log such as Rekor. A keyless record's signed time comes from the timestamp authority the recorder must name, and the certificate is checked at that time.

docs.title: Delivery reference: run records
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

The promoter can publish a run record of every operation it concludes: its type, outcome, gate results, how long it was held, the class of who asked, the Stage and the digests, never a name. Records are unsigned statistics for pacto stats. Turn delivery on first (Install). Recording needs neither the recorder nor signing, and it works on GHCR.

Publishing is best effort and never changes an outcome. A record that could not be published is counted in pacto_delivery_stats_dropped_total (metrics). A promoter that stops between concluding an operation and queuing its record loses that record; one that stops with records queued logs run records not published at shutdown.

The repository must be private: pull access to it equals read access to the delivery history of every Stage that records to it, so grant pull only to the identities that run pacto stats or the dashboard. On a registry without the Referrers API, such as GHCR, run records share one referrers tag, and concurrent writers can lose records uncounted; signed records use write-once tags there. The service on a record is what the Stage declares in spec.service and nothing verifies it, so statistics key delivery rates by Stage.

helm upgrade pacto-operator oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set delivery.stats.repository=ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats

The promoter's own registry credentials are usually read-only. Give it push access to the stats repository with a separate Secret:

kubectl -n pacto-delivery create secret docker-registry pacto-stats-push \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token>
helm upgrade pacto-operator oci://ghcr.io/trianalab/pacto/charts/pacto-operator \
  --namespace pacto-operator-system --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set delivery.stats.registryCredentials.secretName=pacto-stats-push

After the next concluded operation, list a service's records:

oras discover ghcr.io/acme/pacto-stats:pacto-stats-$(printf payments | shasum -a 256 | cut -d' ' -f1)

The run record reference lists every field of an operation record.

docs.title: Delivery reference: security model
docs.text:
Alpha

Delivery is new: its settings and commands may still change.

Every change Pacto delivery makes goes through an Operation. A person, a CI job and an AI agent over MCP each create one, and the promoter plans and checks it. The operator chart's admission policies check who writes each Operation and Approval and who moves a Stage's pointer. This page lists what those policies close and what your platform closes itself.

docs.title: How Pacto tells who is acting
docs.text:
Admission and the promoter read the identity the Kubernetes API server authenticated. They sort it into four classes, and the first row that matches wins:

Class Who Promoter The promoter's own ServiceAccount Break-glass Members of delivery.identities.breakGlassGroups Agent Any other ServiceAccount, any other system: user, an unauthenticated request, members of agentGroups and, when you set the deprecated humanGroups, anyone in none of them Person Every other signed-in identity

A CI job that runs under a ServiceAccount counts as an agent. An agent that holds a person's credentials acts as that person. Approvals and agents sets the groups.

docs.title: What each admission policy checks
docs.text:
The chart installs these ValidatingAdmissionPolicies whenever delivery is on. Each one fails closed.

Policy What it checks operation An Operation's actor is the user who creates it. Only the promoter raises a witnessed operation (an override it records for a digest it did not write; see Plan, propose and approve). Only break-glass raises an override, apart from the promoter's witnessed override. Agents may not freeze, unfreeze, acknowledge or lower a Stage to observe. An agent's Operation names the person it acts for in spec.onBehalfOf, never itself, a service account, a system user or the promoter (agents). A spec.correlationID is at most 128 printable ASCII characters. cancel An agent cancels only an Operation it proposed. Once the pointer has moved, nobody cancels the Operation, and only the promoter or the namespace controller deletes it after it concludes. approval An Approval's author is the user who creates it. Agents and ServiceAccounts may not approve. pointer On a labelled Flux OCIRepository, only the promoter or break-glass changes spec.ref.digest. Only break-glass changes its URL, layer selector or ignore rules, or removes the label. pointer-argocd The same rules for spec.source.targetRevision on a labelled Argo CD Application. Only break-glass changes its source, destination or project. Installed when delivery.argocd.enabled is true, or auto on a cluster that serves Applications. applier On a labelled Flux Kustomization, only break-glass changes what it applies or removes the label. applier-helmrelease On a labelled Flux HelmRelease, only break-glass changes its chart, chart source, values, post-renderers, target, service account or suspend, or removes the label. Installed when the promoter applies through HelmReleases (delivery.flux.enabled is true, or auto on a cluster that serves HelmReleases). status Only the promoter writes the status of a Stage or an Operation, apart from the recorder's record fields and system:masters. A person may clear a Stage's status.upstreamSeen. records Only the recorder writes record fields, and it writes nothing else. Installed with the recorder. promoter-writes The promoter writes only to labelled pointers, and only their digest. promoter-writes-argocd does the same for the target revision of an Application, installed with pointer-argocd.

Only break-glass, system:masters, the GitOps controllers in delivery.admissionPolicies.gitopsUsers, the namespace controller and the garbage collector create or delete a labelled pointer, Kustomization or HelmRelease.

docs.title: When a policy is missing
docs.text: The promoter reads its policies before it acts. If one is missing, fails open, has a binding that does not deny or binds another policy, or is narrowed by matchResources or paramRef, the promoter holds every operation and counts no approval. Cluster-admin and system:masters can delete the policies. The promoter then holds every operation until they are back. A promoter started without --admission-policies admits nothing, and every Stage shows Unguarded.

docs.title: The checks each operation type runs
docs.text:
Every Operation of the same type runs the same checks, whoever raised it. Who must approve it can depend on who raised it. The types run different checks:

  • A promote runs the published, diff, impact and suite checks before it applies, and the contract check after.
  • Before it applies a rollback, the promoter runs only the impact check, which holds it for the consumers' owners when a consumer does not accept the older version. The impact check skips the promoter's own rollbacks.
  • A break-glass override runs no checks and freezes the Stage until a person unfreezes it.

Plan, propose and approve lists every type.

docs.title: Which publishers Pacto accepts
docs.text:
A first Stage that reads spec.candidates.registry lists the newest 20 version tags of its repository and verifies each digest's Sigstore signature itself, so it needs no Flux (Argo CD clusters).
